News.title: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy and 80-year-old man have died following a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash near Drymen in Stirling at about 16:45 on Friday.

The boy and man were pronounced dead and their next of kin have been made aware, police said.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) conduct their inquiries.

An AAIB spokesperson said: "A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation."

News.title: Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
News.content:
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.

These were not the best of circumstances.

Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

In just five days, she was out â the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.

The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered â in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.

"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."

He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".

In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.

News.title: Swinney insists 'stars are aligning' for Scottish independence
News.content:
The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff last month where they signed an agreement, which is not legally binding, that said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

Swinney will tell his party's supporters that "one by one, the stars are aligning in our favour".

He will say that if the SNP lost May's Scottish Parliament election, the case for independence "would have been set back decades".

While the SNP won the Holyrood ballot, the party failed to win the overall majority Swinney had set as a target for trying to force a second referendum in the face of Westminster opposition.

Despite that, Swinney will declare that "there is no turning back".

He is expected to say: "The SNP is making the weather.

"And make no mistake â the wind is now firmly in the sails of Scotland's independence movement."

The first minister will go on to claim that the unionist parties at Westminster are "weaker than they have ever been".

News.title: Harry Styles debuts new track in memory of Liam Payne
News.content:
Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne.

The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, called What Is Enough, during his sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden, on the second anniversary of Payne's death.

Styles is currently performing at the New York venue as part of a residency on his record-breaking Together, Together tour.

Addressing the packed crowd on Friday night, the singer paid tribute to Payne as a friend and someone he "wouldn't have been able to do this without".

As a spotlight shone over him, Styles made a moving speech, in which he honoured Liam Payne, who died two years ago after falling from from a hotel balcony in Argentina.

"I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York, and this building means a lot to me," said the artist.

"There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without," he continued.

"And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends."

This was met with cheers from the audience, who were hearing What Is Enough for the first time.

Wearing a royal blue jumper with a red collar, the musician then urged fans to keep an eye out for and support each other.

"I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven't.

"But really, it's just about looking after each other."

He added that there were "so many more people who have touched my life in such special ways", thanking those who helped him get to where he is.

"I'm gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that's all right."

As he paused, passionate cheers and clapping could be heard from his fans.

The singer then began to play his guitar and perform What is Enough, which featured emotional and reflective lyrics.

As he sang out to the crowd, his band played a melodic accompaniment.

Sharing their reaction to Friday night's performance on Instagram,, external Harry Styles' fans described What is Enough as "beautiful".

Styles launched his solo career in 2017 after becoming a global star in One Direction.

His first album and single were both UK number ones, while his record Harry's House won a Grammy and a Brit Award after its release in 2022.

News.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
News.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

News.title: Vapes were meant to help people quit cigarettes. Now a million non-smokers are vaping
News.content:
When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data â and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

News.title: Not sure what to wear for Halloween? These outfits are set to be the most popular this year
News.content:
If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026.

"People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now.

And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices.

So, here are some spooky ideas to try.

News.title: Two-week half terms: The school holiday no one can agree on
News.content:
Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term.

Buckland has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed.

"What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days."

But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break.

There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days.

As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids.

News.title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of Â£33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

News.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
News.content:
A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says.

Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses.

The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent.

The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych.

Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences.

"This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days out.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
News.content:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

News.title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
News.content:
The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.

It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings.

Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.

It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.

The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save Â£500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.

A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore.

"DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

News.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

News.title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
News.content:
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.

Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.

On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.

"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."

Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.

The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".

"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.

However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."

He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".

Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.

Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".

Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing Â£1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.

In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.

The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.

Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.

Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.

In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

News.title: The woman who remembers everything: What it’s like to live with memories of your best days — and worst nightmares
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rebecca Sharrock remembers almost every day of her life.

The 36-year-old has a rare condition called Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory, or HSAM, which means she can remember vivid details from her past — even back to when she was a young child.

“I live with constant random flashbacks of a clutter of experiences — negative, positive, mundane — and they just flash through my head all the time from random ages, such as they can jump from three years old to 20 years old to seven years old to 16 years old, and it's very difficult for me to get to sleep at night,” Rebecca told The Independent from her home in Brisbane, Australia.

For Rebecca, who also has autism, anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder, it can be hard to let go of disturbing memories. She said HSAM and OCD “get along like a house on fire” and that the two conditions feed off each other.

“I find it hard to just let go of emotions, let go of thoughts, and with HSAM, it then extends to more and more memories that I can't let go of,” Rebecca said.

open image in gallery Rebecca Sharrock, a 36-year-old from Brisbane, Australia, has a rare condition called Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory, or HSAM, which means she can remember vivid details from her past — even back to when she was a young child ( Rebecca Sharrock )

open image in gallery Rebecca recalled the day Princess Diana died in 1997, when she was just seven years old. ‘Me and my sister were having a bath, and mum was washing our hair, and then my auntie just called out, and she said, “Oh, the Princess of Wales has died”’ ( Rebecca Sharrock )

While many people might retain a hazy memory of a day when a global event occurred, Rebecca can recount it with extraordinary precision.

When asked about August 31, 1997, the day when Princess Diana died, Rebecca remembered in detail how her family reacted to the tragic news.

“I was seven. I wasn't allowed to watch the news until I was 11 because mum said that it may be a bit scary for me, but I did catch a news story because my mum and my auntie were over, and me and my sister were having a bath, and mum was washing our hair, and then my auntie just called out, and she said, ‘Oh, the Princess of Wales has died,’” Rebecca said.

Dr. Craig Stark is professor of neurobiology and behavior and principal investigator of Stark Lab at the University of California, Irvine. His team study HSAM and diagnosed Rebecca with the condition in 2013 when she was 23, after two years of testing.

Stark says that he and his team have validated memories of people with HSAM by asking about both public and private events.

“For a number of these folks...we can verify against actual public kinds of things,” he told The Independent. “Some of them have had diaries, and it's like, ‘Oh yeah, they could go back and study their diary.’ Yep, they could, and then they show up with multiple boxes of diaries, and you’re like, ‘Oh.’”

open image in gallery For someone like Rebecca, who also has autism, anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder, disturbing memories can be harder to let go of. She said HSAM and OCD 'get along like a house on fire’ ( Rebecca Sharrock )

HSAM is a rare condition where people have an exceptional ability to remember autobiographical memories. While Stark says that it’s impossible to truly answer how many people have HSAM, researchers have identified about 100 people worldwide with the condition.

One famous example is the actress Marilu Henner, best known for the sitcomTaxi that ran from 1978 to 1983.

Henner offered a positive outlook on HSAM for students at the University of California, Davis, during a visit to one of psychology professor Charan Ranganath's classes last February.

“Developing a better autobiographical memory is the strongest defense against meaninglessness that we have. Because then our lives count for something,” she said, according to the college’s magazine.

open image in gallery One famous example is the actress Marilu Henner (pictured right) best known for the sitcom Taxi that ran from 1978 to 1983 ( Getty Images for Hallmark Media )

Stark said that he and his team found that people with HSAM score high on obsessive-compulsive tendencies. The professor explained the process that people he’s studied with HSAM go through to remember the days of their lives.

“They turn the day into basically the diary or the social media post version of the day,” Stark said. “And that's what they remember very, very well. They think about it multiple times — repetition over time, repeated practice. They have a structure and everything to it. They link it to other events.”

“We've known for thousands of years that these things improve your memory. And Marilu Henner is kind of right that the rest of us just don't do this. [People with HSAM] do, which then makes their memory for autobiographical events better,” Stark explained.

open image in gallery Dr. Craig Stark said that he and his team found that people with HSAM score high on obsessive-compulsive tendencies ( Craig Stark )

Rebecca said that she loves to organize her memories, which she attributes to her OCD.

“It's as if in my head, hypothetically, I've got a filing cabinet, and I like to organize them into months, years and days,” she said. “I had a fear as a child with my obsessive-compulsive disorder about forgetting things. So, when mum would say, ‘You need to just put your memories into a box,’ I'd say, ‘But I'm scared that I'll forget them, and then a part of my life will be missing.’”

Rebecca is a lover of classical music and foreign languages, using her passions as a distraction from unwanted memories that constantly pop into her head.

She said that when she struggles to go to sleep at night, she listens to classical music. “I anchor my mind into relaxation by just imagining that my thoughts and feelings are the notes of the music, and that helps me a lot,” she said.

Rebecca has taken medication to manage her OCD since she was 16 but stress can make some days harder than others.

open image in gallery 'I live with constant random flashbacks of a clutter of experiences — negative, positive, mundane — and they just flash through my head all the time from random ages, such as they can jump from three years old to 20 years old to seven years old to 16 years old, and it's very difficult for me to get to sleep at night,' Rebecca said ( Rebecca Sharrock )

Rebecca can’t drive or have a traditional career because of her conditions.

“If I was to just have to be in one place all day and do what I have to do, I'm constantly having to ground my mind due to flashbacks,” Rebecca said. “I've had to pick a job which is writing and doing creative work that relaxes my mind. So it still occupies me, but relaxes me. And learning languages distracts my mind from flashbacks because I have to focus on either learning the instrument or learning the language.”

She has been taking classical guitar lessons for three years and will start violin lessons next year. She’s also learned how to speak Spanish and French and is almost finished with her courses in Italian.

Rebecca released her first book, My Life is a Puzzle, in 2024, which gives a chronological account of her experiences from birth to age 30. She is working on her next book titled My Life in Sketches.

“For many years, I did wish that I was like most other people. I did wish that I didn't have OCD, didn't have these experiences of HSAM, didn't have my issues with autism, and that causes my anxiety primarily,” Rebecca said. “I have thought over the past five years that because I've never known life to be any different…it would be unsettling to just have to suddenly adapt to a different life.”

Rebecca hopes more research into HSAM can help better understand the brain. “We need to learn a lot more about what's in our world rather than what's outside of our world,” she said.

News.title: Sonay Kartal makes history by reaching biggest final of her career in Wuhan
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Great Britain’s Sonay Kartal made WTA history as she defeated Jelena Ostapenko to reach the biggest final of her career at the Wuhan Open in China.

Kartal began the tournament ranked No 170 in the world having missed six months of the season due to a back injury, but has made up for lost time superbly in what is just her second tour-level tournament since March.

The 24-year-old has become the lowest-ranked WTA 1000 finalist since the format was introduced in 2009, with victory over former French Open champion Ostapenko adding to impressive wins against world No 6 Elina Svitolina, former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic and former Wimbledon finalist Jasmine Paolini this week.

It took another gutsy display from Kartal, who trailed in both sets against the big-hitting Ostapenko but prevailed in a rollercoaster encounter to win two tiebreaks 7-6 (11-9), 7-6 (7-5), saving all six set points she faced across the two-hour battle.

Kartal, whose only career title came in the WTA 250 event in Monastir, Tunisia two years ago, will play either six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek or French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska in Sunday’s final, with the all-Polish semi-final taking place later on Saturday.

“Wow! That was probably one of the toughest of matches I've played,” Kartal said after converting her second match point. “I knew exactly how she was gonna play. At times, she's unplayable, and sometimes you just have to ride that wave.

“Mentally, I think this is one of the best performances I've had in my career, so, I’m very, very proud of that one.”

open image in gallery Sonay Kartal defeated Jelena Ostapenko to reach the biggest final of her career in the Wuhan Open ( Getty )

The Brighton-born Kartal had triumphed against Ostapenko before and defeated the expressive Latvian in the first round of Wimbledon in 2025, where she reached the fourth round at her home grand slam.

And as Kartal admitted during her post-match interview, the pattern of her match against Ostapenko was entirely predictable: the match was dictated by Ostapenko’s racket and she finished with 50 winners to 41 unforced errors, compared to a ratio of 13-13 for Kartal.

Ostapenko raced out of the blocks with the opening break and twice served for the opening set, but Kartal broke back on both occasions and saved her first set point as she made it through to the first tiebreak. Kartal had to save two more set points before converting her third set-point opportunity to take the lead.

The second set followed the same rhythm and Ostapenko broke Kartal’s serve early before errors crept back into her game. Kartal recovered the break but was forced to save three more set points on serve to make it through to the second tiebreak, where she held her nerve to reach her second career final.

open image in gallery Kartal described her victory as a 'huge milestone' after returning from injury to enjoy the best run of her career ( Reuters )

After Kartal’s back injury forced her to miss the middle six months of the season, including Wimbledon and the grass-court campaign, the former world No 54 opted to use her protected ranking to enter the two WTA 1000 events at Beijing and Wuhan in China.

Kartal admitted she was “throwing herself into the deep end” but her gamble has paid off handsomely, first reaching the third round in Beijing before winning five matches in a row, all against top-50 opponents, to advance to the Wuhan final.

“I was dreaming of playing these matches when I was fully fit, so before the injury,” Kartal added. “So to be able to come back here in my third event, and to achieve this, regardless, is a huge milestone for me. I'm gonna recover and enjoy every second of it tomorrow.”

The series of WTA 1000 tournaments sit in the rung below the four grand slams and Kartal is just the second British player to reach a final at that level. Former world No 4 Johanna Konta won the Miami Masters in 2017, and also reached finals in Beijing and Rome.

Meanwhile, by reaching the final in Wuhan, Kartal will jump 120 places in the WTA rankings to No 50 in the world. It also means Kartal will replace Katie Boulter as the new British No 1.

News.title: France protests live: Police fire tear gas and 150 arrested as widespread demonstrations turn violent
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it.

More than 150 people have been arrested at protests across France against high prices and inequality.

French Ministry of the Interior says 140 separate actions involving almost 33,000 people had been recorded by early afternoon, and that 166 arrests have been made – including dozens in Paris before demonstrations began.

"The movement is marked by a very strong mobilisation of far-left elements, whose sole intent is to incite disorder," the ministry sais, adding that demonstrations have involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in areas like Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers, it adds.

It accused some protesters of attempts at looting, attacks on police, starting fires and targeting government institutions, as well as damaging a police station in Marseille. Security forces have responded "swiftly and decisively", the ministry said. Tear gas has been fired at protesters in multiple locations.

In an update on X, Paris police said: "We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who come to attack the law enforcement forces." They accused "hostile individuals" of targeting police, adding that officers are facing them "with courage and professionalism".

The protests began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.

A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Avenue des Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.

Hundreds of other protests were planned across France.

A protester holds a placard amid tear gas smoke as clashes erupt at Place de la Republique ( AFP/Getty )

Protesters in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron's previous term, while in Marseille, trash cans were set alight.

"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.

The police have drawn criticism for their response due to a grisly list of injuries among demonstrators, including one teenager who had his hand blown off after picking up a stun grenade.

Prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police had also been injured.

The internal police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases of alleged police violence.

France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday.

"If there were to be clashes, all types of intermediate weapons can be used," he told Telematin TV on Friday.

Mr Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.

A long struggle to reduce rising public debt has not impressed investors, who are ditching French bonds, driving borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.

Mr Lecornu said on Thursday that authorities feared unrest during the protests. The government accused the hard-left France Unbowed of inflaming the protests, an accusation it denies.

Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the fray appear to have worked, suggesting the protests could grow significantly.

The Yellow Vest movement started in 2018 as a protest against taxes on diesel before expanding into an outpouring of anger at high living costs and income inequality.

However, things have been largely quiet since Macron agreed to billions of euros in tax cuts.Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Crèche in western France, joined the Yellow Vests in 2018 and remains involved in the movement.

He said there were several nearby meeting points for protesters on Saturday, with unions also calling for participation.

News.title: England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes already hang by a thread after brutal Tonga defeat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes are hanging by a thread after a crushing 30-12 defeat by Tonga in their opening match of the competition in Perth.

Brian McDermott’s men were undone by the brilliance of Dolphins half-back Isaiya Katoa who masterminded his side’s stunning win and contributed a crucial 14 points with the boot.

It means England realistically now need Tonga to beat Samoa in a fortnight’s time to stand the slimmest chance of progressing to the semi-final stage.

England failed to capitalise on some serious first-half momentum and the Tongans exposed their weaknesses after the break to gain emphatic revenge for their trio of test defeats in the UK in 2023.

England’s flat pack were comprehensively out-muscled and full-back AJ Brimson – preferred to St Helens number one Jack Welsby – was turned inside out by Katoa, who will team up with England captain George Williams at his NRL club next season.

For McDermott it was a massive wake-up call and he must now rebuild his shattered side for upcoming group games against Papua New Guinea and France, both of which are already in danger of being rendered irrelevant in the complicated cross-group system.

England piled on the pressure for much of a high-octane first half but they failed to find a way through an heroic Tongan rearguard and it was the South Sea islanders who reached the interval 10-0 in front.

Kai Pearce Paul was denied an early opener by a superb saving tackle from Latu Fainu, and Brimson was hauled back by Lehi Hopoate, and Tonga suffered a major blow when playmaker Fainu was forced off injured.

But after soaking up half an hour of pressure, Tonga pounced when Katoa’s inch-perfect offload sent Stefano Utoikamanu galloping over for their opener.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Tonga would stretch their lead into double figures through two kicks from Katoa, but McDermott’s men looked to have forced their way right back into the contest when Hugo Savala sent Brimson over within six minutes of the restart.

Savala’s subsequent kick took England within four and they looked to have all the momentum until a needless penalty sent Tonga back up the other end of the field and they seized on a slice of fortune when Katoa’s kick ricocheted through and Haumole Olakau’atu touched down.

It got much worse for England as a clever kick through by former Huddersfield man Tui Lolohea sent Tolutau Koula over for his side’s third. Katoa’s sixth successful kick stretched Tonga’s lead to 18 as the game edged beyond the hour mark.

Dom Young gave England hope when he raced over on 63 minutes, but it was to prove a fleeting moment of hope as another Katoa kick sent Olakau’atu sent over for his second, and Tonga cruised through the final minutes to wrap up a richly deserved win.

England ease to opening Women’s World Cup win over Wales

Earlier, Winger Anna Davies and debutant Connie Boyd both scored hat-tricks as England eased to a 70-6 win over Wales in their Women’s World Cup opener in Perth.

Debutants Wales had their moment when Paige Travis bundled over to cancel out Amelia Brown’s opener for England and briefly haul her side level in the early stages.

But after that it was all one-way traffic as England proceeded to score 13 tries supplemented by nine successful kicks from Izzy Rowe – who crossed for two of her own.

The World Cup is set to get much tougher for England, whose next match is against hosts and defending champions Australia next Saturday.

News.title: Fishermen recover ‘iPhone and perfume’ haul from ship sunk in Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
Scores of cargo goods, iPhones and luxury perfumes reportedly among them, have been recovered by locals after a shipping container was sunk in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride was sunk on Wednesday (October 14) after being hit by a projectile according to maritime authorities, with Iranian state media reporting Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claims it had been sunk by a naval mine.

Footage circulating social media shortly after the incident shows skiffs congregating near floating shipping containers, with hundreds of pieces of small cargo scattered across the water.

In one video, a man is heard saying “we heard a container ship sank, so we’re going to collect iPhones and perfume,” report The Telegraph.

News.title: Ten people killed as fire rips through Bangladesh beach resort
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A fire destroyed a coastal resort in southeastern Bangladesh on Saturday morning, killing 10 people and injuring four others, officials confirmed.

The blaze broke out at the Tuptup Resto and Resort in Inani, situated within Cox’s Bazar district near the Bay of Bengal.

The area is a popular destination for local holidaymakers.

Syed Mohammad Morshed Hossain, deputy assistant director of Fire Service and Civil Defense in the district, said the flames quickly spread through the three-storey wooden structure.

Children were among those killed in the incident, though further details were not provided.

It currently remains unclear what caused the fatal fire.

News.title: SNP members back resolution supporting UK-wide ban on X
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A motion in support of a UK-wide ban of the social media platform X has been backed by the SNP – with party members also calling for the Scottish Government and Holyrood authorities to remove themselves from the site.

SNP members at the party’s annual conference in Aberdeen overwhelmingly passed a resolution stressing the need for “responsible use of social media”.

It insisted the SNP, elected representatives, councils, the Scottish Government and other public bodies, should “not make use of harmful platforms that harbour abusive content”.

Formerly known as Twitter, X was acquired by the billionaire Elon Musk in 2022, with the platform now owned by SpaceX’s artificial intelligence subsidiary SpaceXAI.

Moving the resolution, SNP member Erin Lux insisted: “There are so many reasons we need to remove ourselves and our services from this platform”.

The party has almost 320,000 followers on X and regularly posts on the platform, including several updates from the conference in recent days.

But Ms Lux claimed that X and its artificial intelligence chatbot Grok “continue to host and produce child sexual abuse material”, going on to state that X is a “hotbed of mis- and disinformation”.

Adding that research had showed using the platform “shifted views rightwards”, Ms Lux asked delegates: “Why on earth are we continuing to post there?”

She insisted: “It is indefensible we are lending our credibility as a party, and the credibility of our elected officials to a site that has become a hotbed of misinformation and abuse.

“Do we really want our party messaging appearing alongside nudified images of our fellow politicians?

“Do we think it is acceptable to force people to log into a site that shares child sexual abuse material to find out if the trains are back on?

“Is it really in our interests to keep driving traffic towards a right wing radicalisation machine?”

Adding that there was a “growing consensus” in favour of leaving the platform, she told fellow SNP members: “We need to show moral strength and the courage of our convictions and choose to use social media responsibly in a way that aligns with our values.”

Fellow SNP member David Birkett argued against a ban, saying he could “understand why people don’t like” the platform, but the party should remain active on it because of it has larger user numbers than rival social media sites.

He told the conference: “Bluesky has 10.4 million active monthly users, X has 551 million. Bluesky has three million daily active users, X has 251 million.

“Those numbers speak for themselves.”

Mr Birkett continued: “I also believe in treating party bodies, candidates and elected members like grown-ups, who can make their own assessment of which platforms they choose to join without some edict.”

He highlighted the role X can play in informing travellers about delays and disruptions to ferries, train services and on the roads.

Mr Birkett said: “Maybe one day Bluesky and others will have the reach that X does and we can rethink this. But until it does, we should keep the party, the Government, the Parliament and other public bodies on the platform.”

X has been contacted for comment

News.title: England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes in tatters after Tonga defeat
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of England’s opening Rugby League World Cup 2026 outing as they face Tonga at HBF Park in Perth.

England have come agonisingly close to lifting the trophy in recent tournaments, losing the final to Australia in 2017, before being edged out by one point (27-26) by Samoa in a thrilling semi-final on home soil in 2021.

Head coach Brian McDermott will take charge of his first tournament as England return to competitive action for the first time since last Autumn’s Ashes series.

Despite the excitement around the World Cup, McDermott remains grounded and is aware of the challenges ahead for his side.

“We’ve got to take Tonga on, we’ve got to meet fire with fire in that regard, but there’s a version of doing it where you don’t just stay doing that for 80 minutes,” he said.

“They are physically going to be a challenge for us, and we’ve got to remain clever and smart while dealing with their physicality.

“I think to go deep in the tournament we have to do something special. There needs to be some moments where we come through a level of adversity, levels of fatigue, and levels of turning them away from our try-line. It’s a big challenge.”

This has been some significant team news as Morgan Smithies was forced to withdraw from England squad due to injury, with Kallum Watkins drafted in as his replacement. However, the 35-year-old is not in the squad for this one. Morgan Knowles is another injured absentee so Luke Thompson starts instead.

Mikey Lewis won’t feature today either, having been left out of the squad, and Jack Welsby is on the bench. George Williams captains England, while Zach Eckersley, Hugo Savala and Max King are all poised for their international debuts.

England dominate the head-to-head record, winning all six of their previous encounters against Tonga, including the 2017 World Cup semi-final and the three-match series in 2023. But can they deliver with all eyes on their 2026 tournament opener in Perth?

Kick-off for this Pool B clash is at 10:05 BST, with team news following now.

News.title: Kiss blasts ‘unacceptable’ Wallabies performance in All Blacks thrashing
News.content:
New Zealand blew Australia off the field in an extraordinary first-half display in Sydney as they claimed a 13th successive win against the Wallabies and completed a 2-0 Bledisloe Cup clean sweep.

The annual series had already gone New Zealand’s way for a 24th successive year at Eden Park last weekend, but Australia did enough in a highly competitive first half in Auckland to suggest they could give the All Blacks a game on their home turf. And in a breathless opening six minutes in Sydney, it looked as if they might.

The ball-in-play time during that opening spell was incredible as both teams committed to fast, attacking rugby, offloading from everywhere. Like two heavyweights going toe-to-toe in the opening round of a boxing contest, throwing haymakers to see who would get knocked out first.

Ryan Lonergan produced an excellent turnover for the Wallabies to trigger an Australia counter, the irrepressible Peter Lakai responded with one for the visitors, as the ball travelled from one end of the pitch to the other in one long unbroken spell.

But after New Zealand wing Josh Moorby finally broke the deadlock, it was Australia who found themselves out on their feet, punch drunk.

News.title: ‘The boats don’t stop’: The deadly coastline that has become a trafficking superhighway
News.content:
The fishing village of Khor Angar does not look like a site on one of the world’s main maritime migrant smuggling routes.

Nestled between the desert and the Red Sea, the whitewashed buildings seem to slumber in the searing heat and give no indication of the life-and-death drama witnessed along this coastline.

Maps claim there is a road from the town of Obock 40 miles away, but the occasional cars and bikes must instead venture over baked sand and mudflats to get there. Camels watch as they pass.

But if you scan the remote beaches along this stretch of northern Djibouti’s coastline clues to the scale of its intercontinental human traffic emerge.

Half buried in the sand are abandoned shoes, clothes and even identity documents.

The dropped personal possessions are reminders of hurried embarkations in the surf, or of terrible panicked capsizings in a perilous strait known as the ‘Gate of Tears’.

On some beaches there are mass graves of those who have drowned, marked out by stones among the sand dunes.

News.title: Asia’s vaccine self-sufficiency drive gets $650m boost
News.content:
An “innovative” partnership to boost vaccine security across Southeast Asia will inject up to $650 million into regional manufacturing, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported shots.

The five-year initiative, announced at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok on Friday, will see major lenders, non-profits, and the private sector come together to invest in the region’s vaccine industry.

Currently Southeast Asia’s production base remains limited and exposed. The majority of shots are imported, and any capacity the region does have is highly concentrated – one analysis this year estimates 60 to 90 per cent sits with a single vaccine manufacturer.

Even before Covid-19 hit, this vulnerability was recognised. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), a regional bloc of 11 countries, endorsed a vaccine security and self-reliance initiative in 2019, driven by Thailand’s National Vaccine Institute (NVI).

These concerns have mounted since the pandemic, but up until now investment as well as political will has been lacking. The partnership announced on Friday, led by NVI, hopes to remedy this, and develop a model that can be copied worldwide.

​​“If we can do it here in Asia, then that really provides a model for the world,” said Aurélia Nguyen, deputy CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a a vaccine research non-profit. “We can build it out in Africa, in Latin America, and that really gives us the resilience that we want the next time we have a major epidemic.”

Cepi has committed up to $20 million of “catalytic funding” for the programme, which is backed by the World Bank as well as organisations like the Singapore-based AVPN investment network.

In all, the package of loans and grants will include at least $174m in public financing, and up to $460m in private capital mobilisation for regional vaccine manufacturing. Further details, including recipients, have not yet been announced.

But Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, told a panel in the Thai capital that “we believe this has the ability over time to mobilise up to $650m of finance”.

He added that the group would use public loans and grants alongside investments by its private-sector arm, the IFC, while its guarantee arm, MIGA, would help cover investors against risk.

“It’s really important because each element of the World Bank Group is involved in it,” Donohoe said. “We’re not just talking the talk, but walking the walk.”

Speaking to the Telegraph after the event, Nguyen added: “Innovative models and partnerships like this, where we’re each bringing a piece to de-risk scientific technology, [allow us] to leverage larger quantities of capital.

“But I think what’s also helpful in this model is, beyond the financing, [we] have a sort of coordinating umbrella through Asean,” she said. “So you can be smart and [avoid] duplicating investments, which brings commercial sustainability and resilience for health systems.”

Nakorn Premsri, the director of NVI, added that the investment model will help “build a more sustainable and resilient regional vaccine ecosystem, to meet both routine needs and the demands of health emergencies”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Bank tax would raise mortgage costs, warns UBS
News.content:
John Healey’s bank tax raid would drive up mortgage rates and worsen the cost of living crisis, the City has warned.

Analysts at UBS said banks would pass on the cost of higher taxes to customers, in the form of higher mortgage rates and lower savings rates.

It threatens to undermine Mr Healey’s and Andy Burnham’s vow to give households more “breathing room” in the Budget.

The average mortgage rate on offer in the UK has already risen from 4.9pc before the outbreak of war in Iran to 5.88pc today, according to Moneyfacts.

UBS analyst Jason Napier warned that a raid on banks would also “disincentivise” investment and “bring in less money than moves the needle” on public spending and debt.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan, warned earlier this year that his bank could pull investment from the UK if the Labour Government chooses to “become hostile to banks again”.

The UBS warning comes as the Chancellor is poised to launch a raid on banks, despite describing them as “the jewel in the British economic crown”.

Mr Healey is said to be considering raising the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 8pc. UBS said NatWest stands to be hardest hit and would face a £263m a year blow, based on an increase in the surcharge to 6pc.

Shares in banks fell on Friday, with Lloyds and NatWest both more than 2pc lower, making them the worst performers on the FTSE 100.

News.title: Are my smart home devices always watching me? How to stay safe (and private) in a connected house
News.content:
The past decade has seen a huge rise in the number of smart devices in the home, from video doorbells to robot vacuum cleaners.

Smart connectivity offers many useful upsides, from letting us keep an eye on package deliveries to streamlining household chores. However, concerns remain about whether these devices are safe from hackers and how they might impinge on our privacy.

As a technology journalist for almost 20 years, I have reviewed many smart appliances and have lots of connected devices in my own home, so I’m an experienced user. To find out more about their potential downsides, and how to keep yourself protected, I’ve also spoken to an expert from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, a board member at the Connected Standards Alliance (CSA) – which promotes openness and safety within smart-device networks – as well as other leading brands in the space.

What is a smart appliance?

A smart appliance connects to your home network, often via Wi-Fi, to allow for a wider range of interactions. That might be a washing machine that notifies you when it’s finished, or a fridge-freezer such as the Samsung Family Hub with a screen and voice controls.

But smart appliances don’t have to be huge: connected lightbulbs, baby monitors, smart plugs and more can all link up with your home network, in many cases integrating with voice assistants such as Amazon’s Alexa or Apple’s Siri.

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”

Sports.title: Inside the amazing rise of Kai Rooney, 16 as he makes Man Utd U21 debut but can Wayne’s son be as good as iconic dad?
Sports.content:
Next

KAI ROONEY made the next step on his career journey when he made his debut for Manchester United’s U21s on Friday night.

The 16-year-old jumped up multiple age groups for the fixture against Nottingham Forest‘s youth side in Premier League 2.



He started on the bench but was brought on in the second half of the 3-2 defeat, and posted an excited story to his Instagram account before the clash.

And the milestone came just days after debuting in the Uefa Youth League for the U19s against Atletico earlier in the week, with fans beginning to get excited about his sudden meteoric rise.



His progress has naturally drawn comparisons to his father, United and England icon Wayne Rooney.

And while the youngster still has a daunting task trying to emulate his predecessor, he is taking all the right steps towards being handed his breakthrough.



It has not been a straightforward journey for the teenager – who will turn 17 in two weeks.

He had stints with United and Manchester City, as well as a brief spell in Maryland, USA during his father’s time in the MLS.

But in 2020 he re-joined the Red Devils, who were just one of a number of teams believed to be interested in his services.

He excelled immediately playing as a forward, scoring 56 goals for the U12s in the 2021/22 season – a record for the age group – as well as producing 28 assists.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

He rose up the ranks to the U18s squad while he was still 15 in the 2024/25 season.

But a brutal injury left him on crutches and unable to play for a number of agonising months, with Rooney revealing the injury alongside the caption “life can’t get worse.”

But he rallied back to health last season and became a regular feature for the U18s side, and was even able to play at Old Trafford for the first time earlier this year.

He was finally able to wear his sponsored boots in his new age group, after signing a lucrative deal with Puma at the age of 12 but being banned from wearing their shoes at U16 level.



His game style evolved with the jump as well, with the youngster drifting to become more of a winger than the traditional striker role in which his father excelled.

He even revealed the surprising wide man that inspired his new style – former Arsenal star Gabriel Martinelli.

It would be almost impossible to emulate his father’s early career, with the legendary forward’s first Premier League goal coming at just 16, and his England debut following less than a year later.

But after making his U21s debut, his eldest is still enjoying a brilliant start to his career, and is on the right track to become a breakthrough star in the coming years.

Sports.title: ‘Most useless football technology ever’: Referee stuns fans by ditching yellow cards for iPhone-style device
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL fans have been left stunned after a referee ditched traditional yellow and red cards for a bizarre iPhone-style device.

The extraordinary experiment took place in Uruguay, where officials are trialling technology that could change how players are booked and sent off.



Referee Eduardo Varela used the electronic gadget during Nacional’s Copa AUF Uruguay last-16 clash against Rentistas on October 15.

And the historic moment came just 12 minutes into the encounter at the Gran Parque Central stadium in Montevideo.



Rentistas star Juan Pablo Plada became the first player to receive a digital yellow card following a challenge on Maxi Silvera.

Instead of reaching into his pocket for the familiar plastic card, Varela produced a smartphone-like device displaying a bright yellow screen.



The unusual sight quickly attracted attention, with footage of the incident circulating on social media.

One fan said immediately: “Most useless football technology ever.”

Another said: “Soon there will not be a referee on the pitch.”

While a third said: “This is technology and if he trips and falls he could be set on fire.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The technology has been developed through a collaboration between the Uruguayan Football Association and a private technology company.

It allows referees to issue yellow and red cards digitally while automatically recording disciplinary decisions.

And the device does far more than simply replace the traditional cards used by officials for decades.

It can also register goals, substitutions and penalties, sending match information directly to the competition’s management system.

Uruguayan refereeing official Marcelo De Leon explained that the long-term ambition is to make match data available instantly to football authorities and eventually media organisations.



Remarkably, the technology has also been designed to operate without a conventional WiFi connection.

That could make it particularly useful at smaller stadiums where reliable internet access is not always available.

But the revolutionary experiment has already encountered some embarrassing problems.

The 23-year-old suffered a stress fracture in her lower right leg and was forced to miss both Wimbledon and the US Open.

Raducanu has dropped to world No 107, her lowest position in two years, but Evans, who retired at this year's Wimbledon after controversially being denied a singles wildcard, has backed her to win the grass-court title on home soil.

"I genuinely think she will win Wimbledon one day," Evans told The Telegraph.

"Yeah, I don't know why. She's good, and I think - I'm saying this in as nice a way as possible - I think she thinks she's good.

"Not in an arrogant way, but when she plays big matches, she's like 'Whatever. This is just another match.' And yeah, I just think one day she'll get it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Both Tim Henman and Laura Robson believe Emma Raducanu reuniting with her former coach that helped her clinch the US Open, Andrew Richardson, is a good move

It has been a frustrating 12 months for Raducanu with more persistent physical issues. After a foot injury severely hampered her pre-season training, Raducanu then spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness after initially falling unwell in early February.

She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair's time on court together has been limited.

Raducanu was not among the players named in Great Britain's team for the Billie Jean King Cup Finals in late September and with question marks over whether she will compete again in 2026.

The former world No 10 could benefit from ending her season early to focus on recovery and secure a protected ranking before making her return next year.

"There's no doubt she needs to have a racket in her hand a bit more," said Evans. "I'm sure she's getting pushed side-to-side by endorsements, and there's a bit of tug of war on what she needs to do, what she doesn't.

"I admit I've not watched her practices very often, but from what I'm told she's a good trainer: she works for two, three hours in a row with hardly any break."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tim Henman feels Emma Raducanu should remain positive despite losing the Queen's final to Donna Vekic

A protected ranking for Raducanu?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at Emma Raducanu's incredible win at the 2021 US Open

Should Raducanu miss at least six months of competition due to injury, she can use a special ranking for a select number of events upon her return.

This would be her top-50 ranking from during the grass season - the last time she competed and received prize money for a tournament.

What is a Protected Ranking?

It is a provision in tennis that enables players who have been absent from the sport for an extended period to qualify more easily for tournaments upon their return.



The ATP and WTA Tours have different rules when it comes to protected rankings.



For ATP Tour or other men's tournaments, an eligible player could use a protected ranking calculated over the three months after they suffered an injury.



WTA Tour players see their protected rankings fixed as the same as it was at the time when the injury was first suffered.



A WTA player can use this protected ranking for eight tournaments in a year, or 12 if they miss more than a year.



Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, former player-turned-TV analyst Annabel Croft said:

"It wouldn't be a surprise if she made that decision [close down her season]. That wouldn't be such a bad decision to take because you can fully heal, rest up, get as much treatment as possible and then come out fully fit, raring to go at the start of next year.

"Maybe if there's a worry about the ranking drop with so many points to defend and potentially that ranking could plummet, although she might benefit from the protected ranking.

"All of these factors have to be considered, don't they? But at the end of the day, your health is your wealth, as they say, and that is the most important factor and she just needs to get herself fit.

"It's an unusual injury. I mean, I've had calf muscle injuries, which were not nice at all. And the minute you push off, you tweak it and it feels tight but the one thing that I've always thought about Raducanu, particularly when we saw her at Queen's Club on the grass where she played such beautiful tennis, is that she's very light on her feet. Movement has always been one of her strengths.

"She's such a great athlete. She moves around the ball. She's light on her feet and gets into great positions where she never looks off balance. But movement will be part of a major strength of what she brings out onto the court. That needs to be absolutely 100 per cent."
