Sports.title: South Africa look to re-establish Test credentials after Australia mauling
Sports.content:
South Africa will seek to show their heady ascent to the ‌top of the Test cricket pile was no accident as they bid to level the series against ​Australia in the second Test, starting on Sunday in Gqeberha.

The hosts suffered a 214-run defeat to Australia in the first Test that ended in Durban ​on Tuesday, a setback that left their status as world Test champions looking increasingly fragile.

South Africa secured a dramatic five-wicket victory over Australia to win the World Test Championship last year ​at Lord's in London, but their qualification for the final prompted debate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from day five of the first Test between South Africa and Australia

They played fewer Tests than the likes of England and India and faced what was widely regarded as an ​easier schedule in the qualifying period.

Their winning form leading up to the ⁠WTC final also masked some poor batting performances, ⁠which coach Shukri Conrad acknowledged finally caught up with them against Australia at Kingsmead, where they looked anything but world champions.

"We've been ‌heavily reliant on (captain) Temba (Bavuma) and (opener) Aiden Markram and then the lower order runs," he said after Australia exposed their batting fragility.

Several changes are expected for the second Test where Matthew Breetzke is ‌set to be given a renewed chance to open alongside Markram.

Ryan Rickelton is primed to take over as wicketkeeper from Kyle Verreynne but move down the order.

Tristan Stubbs, who batted at number five for the first Test, has been omitted, which could open the door for Marques Ackerman ⁠to make his Test debut.

South Africa will welcome ​back paceman Kagiso Rabada for his first outing since the Indian ​Premier League in May, placing considerable expectation on his shoulders despite his lengthy ​absence. That means they will drop one spinner.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain discuss why Test matches are finishing so quickly

Australia's selection is also keenly anticipated but ⁠with Cameron Green's return from injury likely delayed, they might resist the temptation to make any changes after such an emphatic win.

One possibility, however, is that Scott Boland is brought into the attack as ⁠Australia monitor the workloads of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood ​and Mitchell Starc after all three bowled at least 29 overs in the first ​Test.

Persistent rain and damp conditions are forecast for Gqeberha, particularly on the opening two days, which raises the prospect of delays or a shortened ‌match at St George's Park.

South Africa XI (possible): Aiden Markram, Matthew Breetzke, David Bedingham, Temba Bavuma (c), Marques Ackerman, Ryan Rickelton (wk), Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Kagiso Rabada, Gerald Coetzee.

Australia XI (possible): Travis Head, Nic Maddinson, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Matthew Renshaw, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitch Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood.

Hazlewood says reverse swing may be a factor

Image: Josh Hazlewood's 6-49 helped Australia wrap up a comprehensive win over South Africa in the first Test

Australia fast bowler Josh Hazlewood predicts reverse swing may be crucial to the outcome of the ‌three-Test series, where abrasive pitches are helping revive a fading art.

The art of reverse swing has faded in recent years with greener wickets and lusher outfields keeping the ​ball newer and less likely to rough up.

"The ball still looks new late in the innings if it gets that far," said Hazlewood about playing back home ​in Australia, but it is a different story on tour ⁠in South Africa.

"It's abrasive wickets. It's very ⁠hard underfoot," he explained.

"We probably got a hint of swing in the first innings and then as the game goes it ‌just deteriorates more and you get a bit more. So we knew it was crucial," he said of their success in Durban, where he returned carer-best figures of ‌6-49 in the last innings to secure Australia's triumph.

"If the wicket is hard, firm, deteriorating and not much seam movement, you're probably going to get that reverse swing," Hazlewood told a pitch-side press conference on Friday as Australia prepared for Sunday.

"You probably want ⁠the ball a bit harder and a little bit of ​reverse swing rather than a lot of reverse swing and ​the ball's soft. That's much easier to navigate as a batsman," he ​added.

Hazlewood, now 35, produced his performance in Durban after missing all of last ⁠season's Ashes series through injury.

"I just play every Test match that comes," he said of his longevity. "Could be your last one whenever. I don't think about it much.

"I think you ⁠know it was great fun last week playing ​with the same guys. Doing the work in the last innings and ​taking the 20 wickets for the game on what was a pretty flat wicket for the majority. I don't look too ‌far ahead these days."

Sports.title: England thumped by Tonga in World Cup opener
Sports.content:
Haumole Olakau’atu scores two second-half tries against England

England were handed a Rugby League World Cup reality check after a 30-12 thumping by Tonga in their tournament opener.

Brian McDermott's reign as England head coach got off to a dismal start as Isaiya Katoa inspired Tonga to a famous victory in Perth.

Half-back Katoa provided the precision behind Tonga's powerful forward pack. He proved the difference between the teams during a physical first half, creating a try for Stefano Utoikamanu and kicking three goals to give Tonga a 10-0 half-time lead.

England had their moments in attack despite a scoreless first half and AJ Brimson got them back into the contest with a well-worked score but two Tonga tries in three minutes, followed by another Katoa penalty, left them trailing 24-6 with 19 minutes remaining.

Dom Young's 63rd-minute try gave England hope but Haumole Olakau'atu's second try, again created by Katoa, condemned them to a chastening defeat.

England line up to face Tonga's Sipi Tau

England are back in Perth next Saturday where they will be expected to defeat France, but there will be plenty to ponder before then.

Their struggles under the high ball will be a concern for McDermott, with Zach Eckersley constantly targeted by Katoa during a blood-and-thunder first half.

England did enjoy plenty of possession and territory during the opening period, with George Williams and Hugo Savala both denied just shy of the tryline, but they were living on the edge at the other end and were carved open on 24 minutes.

Tonga winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak is tackled by Victor Radley, Harry Smith, Sam Walters and Brad O'Neill

Katoa, who lost half-back partner Latu Fainu to injury early on, received the ball in space and drew in two defenders before putting Utoikamanu through a gap to break the deadlock.

Katoa converted and slotted another kick two minutes later after Harry Smith obstructed the ever-dangerous Dallin Watene-Zelezniak.

Savala was again denied by a huge hit from Jojo Fifita while Herbie Farnworth was caught high as he charged for the line. England failed to capitalise from the penalty and things got worse for Farnworth when he was pinged for tripping Watene-Zelezniak as he again chased a Katoa kick on top of Eckersley.

Katoa's penalty made it 10-0 at the break.

Dom Young's try briefly gave England hope

England needed an early response after the restart and they got just that as another strong run from Young saw Williams and Savala put Brimson away, with Savala converting to cut arrears to four.

But they shipped a second try when Olakau'atu poked a toe at Katoa's blocked grubber, the ball ricocheting back into the path of the second rower, and Tolutau Koula bagged a third three minutes later after an inch-perfect grubber from ex-Huddersfield Giant Tui Lolohea.

Katoa converted from the touchline and added a penalty to make it 24-6, only for England to immediately hit back as Williams and Savala again combined to tee up Young.

However, any hopes of a comeback were quickly quashed as more magic from Katoa created a second try for Olakau'atu.

England are left requiring wins against France and Papua New Guinea in their remaining pool games, plus a favour or two elsewhere, if they are to reach the knockout stages.

What's next?

England must regroup ahead of facing France in Perth next Saturday, kick-off 7.35am (UK and Ireland time).

Sports.title: Red Roses' 41-game unbeaten run ended in dramatic fashion
Sports.content:
England's 41-game unbeaten run is over after they were stunned by a late rally from Canada, the Red Roses falling 24-21 in their WXV Global Series clash in Toronto.

Shoshanah Seumanutafa came off the bench to score the match-winning try in the 77th minute to hand England their first defeat since the 2022 World Cup final.

Following a draw in their previous clash last month in Exeter, Canada looked up for the challenge early as they opened the scoring through Savannah Bauder in the 15th minute.

Quickfire tries to Maddie Feaunati and Zoe Harrison just before half-time put England ahead 14-5 at the break.

The points kept flowing as both teams crossed just after play resumed, but DaLeaka Menin's 63rd-minute try kept the door open for Canada.

A raucous home crowd exploded for Seumanutafa's match-winner shortly after, with Canada able to hold on from there and quell England's historic run.

Speaking after the match, England's head coach John Mitchell said he was focused on taking what positives he could out of the loss.

He said: "We're not driven by outcome. We're disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance tonight. So we'll stick to our processes.

"I guess (the loss) frees us up and allows us all to find more.

"I know this group has got more in them but sometimes it requires the context that we've just received to dig deeper and find something more.

"Maybe everyone in the group can probably review their 'why's and re-establish those as well because I'm sure they're changing and evolving as they experience what we're going through."

The opener of a two-game Rugby Rematch Tour between the growing rivals drew an electric crowd to BMO Field as Canada returned to home soil for the first time since ​finishing runner-up to the Red Roses at last year's World Cup.

"I think it's a ⁠little bit more than just the score at ⁠the end because we won on so many levels today," Canada's Justine Pelletier said.

"Off the field, just the crowd, being home, and there's so much ‌going on around. And I think that win at the end on the pitch was just the cherry on (top).

"It was good to beat England, but I think for a few years now we knew ⁠that we could beat them. It was just a matter of time ​and a matter of putting every detail together."

"The bit we always remember is we're at the ​top, and when you're at the top, people want to bring you down as quick as ⁠they can," England captain Megan Jones said, adding that the team take "huge pride" in their unbeaten run.

Sports.title: Savaged by Simon Jordan – and thanks to the algorithm I want to be savaged again | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Yet again the mainstream wokealorium is preachifying from its pulpitrex. It’s egregious. It’s sanctiforial. It’s a wangitude of complete retardifaction.

This has not been an easy column to write. It has been difficult, gruelling in parts, but also warm, exhilarating and at times deeply erotic. Yes. I was SAVAGED by Simon Jordan. And I’ve never felt so alive.

You know who Simon Jordan is. Used to own Crystal Palace. Now a very good and listenable pundit on TalkSport, where he does the grown-up topics. Simon Jordan has strong opinions. This is his thing. His worldview says: the world is bad. The world is in need of correction. And he’s right about that, as he often is about things.

That’s what makes this all a bit surprising because I like Simon Jordan! I listen to his morning show with Jim White and it’s often really good. I respect the fact he has industry knowledge because he ran a football club. And yes that involved lots of dealings with Steve Bruce, Iain Dowie or similar, but it’s still basically the same thing.

I like the way he pops up in clips looking like an exquisitely powdered 17th-century Umbrian count, some gorgeous little angry blond glove-puppet I want to sit on my knee and pet and cosset and whisper in his ear about granditudinous hypocralism, in a way that’s just warm and fond and not, for me, in any way sexual, but which definitely is for him.

View image in fullscreen Simon Jordan in 2005 when in charge at Crystal Palace and busy dealing with the likes of Steve Bruce and Iain Dowie. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian

I like the way he talks. It reminds me of Jackie Chiles, the lawyer in Seinfeld, saying it’s outrageous, egregious, preposterous. Sometimes this can have a Mrs Malaprop edge. But that’s also fun and even then you get his point, which is usually good, even if you didn’t expect to agree, or can only agree secretly. When you’re right you’re right. When you’re veritudinously superfactual you’re veritudinously superfactual.

By now you’re probably wondering what happened. Well, I was definitely savaged. No one can take that away from me. And yes this was a week ago, but other stuff happened in between and I forgot about it for a while. I also haven’t fully listened to the savaging. It’s two minutes long and life is short.

In fact I only know about it because my friend and colleague Barry Glendenning is very reliable in this respect. If you’re ever cancelled, owned, or significantly beasted on the internet then Barry will let you know, as an act of love and kindness, and not, repeat not, because he enjoys it and is killing time in the pub on his phone. It’s like having a faithful and attentive online Lassie. What’s that? Slow down boy. Wait, you’re saying Michaela Strachan has called me a nonce? On LinkedIn? Good boy. Easy. There you go. Here’s a lovely bowl of vape oil and Guinness.

I have to admit I am also amplifying this, promoting myself as genuinely savage-worthy. In reality I was savaged in a minor, offhand way that I still don’t really get. I was at Croatia versus England in Rijeka. The game was meant to be played without fans as punishment for some Croatia-related disorder in Paris last year, which included accusations of people making Nazi salutes.

In the event the Croatian FA filled the ground with children, which is allowed under a loophole in the rules. It felt a bit weird in the moment. At the very least it didn’t seem to fit the spirit of the offence. Nazism, yes, bad. But also: a lovely day out for Year 8.

I still don’t really get why anyone would strongly disagree with this. It seems obvious enough. Yeah, everyone likes happy jolly children. Personally I believe the children are our future. I’ve always said that. But they’re not some kind of smart bomb that disintegrates the capacity for logic.

View image in fullscreen Hajduk Split fans disgraced themselves this week. Photograph: Ante Cizmic/AP

The counter-argument seems to be that this is joyless liberal Guardian stuff. It’s the woke mind-virus. It’s being too interested in not promoting nazism, when you should simply enjoy the laughter of little boys.

And yes Simon Jordan is right. It is annoying to be preached at. But we’re not talking libtard snowflake stuff here. We’re talking actual Nazis, people who just like and enjoy swastikas, who talk fondly about the Ustase, arguably the most vicious sect of the Third Reich war machine. I don’t know, man. The more I hear about the Nazis, the less I like the sound of them.

Plus we now have the sight of Hajduk Split fans this week walking behind an actual coffin and chanting “Auschwitz”. Does this seem like the message is being hammered home? At the very least we’re going to need more children. How many is this one going to take? Ten thousand? Maybe if we can get children to carry a coffin through Amsterdam then it’s fine and just a heartwarming event that shows lessons are being learned.

This is how it goes you see. You are supposed to LASH BACK in these situations. But it’s all a bit weird. Suddenly Simon Jordan is attacking me with children. He’s barging me out of the way in Starbucks with his mega-buggy, one hand clutched to his pearl-draped throat, saying, what about the children, the children, the children?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

You see? I’m being sucked in. Because this is what the internet will do to you. I wasn’t even the main savaging that day. I was a side-beef, an afterthought. By now the algorithm is already filling my feed with fresh SJ face-offs, the latest a “heated exchange” with Dale Vince about Robbie Savage, in itself a mouthwatering trio, perpetual savaging motion in action.

In the end this is the only real point of interest here. This stuff is utterly addictive. And with good reason: it’s designed to be. Vast amounts of expertise and resources have been poured into this irresistible machinery. David Squires did a brilliant cartoon this week about the rise of the celebrity football chat-cast, the industrial-scale, seed-funded waffle that must now justify its space by shouting above the noise, and which will always tend towards beef-culture and a narrative of opposition.

I’ve tried really hard to stay out of this. I don’t do radio or TV stuff, because, well, what’s the point, but more because nobody’s clean, nobody escapes, suddenly you’re having a charity boxing grudge-match with Stephen Warnock.

But it is worth logging for the record that we are at fever pitch. The level of rage around football right now is genuinely astonishing. The story of the Manchester City verdict is, in part, a regulatory ruling over a breach of financial rules. But really it’s the astonishing post-truth online response, the urge to assail and objectify and dehumanise over a tribunal’s interpretation of accountancy practices.

View image in fullscreen Emotions over a tribunal’s verdict on accountancy practices have reached fever pitch. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Just going to report on a game at the Etihad this week involved BRAVELY DEFYING assorted threats of violence in response to articles written in these pages. And yes, these are clearly the work of a 77-year-old hunchback in Jakarta, or a drunk and bored corporate lawyer taking a break from surfing porn on the family computer.

But it is all part of the design too. This is meant to happen. A new book called Our Minds Under Siege by Bruno Giussani, a former global curator of TED, describes the way algorithm life is actively changing human behaviour. This is not a secret. Marketing has wanted to do this since the early 20th century.

Walter Dill Scott’s Theory of Suggestion. The Drive Theory of Motivation. The deliberate creation of want and anxiety into the way we sell things. And now we have a new and commercially irresistible language. Dopamine craving. Variable social validation. The feedback loop.

The way even random scrolling is controlled and metered, designed to create a craving that’s always there inside your head, and controlled by tech platforms that openly define humans as eyeballs, want, need, hunger.

In the end, this is why Simon Jordan seems to care so violently about someone else’s opinions on the children-washing of Uefa sanctions. It’s why I’m just incredibly excited by this as an outcome, why I want more not less. Savage me again. Make me feel something. Let me exist inside the machine with you, egregious, preposterous, vibramoniously alive.

Sports.title: ‘It’s really not a drama’: Carrick sticks to the script after Martínez storm
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup, and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football, Jason Wilcox.

All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for the former United midfielder.

On the final day of last season, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as head coach.

By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls closed in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.

A game at Leeds in January proved to be Ruben Amorim’s last in charge at Manchester United after he greeted the 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job”. With an uncanny circularity Carrick heads to Elland Road on Sunday after Martínez made similar comments. Amorim’s team were sixth going into that game; Carrick’s start the weekend 13th.

On Friday, though, came a masterclass from Carrick in dialling down emotion as Martínez’s explosive comments about Wilcox – “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director” – were addressed and he repeatedly referred to the “really good feeling” at the club.

“It’s really not a drama for us as a group,” he said. “The boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad … so we’ve moved on pretty quickly.”

If this seems less than credible, and almost certainly a stance coached by United’s PR mandarins, what else would Carrick be expected to say? More obvious was how the zen-like performance required from the club’s leader was being delivered. Even when he broke from the script to interrupt an inquisitor this strengthened the sense of Carrick being in control – hardly easy given the heightened glare on United since Tuesday evening.

When the positive vibes trope was challenged by a questioner saying: “We’ll have to take you at face value”, Carrick’s interjection came with a smile. “I’m telling you the truth when I say that,” he said. “Do you not believe me, no? The players totally believe me. I’m telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while, actually, and that’s it, plain and simple, you know? We’re emotional, we’re passionate, we care a lot.”

When signing on to be the permanent United manager, Carrick had overseen only 21 games at elite level – in two caretaker spells at the club. United had 17 league games to play when he replaced Amorim, and Carrick has shown signs of faltering this season when having to compete on four fronts.

Elimination by Brighton at the earliest stage of the Carabao Cup was not a great calling card regarding an ability to juggle competitions, and there was a surprising reaction from him after the 2-0 opening-day loss at Hull. He bridled at the suggestion United had lacked “passion” during a first-half horror show. “Oh come,” Carrick said. “That’s ridiculous.”

View image in fullscreen Lisandro Martínez caused controversy for his post-match comments after Manchester United’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid. Photograph: Florencia Tan Jun/Uefa/Getty Images

A faulty United rearguard is hampering an attack that is functioning far better and has the most shots (125) and most touches in the opposition box (205) in the Premier League. Nine goals from six matches is not paltry but greater ruthlessness would transform a promising front six into a potent one. Carrick has to find the right blend from Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Baleba has sparkled in his first two appearances – against Spurs and Atlético – and might have provided the shield from the No 6 berth to ensure a less leaky defence had he not arrived injured.

This has to be the hope for Carrick. Playing Tielemans at No 10 at Atlético suggests the manager may doubt the 29-year-old’s legs, and questions have been raised about whether United are putting in enough of the hard yards. Their 671.4km distance covered in the league is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2km is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

The trip to an always febrile Elland Road that saves a particular welcome for their cross-Pennines rivals presents a stern challenge. Leeds are ninth and have lost once.

“It’s a great rivalry,” Carrick said, who was full of praise for his Leeds counterpart, Daniel Farke. “There’s big history between the clubs, the areas. That’s what makes these types of games special. You’ve got to embrace the history, what it means.

“I’m sure it will be a fantastic atmosphere on Sunday. It brings an intensity and it’ll be a little bit extra again, on Sunday against us … Of course, we have to be ready, and the boys will be.”

Carrick requires a positive result, though in denying this, he again sounded the right note. “I don’t need results, we all need results,” he said. “It’s not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me, bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this club. It’s not about me, so please …

“I don’t go into every day at work, in this situation, this game, thinking about me. It’s about what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to, and that’s what drives us. So whatever’s best for the club and for the team on Sunday is the most important thing.”

Sports.title: Wolves extend Burnley’s home woes to a full year as Vardy strikes in vain
Sports.content:
The Wolves substitute Tawanda Chirewa struck within seconds of coming off the bench as César Peixoto’s side came from behind to extend Burnley’s home misery at Turf Moor to 21 games without a win.

Chirewa had just replaced Sean Neave in the 72nd minute when Mateus Mané pounced on Igor Julio’s heavy touch and sent the 23-year-old Zimbabwe international through to strike an angled shot, which flew into the net despite Grégoire Coudert getting his hands to the effort.

It was a vital victory for the visitors, who had fallen behind to Jamie Vardy’s first Burnley goal before levelling through Fer López.

For Burnley it was a huge blow. Their last league win at home was when they beat Leeds in the Premier League on 18 October 2025, meaning their horror run will extend beyond a year. Sheffield Wednesday established an unwanted English Football League record last season by going 23 games without a win at Hillsborough.

Burnley’s head coach, Nicky Hayen, admitted he does not know what the future holds for him. “I will not give up,” he said. “I am not thinking about [his future] because I don’t want to lose energy. That’s a question for other people.

“We played with a lot of courage in the first half, scored one good goal, and could have scored more. But then we made a mistake before half-time and it gave the opponent energy.

“It was more equal in the second half, but Wolves didn’t create many chances until we made another mistake. Then you could feel the atmosphere change in the stands – and I understand why.”

Burnley’s next home game is against Portsmouth, with their bitter rivals Blackburn then scheduled to visit Turf Moor on 22 November. The Clarets were denied victory on home soil on Tuesday night when Ivan Mesik equalised for Charlton in the sixth minute of added time.

Vardy, who celebrates his 40th birthday in January, illustrated that his finishing instincts are as sharp as ever with a low 20th-minute strike that gave Wolves keeper José Sá no chance.

View image in fullscreen Jamie Vardy gives Burnley an early lead. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

However, the home side failed to turn their first-half superiority into more goals and were hit by a sucker punch when a mistake by Kyle Walker, the captain, led to López side-footing an equaliser before the break.

Wolves, weakened by an injury crisis that worsened this week when Raúl Jiménez and Adam Armstrong joined the list of absentees, travelled north having lost their previous two games. They improved after half-time and Coudert saved Fer’s free-kick and Rafiki Saïd’s snap shot, before Chirewa came on to score the winner.

“Sometimes substitutions don’t work and sometimes they do,” said Peixoto. “The important thing is that the players are ready for when they come on. They must have the right mentality to help the team – and Tawanda showed he has the right mentality. It is an important three points, but that’s all it is.”

Tommy Doyle spurned a golden chance to add gloss to the scoreline late on, but Wolves held on for three much-needed points before boos rang around Turf Moor at the final whistle.

Sports.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
Sports.content:
“The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.”

McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.”

But there’s sadness, too, in the way his life and career were scarred by his refusal to wear the poppy when playing games around Remembrance Sunday in England. “It’s completely changed me as a person,” McClean says. “It’s made me a bit of a recluse because I don’t trust a lot of people now. I’ve been stung bad.”

McClean’s autobiography, The Walls, is one of the best sports books of the year. It’s a powerful and sometimes disturbing read elevated by McClean’s willingness to show himself in an unflattering light.

I have written a lot about Derry and boxing, and Bloody Sunday, but it helps to be back here to understand how McClean can respect the millions of soldiers who died in two world wars while refusing to forget how the British army killed so many Irish people in this city.

View image in fullscreen James McClean celebrates after scoring for Sunderland in August 2012. Three months later his career and his life would drastically change. Photograph: Scott Heppell/PA

He comes from Creggan, the estate affected most on Bloody Sunday in 1972 when 14 unarmed civilians were killed by the British army in Derry. Six of the fatalities were from Creggan. In 2010, after the Saville report finally concluded that all the victims posed no threat, the British prime minister David Cameron apologised for the “unjustified and unjustifiable” massacre.

McClean was born in Derry in 1989 and he writes that “learning how to make a petrol bomb was one of my first life lessons. I was 11 before I’d properly mastered it.”

He pauses when asked how he would feel if any of his three daughters or his son, who is 11, ended up making petrol bombs. “I’m very thankful they don’t have to. It’s a different era now. I just want them to be proud to be Irish.”

The 37-year-old spells out the contrast with his youth. “I grew up in a very Republican community still dealing with the effects of the Troubles. You would see gunmen on the street. People got shot, kneecapped. To get access to my street you had to go through a lane where you sometimes saw masked men doing punishment beatings. But you weren’t scared. You knew you’d done nothing wrong. That was the norm … but it’s not normal.”

His biological father, Joe Kelly, was an alcoholic in Creggan and McClean spoke to him only once – when he shouted at him in the street to stay away. But he remembers a happy childhood and, when his professional career began with Derry City, “I was very carefree”.

McClean was 22 when Steve Bruce signed him for Sunderland in August 2011. He made his Premier League debut that December after Bruce was replaced by Martin O’Neill. McClean soon became a regular starter and that first season in English football was full of joy and praise. He was fast, skilful and disciplined. Apart from wasting money his biggest vice was typing his name on Twitter where he would revel in glowing reports of his play.

View image in fullscreen McClean says he always opted to fight fire with fire. ‘I went into some games in the wrong frame of mind.’ Photograph: Charles McQuillan/The Guardian

“It was amazing,” McClean says. “I never thought about the politics when I first got to England so up until November 2012, when the poppy thing started, I never experienced any bother.”

Everything changed when he told Sunderland he wouldn’t wear the poppy because it also represented the British army which had occupied Derry for so long. “There was never a decision for me to make,” he says. “Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen. It was a very difficult year and I felt a lot of that could have been handled better by the club. But Sunderland came out with a statement before the game which drew all eyes on me. It was there to protect the club. They basically said this is James’s personal decision but we, as a club, wholeheartedly support the poppy appeal.

“I wanted to make my own statement but I was constantly told by the club that: ‘No, no, it’ll die over. Just leave it.’ I’d just turned 23 and I thought the club had a duty of care to look after me and that’s what they were doing. I’d won the player of the year the previous season but I felt they hung me out to dry.”

McClean recalls that: “The next game was away to Fulham on a Sunday, on Sky. A threat was made that I would be shot if I came on to the pitch. I remember [his wife] Erin panicking. It sounds extreme and people might say: ‘Oh, wise up, you’re not going to be shot on TV.’ But the night before the game I was assigned two police officers to stand outside my door. So the Met police took it seriously and that made it more real.”

O’Neill brought him on in the second half and his every touch was booed – by the Fulham and Sunderland supporters. The vitriol poisoned his world but McClean kept searching for his name on Twitter. He became furious whenever, after a mutually respectful encounter with a member of the public, the person would go online to abuse him.

Sometimes McClean would track the person down and demand an apology. “Maybe that madness was always there, but it got stronger,” he notes.

McClean moved to Wigan before joining West Brom where, in “the best kind of madness” he earned £42,000 a week while he had his best spell in the Premier League. But as one poppy season blurred into another, the death threats kept coming, as did the warnings that Erin would be raped. McClean says: “My reaction was always to fight fire with fire. I went into some games in the wrong frame of mind. It wasn’t: ‘Can I help the team?’ It was: ‘I hope I score today so I can shush them up.’”

View image in fullscreen The winger is sent off while playing for West Brom in December 2015. Photograph: Alan Walter/Reuters

McClean admits: “There were days where I went looking for the conflict.” He posted a photograph of himself listening to his favourite Wolfe Tones song, The Broad Black Brimmer. “I knew exactly what I was doing,” McClean writes. “It was an IRA song – and I was sure it would rile a certain type of person up.”

By the time he reached Stoke, for whom he played 111 games between 2018 and 2021, his problems in English football reached a new low. “Brexit made the idiots louder” and “the poppy season seemed to be getting longer every year”. He had also made a stupid mistake during lockdown when he posted a photograph of himself, wearing a balaclava, with his two eldest children below a caption which read: ‘Today’s school lesson – History.’”

McClean thought he was being funny but his choice not to wear the poppy, in contrast, was heartfelt. “I thought others might have followed suit but it never turned out to be the case.”

Did he feel that a more rounded understating of his stance had emerged by the time he enjoyed his happiest seasons in English football, while playing for a Hollywood-tinged Wrexham from 2023 to earlier this year? “A wee bit, aye. When you explain it to footballers you’ve played with, and to people on a personal level, it opens their eyes and they say: ‘Oh, I understand that.’ But the overall British population? I don’t think so.”

Reflecting on his Premier League years, McClean marvels at the brilliance of Kevin De Bruyne and Eden Hazard. “You had to accept there were lads capable of doing things that were beyond you,” McClean writes. “But there were also games where I thought I was coming up against a physical strength that I found suspicious. Coming back into the Premier League after a break convinced me that some players had to be benefiting from some kind of performance-enhancing support.

“I remember coming up against one player that I’d encountered at Sunderland who I always felt that I’d been able to match in terms of his speed and power. While I’d been away from the Premier League, he’d gone to a bigger club, and now he was a different animal completely.”

These are startling allegations and, while McClean has no concrete evidence to support his doubts, he trusts his gut reaction. “I’ve always been very fanatical about my fitness,” he says. “But when you come against the top Premier League clubs, no matter what height, what size, they’re just faster, they’re stronger, and you’re thinking: ‘How is that possible?’”

After their daughter Willow was diagnosed with global development delay and autism, Erin persuaded him to be tested for autism. He was found to be “at the high-functioning end of the spectrum” but he still struggles with the fact that “I’ve probably got body dysmorphia or some kind of bulimia. Maybe it’s the autism thing, because I’m so strict with my diet 95% of the time. But when I can’t work out I binge. So if I’m travelling and flying, I’ll just eat that much shite to the point where I have to make myself sick. I still feel really guilty, because the next day I’ll punish myself in the gym – which is not healthy.”

View image in fullscreen McClean is the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win more than 100 caps for the Republic of Ireland. Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty Images

Life has become even more complicated since he returned to Derry City in January. “I was meant to be coming home for the fairytale ending. But you quickly realise the promises are just bullshit.”

McClean has not played for the club since July and, asked about the situation, he says: “It’s not good. It’s a player against owner and there’s only one winner. I think that’s it in terms of Derry City. You never think you’ll be betrayed by your own so it’s painful.”

When contacted by the Guardian, a spokesman for Derry City said: “The club cannot speak to, or comment on, how James feels.” He also rejected the suggestion that Derry City had failed to fulfil any promises made to McClean.

Earlier this month, McClean said he couldn’t “understand or accept” the way he was being treated by the club and that he was fit to play despite being left out of the squad by interim manager Mark Connolly. Derry City then released a statement in which they said: “The club has sought to resolve this internal matter privately. Out of respect for confidentiality and the fact that this dispute involves sensitive medical details regarding James’ hip condition, the club have previously refrained from making any public statement on the matter.”

McClean insists he could play football elsewhere but how does he feel if this is the end of his career? “It doesn’t unsettle me because I’ve been boxing off and on for 10 years and in the past 18 months I’ve really thrown myself into it. I’m not going to start a pro boxing career because it’s just not feasible at my age. But I’ve been in contact with Misfits and they want me to fight.”

Misfits Boxing was set up by KSI and the Sauerland brothers, who made their name in the traditional fight game, and it features YouTubers and former athletes who want to become boxers. It is dismissed by boxing purists but McClean sounds enthusiastic about making his debut in the ring once his contract with Derry expires: “Boxing is giving me that purpose to wake up and train hard.”

What kind of boxer would he like to become? “I’m a pressure fighter. I like to be constantly in someone’s face because I’ve got the fitness to maintain that. I’m not saying I’m by any stretch of the imagination a [Gennady] Golovkin or a Canelo [Álvarez], but I love watching them. I’m not looking to have a career in boxing but three or four fights a year is perfect. The dream was always to be a footballer but this is a new excitement, a new challenge.”

As we prepare to step out into a rain-sodden Derry, there seems little chance of any reconciliation for him on the football field. But he looks up and his taut fighter’s face suddenly relaxes into a smile. “It could be a blessing,” McClean says softly. “It could end up a blessing in disguise.”

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta defends job cuts at Arsenal to help club ‘evolve and create success’
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has defended Arsenal’s decision to cut up to 60 jobs and insisted it was felt to be necessary to ensure they can continue achieving success.

The Premier League champions are understood to have informed the staff whose positions are at risk after a consultation process started by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) before the end of last season. Arsenal hope the number of redundancies can be reduced and will attempt to redeploy affected employees wherever possible, although some job losses may be unavoidable.

It is understood the catering and travel departments are among the affected, and that the men’s and women’s first-team performance and coaching staff will not be impacted. The academy, Arsenal Women, Arsenal in the Community, the Arsenal Foundation and site security teams are also exempt, although other areas of the wider football operation are included in the review, which was overseen internally by the managing director, Richard Garlick.

The timing of the proposed cuts has attracted scrutiny after last week’s announcement of Arteta’s new contract, worth more than £20m a season. Arsenal say the restructuring process began before the deal was announced and the manager said he was not the appropriate person to answer questions about the redundancies.

“It was explained to me about the exercise, and the analysis that has been done across the club, and with the intention always to evolve to improve,” he said. “Some decisions have to be taken, to put people in the right roles, and keep investing to achieve what we want to achieve and the success that we want to create. So that has been explained. Obviously I am not the right person to answer that question. That’s for sure. And hopefully everybody will respect that.”

The club refused to allow Arteta to answer any more questions on the subject. Arsenal’s most recent financial accounts, for the 2024-25 campaign, show that operating costs rose from £148m the previous year to £201m, with the owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, keen to cut costs despite winning the Premier League title in May.

Arteta was instrumental in reshaping Arsenal’s medical department over the summer, when the former Aston Villa team doctor Arnaldo Abrantes arrived, and is believed to have bolstered his backroom staff in other areas.

Arsenal travel to Nottingham Forest on Sunday – the first of four away games in their next five matches – and Kai Havertz is again expected to start ahead of Viktor Gyökeres. The Sweden striker has yet to find the net for Arsenal this season and struggled against Lille in midweek after scoring four goals on international duty.

“These are moments in a player’s career, or in a season, I would say,” Arteta said. “And we are trying to help him as much as possible. The other day, I think he had some very good moments. He’s three or four times in front of goal with no keeper and the ball should arrive to him and it doesn’t. But these are the strikers. It’s very small margins. Scoring or not scoring changes the narrative, for sure, not the perception of how much he can help the team.”

Sports.title: The Florian Wirtz mystery: why has he not found Leverkusen form at Liverpool?
Sports.content:
Is Wirtz struggling at Liverpool as badly as most outside observers believe?

Some criticism has been OTT and a fee rising to £116m heightens demands but, yes, compared with his performances in Germany and for Germany Wirtz has underwhelmed at Liverpool. The past week has encapsulated his Liverpool career so far. In the Champions League rout of Lask he was everywhere, exploiting gaps between and behind the Austrian club’s defence and knitting together a dominant display against limited opposition. In the previous game against Manchester City, however, when Andoni Iraola needed big players to step up in the absence of Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai, Wirtz was ineffective, wasteful and withdrawn when his team were chasing the game at 0-1. It also did not help his cause that Rayan Cherki, a cheaper alternative whom Liverpool considered and passed on, completed City’s victory with a sublime goal. AH

What are the main reasons for this?

The physicality and intensity of the Premier League appear to be Wirtz’s biggest issues. He can be swamped, knocked aside, leaving Liverpool’s central midfield exposed. Iraola this week rejected the notion that the playmaker is struggling with English football, although his answer almost veered in support of the argument. “It’s not about whether they are foreign teams or English teams,” the head coach said. “It’s about different kinds of games. Some games are more comfortable, with more time to think, sometimes less. It’s not about the competition.” But, as Brentford are likely to demonstrate on Saturday, there is less time to think and little opportunity to get comfortable in the Premier League. Wirtz produced three assists in 11 Champions League games last season, the same amount as he did in 33 Premier League matches. His passing accuracy this season – from an admittedly small sample – is 80% in the Premier League and 91.5% in the Champions League. AH

Does he have the ‘on-pitch personality’ to succeed at Liverpool?

That is a question that can be levelled at many of Liverpool’s signings since the 2025 title win. The shift towards acquiring expensive “finished products” has left many pining for the hunger and spirit of emerging talent that characterised the club’s re-emergence under Jürgen Klopp. Wirtz does not have an ego to match his price tag. He is a conscientious, dedicated professional who Iraola, like Arne Slot before him, has found to be a good listener willing to put team instructions first. He is also, it seems easy to forget, only 23. Wirtz may not be a demonstrative force but he shows personality on the ball, always looking to receive it and take responsibility. His talent is clear but has not been seen consistently enough in a Liverpool shirt. AH

What needs to happen tactically, and in general, for him to thrive at the club?

Wirtz was sold on Slot’s vision for him as the central, creative force of a new-look Liverpool attack that would turn the slender wins of the title-winning season into dominant, emphatic victories. It never happened, and Slot was sacked without finding a position that best suited Wirtz. Iraola immediately confirmed Wirtz would be his No 10 and got to work on him building a close rapport with Isak. There were some promising signs before Isak got injured again. Wirtz can justifiably argue that forces beyond his control have conspired against him at Liverpool and that, as his relationship with Bradley Barcola and Isak improves, so will his end product. He would also be helped by the addition of an out-and-out defensive midfielder who could offer Wirtz licence to roam and greater protection to the Liverpool defence. Monaco’s Lamine Camara, whose proposed move to Chelsea collapsed on deadline day, is of interest. AH

How good was Wirtz at Bayer Leverkusen?

Unbelievably so. In his final two seasons in the Bundesliga you could make the case that he was the best player in it. He racked up goals and assists in European competition too (he was excellent in the Champions League in 2024-25 before injury halted him in the knockouts) but you can’t just describe it in terms of numbers. He dominated the big matches and acted as the conductor of Leverkusen’s orchestra. Teams who tried to kick him out of games almost universally failed, making the idea he can’t hack the Premier League physically a flawed explanation for his difficulties. AB

How much of his success was down to ‘on-pitch personality’?

Partly it was, but on a technical and tactical level his success was also partly down to the freedom Xabi Alonso allowed him. As Alonso said in November 2023 (during Leverkusen’s unbeaten double-winning season) every player had responsibility to patrol an allotted zone “but Flo is different” – he was given licence to prod opposing defences as he saw fit. Alonso’s rotation of him made sure he remained fresh and impactful, his hat-trick in the 5-0 win over Werder Bremen that clinched the title in 2024 coming after he was brought on as a half-time substitute. AB

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Is the Bundesliga being weaker than the Premier League a factor?

I don’t think we can say that isn’t a factor – but this is something Wirtz himself predicted. Many in his entourage thought he would be better served by joining Bayern Munich instead of Liverpool and he acknowledged he was taking the tougher option. He knew it was a risk but was determined to challenge himself. Another point is how different the Bundesliga is tactically; it has a similarly high tempo but is far more chaotic, which is perfect for a player with his sang froid to exploit. AB

He shone recently for Germany. Is he being used in a notably different way?

He has been given greater freedom (and a little less responsibility off the ball), more akin to his Leverkusen role, but what has been important is having Klopp cheerlead for him. The manager has not missed an opportunity to say how great Wirtz is or how his good international form is “good for Liverpool”. Klopp also gave him the captaincy for the last game (and a half), showing Wirtz and the world that he believes not only in his talent and influence but in him as a leader. It feels like the more contact he has with Klopp, the better for him and his club. AB

Do you have faith in Wirtz being a success at Liverpool?

Wirtz can be a class act, a lovely footballer to watch, and it would be premature to write off a gifted talent who – as the previous answer about Isak and a defensive midfielder suggests – has not had the platform to fully express himself at Liverpool. But the question of whether the Premier League suits him and whether he suits this Liverpool team continues to gnaw away. Wirtz needed a strong start to the season after the difficulties of his debut campaign at Anfield and, with one assist and no goals in six Premier League appearances, that has not materialised. There was encouragement in his overall performance and in his understanding with Barcola against Lask, as there has been on several Champions League nights, but Iraola needs his playmaker to produce a repeat in games such as Brentford away. Wirtz will remain categorised as a luxury player if another difficult Premier League assignment passes him by. AH

Maybe. The deck has been largely stacked against him since he arrived: there were too many changes to a champion team in the summer he arrived, plus he was expected to pull the strings in a side that still had Mohamed Salah. He has overcome big setbacks before, such as the 2022 anterior cruciate ligament injury that took a long while to get over, so he has the character to go with his class. Wirtz has the ability to succeed at Anfield but unless the conditions around him change I think it will be very hard to do so (I can imagine him being great for Bayern in a couple of years, post-Michael Olise). AB

Sports.title: Premier League news: go bananas: Maresca loving fans’ show of defiance; Alonso backs his defence
Sports.content:
1. City manager says ‘we need to make our noise’ Enzo Maresca has called on Manchester City fans to bring inflatable bananas to help inspire the team in their first Premier League home game since being found guilty of financial breaches when they take on Ipswich on Saturday. Supporters packed the away end at Liverpool with the novelty items as a nod to the club’s history last weekend. Blow-up bananas became popular among City fans in the 1980s and 1990s when they spent time in the second and third tiers, and have been revived in reaction to the threat of being punished with relegation and to show there is plenty to reflect on before the 2008 takeover. “Very nice,” Maresca said of the inflatables. “I didn’t know the history behind the banana. I hope tomorrow I can see many bananas in the stadium. I think it creates a nice environment for the fans and for everyone that is in the stadium. I have four kids, they already asked me [for bananas], but tomorrow they’re going to be at the stadium and we’ll see.” It comes after Maresca dropped points for the first time as City manager, losing 4-2 to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League. City are three points clear of second-placed Arsenal at the top of the Premier League and victory would make Maresca the first manager to win their first seven Premier League games with a club. City are playing against a backdrop of being the focus of anger around the country. “We need to try to make our noise,” Maresca said. “And to make our noise means win at Anfield, try to win tomorrow. And this is the way we can make our noise. The different kind of noise, we are not able to control that. I think Rúben [Dias] said that people don’t like the City win. But we like to win. So I think that is a good message for everyone. Probably since the noise, we can see, I can see from my personal point of view, the fans, the club, the team, more together for sure. But we’ll see.” Will Unwin

2. Alonso insists ‘the clean sheets will come’ Xabi Alonso has stressed the importance of clean sheets as he strives to find the right balance at Chelsea and faces up to the absence of Reece James for three months after knee surgery. The manager has been delighted with the attacking output of his team but it is a different story at the back where they have the joint-worst defensive record in the Premier League. Alonso made tactical tweaks for last Saturday’s 5-1 home win over Bournemouth when Moisés Caicedo returned in midfield to play alongside Jordan Henderson in James’s absence. Chelsea announced on Friday morning that James had undergone an operation; it compounds the captain’s reputation for bad luck where injuries are concerned. Alonso’s team defended deeper against Bournemouth and were compact in a 4-4-2 shape out of possession rather than their usual three centre-half system. There were positive signs, which Alonso is determined to build on at Everton on Saturday lunchtime. View image in fullscreen Reece James has had surgery on a knee injury picked up in training before last weekend’s 5-1 win against Bournemouth. Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters “You need a lot of clean sheets to win trophies,” he said. “But you [also] need to score a lot of goals. So it’s about being strong in defence, being good in attack and we are in that process. We are still early days; to do a very deep analysis, it’s too early. We can maybe talk in February. Those tweaks … they need to come naturally and we are not in that moment yet. “The obsession is to win and to compete in the best possible way. The clean sheets will come, I’m pretty sure of that, because we want to play with good balance and good control.” The chemistry in midfield will be key and if Caicedo’s partnership with Henderson showed promise against Bournemouth, Alonso made it clear he would also count on Roméo Lavia and Valentín Barco. He added there would be matches where he played with three midfielders. “In terms of personalities, Moi and Hendo match very well,” Alonso said. “Hendo has this energy to go. He’s very active. He covers a lot of the pitch. And to find the balance with Moi … that he’s more in the position, that he has this stability to be in good distances with everything, it was a good start. “Roméo is in a good moment. He played very well with Belgium [during the recent international window]. He’s super available. It’s been difficult for him [with injuries] but this season he’s been available and has done really well. We need to keep him with the other midfielders because that area is fundamental for our game. And also Valentín. The minutes he has played with us, he has been very competitive. He doesn’t care who is the opponent. He goes. That warrior, fighting spirit he brings is very positive.” David Hytner

3. Moyes backs Pickford to keep England shirt David Moyes believes Jordan Pickford will relish the challenge to his England place from James Trafford and remains the nation’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper. Pickford and Trafford shared goalkeeping duties during the recent four-game international break as part of an arranged plan by manager Thomas Tuchel. The 24-year-old Leeds player is considered the biggest threat to emerge to Pickford’s long-held position with the national team but Moyes insists the Everton keeper has been sharper than ever this season. “When Jordan came back from the World Cup, it might be the best I have ever seen him,” the Everton manager said. “He was lean, he was sharp, his footwork was brilliant, he was fast across the goal and if you look at some of the saves he has made between now and then he has made a couple of brilliant, brilliant saves. “I spoke to him when he came back and said: ‘You know you have a bit of competition now with Trafford, how are you going to deal with it?’ I don’t see Jordan falling away at the moment. I think if it really mattered to England then Jordan would still be the one who was there because he makes saves. He did that in the Argentina game. He has that experience and he is not ageing.” Trafford has won plaudits for his footwork with Leeds and England. But Moyes reflected: “Jordan is a terrific kicker of the ball, he is a better kicker than Trafford, but passing is a different equation. When you talk about that, is goalkeeping now just about the passing? Or are you saying you still have to put your gloves on and make good saves and make good decisions. I think it would be hard to move Jordan off that role. I don’t think Jordan is moving aside at the moment.” Andy Hunter

4. Iraola shares delight at coaching Ngumoha Andoni Iraola has said it is “a privilege” to work with Rio Ngumoha and believes the Liverpool winger is on the path to becoming an elite talent. Ngumoha has shown his versatility this season, with the arrival of the £123m Bradley Barcola prompting Iraola to shift the 18-year-old to the right wing on occasion. Ngumoha helped create Barcola’s first goal for Liverpool when impressing from that position in the midweek Champions League rout of Lask. “For us it is a privilege to have Rio in the team because he has just become 18,” said the head coach. “He has already played some minutes with the national team and that is not normal. Normally you start playing with the national team when you are 20-something and you already have matured a little bit. We have to help him because luckily for us he is not the finished product. He can still improve because he is still 18 and I hope we can help him with these processes.” View image in fullscreen Trey Nyoni is likely to make his full Premier League debut for Liverpool at Brentford. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA Ngumoha won his third cap for England during the recent international break, featuring in both wins over Czechia in the Nations League, and has started four times for Liverpool under Iraola. “I think he knows he is elite at certain things,” Iraola said. “If you want to put someone one versus one then Rio is one of the best players you would choose because he is so difficult to contain. “There are areas he has to improve, especially without the ball. He has to get used to the demands of the Premier League in terms of duels and this happens when you come from the youth system. There you are used to being superior to the others and now you face very strong opposition and it is not easy to sustain those duels, but he is improving a lot. Body-wise he is becoming stronger and I think he is in a good place.” Andy Hunter

Sports.title: Steven Gerrard told to seek different managerial opportunity instead of Wrexham job
Sports.content:
Steven Gerrard told to seek different managerial opportunity instead of Wrexham job

Steven Gerrard deserves another shot at management, but not with Wrexham.

That's the view of talkSPORT's Tony Cascarino, discussing the future of current Wrexham manager Phil Parkinson amid a poor start to the Championship season.

2 Phil Parkinson is under pressure with Wrexham winning only one of their last six games Credit: Getty

Who has been tipped for the Wrexham job if Parkinson leaves?

Former Burnley boss Scott Parker and Gerrard are two names that have been floated as potential replacements for Parkinson were he to be sacked by the Welsh club.

Parkinson joined Wrexham in 2021 and led them to an historic three-straight promotions from the National League all the way to the Championship.

And he very nearly guided them into the second-tier play-offs last season, falling just short on the final day.

However, Wrexham have toiled early in 2026/27, winning just two of their opening 10 Championship games.

As such, talkSPORT understands Parkinson's position is coming under increased scrutiny.

That's ahead of Saturday's home clash against Preston, one of seven teams below Wrexham in the table as things stand.

What did Cascarino say about Gerrard?

On the suggestion of Gerrard taking over in North Wales, Cascarino told the Weekend Sports Breakfast: "Steven did exceptionally well at Liverpool's academy.

"He got the Rangers job — done brilliantly well. It didn't go well at [Aston] Villa — he did okay for a period of time.

"And things then went pear-shaped for him and he went to the Middle East [to manage Saudi side Al-Ettifaq] and he didn't keep his job very long there.

"But I think you have to fail in management; there's going to be failure along the way.

2 Gerrard has struggled to make an impact as a manager since his time at Rangers Credit: Getty

"You're going to learn a hell of a lot by failure as well."

Asked by co-host Shebahn Aherne whether he thought Gerrard should get another crack at coaching, Cascarino continued: "He deserves an opportunity somewhere along the line.

"I don't think he deserves the Wrexham job."

Gerrard has been out of management since leaving Al-Ettifaq in January last year.

The Liverpool and England great previously led Rangers to the 2020/21 Scottish Premiership title.

He subsequently spent just under a year in charge of Villa, his first Premier League role.

Sports.title: Kai Rooney takes giant step in Man United career at same age as dad’s Everton debut
Sports.content:
Kai Rooney takes giant step in Man United career at same age as dad’s Everton debut

Kai Rooney reached an early career milestone by making his debut for Manchester United Under-21s on Friday.

The son of Man United and England legend Wayne Rooney, Kai came off the bench in a Premier League 2 clash against Nottingham Forest.



2 Kai Rooney signed first-year scholarship terms with Man United in July

He's still only 16, the same age as his dad when he made his first-team debut for Everton.

What happened on Kai Rooney's Man United Under-21 debut?

Unfortunately, his Under-21 debut didn't go to plan as United conceded a late goal to lose 3-2 in the game being played at Loughborough University.

Nonetheless, Rooney Jr's appearance represents the next step in his burgeoning career as he looks to follow in his dad's footsteps.



Rooney was among United's new academy intake this summer, signing as a first-year scholar.

Also in that crop was Jacey Carrick, the son of current United head coach Michael Carrick.



Born in Liverpool, Rooney first joined the United youth set-up back in 2016.

After also spending time with Manchester City and then in the USA after his dad moved to D.C. United, he re-joined the Red Devils in 2020.



And ultimately, his goal is quite clear: to reach the first team.

What has Wayne Rooney said about Kai?

Speaking about his son last month, Wayne Rooney told talkSPORT: "Kai has signed a long-term deal at Man United and he's at the place he wants to be, the place I want him to be.

"That's important. He's been at the club a long time and he wants to go and try and play for the first team and be successful."

2 Wayne Rooney says Man United is the right place for Kai to be and will hope to see him follow in his footsteps by breaking into the first team Credit: Getty

But for the time being, he'll hope to continue his development with the Under-21s, who are managed by Adam Lawrence.



United are back in Premier League 2 action away to Burnley in early November.

Meanwhile, the first team's woes worsened in midweek with a 2-0 Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid.

After that game, United defender Lisandro Martinez sparked controversy by openly criticising the club's board.

He has since apologised.

United's search for a first win in six outings takes them to old rivals Leeds on Sunday.

Sports.title: Championship manager admits sack fears just three months after being appointed
Sports.content:
Championship manager admits sack fears just three months after being appointed

Burnley manager Nicky Hayen admitted he has concerns over his future after a 2-1 defeat at home to Wolves on Friday night.

The Clarets will now go one year without a win at home, leading to very loud boos at the end of the game and lots of anger directed at chairman Alan Pace.



3 Burnley are embroiled in a relegation battle Credit: Getty

The Clarets are sitting in the relegation zone on eight points and could drop to 23rd by the time the weekend is over.

And with their next home game not until Halloween, it will be a full year since they last tasted victory at home.

The last time they did so was on October 18, 2025 against Leeds United, winning 2-0 in the Premier League.



They have played 21 matches since and haven't won a single one, with the pressure building on Hayen to turn it around after just three months in charge.

Speaking to talkSPORT after the match, the manager was asked whether he fears for his job.



"I would lie if I said I didn't," Hayen said. "I think every manager in this position feels pressure and difficulties.

"But again, if you saw our first half, that was a really good one. They didn't create even one chance.



"It was a draw at half-time. Even when we came out of the dressing room, we had a few moments where we could lead again. And then we gave the game away.

"You know when the atmosphere starts to change. Players - I don't say hide themselves - but they don't play with 100 per cent confidence anymore.

"They want to try to change it in their own way. They try to do everything positive, but they lose the structure. They're going to play four or five touches instead of keeping the structure.

"We just have to stay together. Something that I said to the fans before the season, just support for 90 minutes and then you can criticise me or the team as much as you want.



"But you feel that the energy in the stadium was changing after it went 2-1. That makes it more difficult, not only for me, because I can handle that pressure, but also for the players.

"If they feel positive support like the first half, then you can do more. When it starts to change, it becomes difficult."

Fan protests

There were banners calling for American chairman Pace to leave Turf Moor, which led to scuffles with stewards as the atmosphere turned sour.

Security staff attempted to remove the flags from view, leading to clashes with sections of supporters.



Pace is the chairman and majority owner of Burnley, and after a dreadful start to the season, he is the target of many fans' anger.

3 Pace is public enemy number one at Turf Moor Credit: Getty

Fuming

One Burnley fan joined the Weekend Sports Bar to rip into the club.

Lee said: "Alan Pace needs to disappear out of my town. Get rid.

"He doesn't know what he's doing. He's way out of his depth.

"Hayen - where do I start? He can't see out a game. His decision making and substitutions are absolutely shocking.

"Then, he takes Vardy off when we are playing well and brings Broja on. Why?"



Story of the game

With Burnley looking to charge up the table and get away from the Championship drop zone, they started very quickly and created chance after chance.

3 It was a night to forget for Burnley and their fans Credit: Getty

Eventually, they grabbed the lead in the 20th minute as Jacob Bruun Larsen provided a perfect pass for Jamie Vardy.

The 39-year-old made a run in behind and didn't even take a touch.

Instead, he just hit it first time across the goalkeeper and into the far corner like he has done his whole career.



But soon after, an error from Kyle Walker allowed Newcastle United loanee Sean Neave to roll the ball across the box for Fer Lopez.

He guided his effort off the inside of the post to level the score.

In the second half, it was the visitors who were on top, but they needed two more individual errors to grab the victory.

Igor Julio took an awful touch that Mateus Mane pounced upon and rolled the pass through for fellow substitute Tawanda Chirewa.

Chirewa had been on the pitch for 21 seconds and rifled a shot at goal that Benjamin Coudert somehow didn't save and tipped it into the net.



From that point, the confidence drained from the home team and the visitors had a few chances to make it more comfortable before Armando Broja hit the bar.

And at the full time whistle, there were very loud boos and chants of 'Alan Pace is a w*****'.

Sports.title: The top five wingers in the world over the last three years
Sports.content:
The top five wingers in the world over the last three years

Bukayo Saka has not been included in the list of top five best wingers in world football over the last three seasons.

talkSPORT's Jermaine Pennant thinks Saka sits just outside the biggest superstars on the planet in his position.

5 Pennant has left Saka out of his top five wingers in the world in the last three years, questioning his numbers and his overall level Credit: Getty

The Arsenal forward has faced some criticism over the last three years regarding his numbers, despite recent success.

He is now a Premier League champion and has played in a Champions League final, but Pennant doubts his output in the big games.

In recent seasons for the Gunners, he has scored just six and seven goals in the league, netting three so far this campaign.

"He's world class, but he doesn't get in my top five," Pennant said.

So if Saka misses out on Pennant's top five of wingers in world football, who makes it?

Mohamed Salah

"World class. He's an elite, world class winger."

That's what Pennant thinks of Liverpool icon Mohamed Salah, who scored 71 goals in the last three seasons, winning the Premier League title, PFA Player of the Year and a Golden Boot.

Across 135 club games altogether, the Egyptian King, who now plays for Trabzonspor in Turkey, also provided 47 assists.

Vincius Junior

Real Madrid's Vinicius Junior is another to make it into the top five wingers in the world across the last three years.

In 150 games in all competitions, the Brazilian superstar scored 65 goals and provided 44 assists.

In every one of his previous three seasons, Vini Jr. hit double figures for goals and won four trophies, including the Champions League, while coming very close to winning the Ballon d'Or in 2024.

5 Liverpool legend Salah has been included in Pennant's top five wingers of the last three years for his incredible stats Credit: Getty

5 Vini Jr. has some impressive stats to his name over the last few seasons, coming close to winning the Ballon d'Or in 2024 Credit: Getty

Lamine Yamal

Of course, Lamine Yamal takes a spot in the top five wingers.

The 19-year-old, who is challenging Harry Kane for the Ballon d'Or this year, has 91 total goal contributions in the last three seasons.

Yamal won the World Cup, the Euros and two La Liga titles in that time, dominating football as one of the best on the planet.

Ousmane Dembele

The only Ballon d'Or winner on this list is Ousmane Dembele, and Pennant had to include him because of that.

Dembele is the reigning winner of the award after scoring 35 goals and providing 16 assists in all competitions in 2024/25.

He has also scored 31 goals in the last two seasons in Ligue 1, as well as netting 18 times in the Champions League, winning it twice.

5 Barcelona's star duo Yamal and Raphinha have both taken a spot in Pennant's top five wingers in the world Credit: Getty

5 PSG's Dembele won the Ballon d'Or last year, so of course he has to take a place in the top five of the last three years Credit: AFP

Raphinha

Yamal's teammate Raphinha, who is also a two-time La Liga winner in the last three years, takes a spot in the top five wingers.

The ex-Leeds man has risen to stardom in recent years, picking up 20 goal contributions in a remarkable 2024/25 league campaign.

He also scored 13 goals and provided eight in 14 Champions League games that same season, which saw him equal Cristiano Ronaldo's record for the most contributions in a single edition.
