World.title: As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
World.content:
Beit Jala, occupied West Bank – Khaldoun Atwan starts each day in the oncology ward at Beit Jala Government Hospital, not knowing what barriers will come his way.

The Nabi Yunis checkpoint in Halhul seems to be “always closed”, so the head of the daytime oncology unit at the hospital leaves his car and finishes the commute from Hebron by taxi.

“More than once, by God, I found the mirror broken. I found the wiper broken,” he said about his journey through an area where settlers are now active.

Traversing a dizzying array of gates and checkpoints opening or closing at will, he does not know whether he will reach the hospital, whether his patients will, or whether the drugs they need will be on the shelf when they do.

Beit Jala is the only government hospital in Bethlehem governorate, home to some 320,000 people. Inside his tiny, spartan office, Atwan is struggling to keep up with his cancer patients who have regressed because they missed crucial appointments or essential drugs needed for their chemotherapy treatment.

Not even during the second Intifada, he recalls, was drug supply an issue. Now, it’s inescapable.

“Everything’s short … whatever’s available we give,” he said. “It’s a disaster.”

The Palestinian Authority (PA)’s finances have collapsed over the last three years due to a reduction in international aid and disruptions in Israel’s transfers of tax receipts. Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including widespread road closures, checkpoints and a series of settler pogroms against Palestinian communities, have also impacted the economy.



As a result, the occupied West Bank’s healthcare system is rapidly deteriorating, with staff receiving just half their salaries, while the PA can’t pay for essential medications.

‘Emergency cases only’

Alongside others nervously pacing in the courtyard, an older cancer patient from a village in Bethlehem governorate stood at the entrance of the hospital, weighing with his son what to do. “Every month they do their best, the doctors and the cleaning staff, but they aren’t provided with anything,” he said.

Ministry clinics are now operating part-time, with doctors seeing well more than 100 patients a day when they are. Now, even a doctor’s visit is rushed and unaffordable: “If we want to go to the doctor for a checkup, we need 200 shekels [$65],” said an older cancer patient.

“It’s not a story of there being no staff,” said Iyad Dari, the attending physician at the dialysis unit at Beit Jala. Getting paid only half their salaries, “the government employee is working just two or three days a week, because he hasn’t got enough to come in for his full hours,” he added. As a result, the hospital ends up covering emergency cases only.

“At first, [patients] were [angry]. But now everyone understands: Everyone’s suffering,” Dari said.

The medical supplies crisis in Beit Jala and across the West Bank is the result of Israel’s withholding of tax revenues earmarked for the PA, an action spearheaded by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

“This crisis is very predictable, and we saw it coming 100 percent,” said Milena Ansari of Physicians for Human Rights Israel. Even before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel was periodically withholding tax revenues, endangering the Ministry of Health’s coffers, Milena said.

According to Yosef Ojra, an internal medicine specialist at Beit Jala, the withheld revenues have depleted the Health Ministry’s funds to pay medical suppliers, who are now withholding their services. The ongoing borrowing of supplies between the public and private arms of healthcare has greatly strained private clinics, pharmacies and hospitals.

Hisham Amle, an oncologist at the hospital, said shortages are “an old problem, not a new one”, but that about 90 percent of important items – for chemotherapy, above all – used to be there. Now, even immunotherapies and biologics are missing, and cancer treatment runs on an unbroken chain. “If the patient misses a session or two, he’s lost all the treatment before it,” he said.



“When I first took over the department, the drugs were available,” said Atwan, the lead oncology nurse. He then began to list all the crucial drugs he was now missing for his patients. “There’s not one single complete protocol I’ve got.”

Khuloud Dweib, the hospital’s director of pharmacy, said the ministry recently managed to obtain eight previously missing oncology drugs and four biologics. This should be enough for between a month and a half and two months. But many other drugs are still out of stock, she said.

Unlike in Gaza, Israel is not blocking medicines from entering the West Bank, Ansari noted. The problem is “strictly” that the PA has no money to buy them. But “Israel has the primary legal obligation as an occupying power,” she notes, to ensure adequate medical care and access to occupied populations.

Denied movement, denied care

For all of the southern West Bank, Beit Jala’s hospital is the only public option available for cancer and dialysis treatment, with patients coming from Bethlehem and Hebron governorates, parts of occupied East Jerusalem and sometimes Jericho.

But as Israeli checkpoints and gates multiply, reaching the hospital has become a nightmare. Dari described a dialysis patient from Nahalin, with an appointment at seven or eight in the morning, whose village was sealed. “He sat about four, five hours at the checkpoint,” Dari said. Then he took the long way round, through Jaba, Surif, Halhul and Hebron, and reached the unit at four in the afternoon. A normal journey costs about 10 shekels. “A detour like this costs more than 100 shekels,” Dari said, and some patients need dialysis four times a week.

The ministry’s central supply warehouse, meanwhile, is in Nablus, Dweib said – and an hour-and-a-half drive can now take six to 10 hours when closures hit.

Often, Atwan’s patients require treatments split between his unit and the Augusta Victoria Hospital in occupied East Jerusalem. Before the war, cancer patients from the West Bank routinely received medical permits to enter Jerusalem. Some treatments are in Beit Jala, while others are only available in East Jerusalem. But there are no guarantees any more that patients can reach Jerusalem. “I’ve got a cancer patient … He waited on a referral, and there’s no treatment, and after all the running around it comes back he’s security-rejected, too,” Atwan said. “I mean, he doesn’t get a permit to go to [Augusta Victoria]? Where’s he supposed to go?”

Atwan recalled patients who became neutropenic due to missed treatment sessions, and one was lucky not to end up with sepsis. “These are disasters.”

He’s not sure exactly how many cancer patients he’s lost due to missed and incomplete treatments; many of the poorer patients, he said, simply go home and die there.

‘I’ve started cutting back, not taking much’

As crowds swell at front desks and people wait at the hospital’s entrance, a nervous exhaustion percolates through the hospital’s aged halls. “People are really tense. Everyone’s scared,” Dari said.



Atwan, who receives half his salary, struggles to cover his commute from Hebron and help support his daughters at university.

“Let’s not talk about our state of mind – we’ll start crying, for God’s sake,” said Atwan. “Our morale is at rock bottom … We smile in spite of ourselves.”

Amid mass unemployment with labour permits systematically revoked, more sick Palestinians are pushed towards public hospitals just as those hospitals have less to give. Hospitals “will prioritise someone who will actually pay them”, Ansari added.

Ahmed, a Palestinian from Bethlehem with a medical degree, would check every couple of days with the pharmacist to see if they had Humira, an injection every two weeks that his sister with Crohn’s disease needs. For three months, the pharmacists were out of stock. Buying directly from the pharmaceutical company would cost about 2,000 shekels ($650) for one or two injections. “We couldn’t afford that,” he said. “So we just struggled until it became available again.”

The elderly cancer patient from a village facing settler pogroms has cut back on his own medication. “It’s not supplied regularly,” he said. A course of it costs 20,000 shekels ($6,500). “I’ve started cutting back, not taking much,” he added.

Amid supply and staffing shortages, surgery backlogs have piled up. Sayed Ayyad, 22, from al-Eizariya, fell during an accident, fracturing his ankle badly last month. With serious operations taking priority, he waited three weeks for a slot.

“They told me there’s 60 people waiting for an operation,” he said. “One day we couldn’t do the surgery because there were no medicines, no painkillers, no anaesthetic, nothing.”

Fates left to chance

Khuloud Dweib, who heads the pharmacy department at Beit Jala, has to manage the worsening crisis as patients struggle with their health and finances. “There’s no security. We don’t have political, or health, or even financial security,” she said.

She’s left thinking of cases like a young man with multiple sclerosis studying medicine in Egypt. The Health Ministry used to provide his medicine through private purchase until the company stopped supplying without payment. His mother came to see her. “I want to sell my house so I can get the injection for my son,” the mother told her. “Because he’s in Egypt, away from home, studying, and … he’s stopped seeing, stopped walking.”

“So, what can I tell you,” Dweib said, fighting back the tears. “God help people.”

The medical staff fear that with their supplies being hollowed out, they could face a similar fate to their colleagues in Gaza who have been kidnapped or killed.

“We know that at any moment we could be targeted as medical staff, just because we’re medical personnel providing services to people,” Dweib said. “We’re a father and a mother in this society.”

Nobody in the ageing hospital wards sees an end in sight. “The longer we stay, the worse the situation gets,” said Dari.

At three o’clock each afternoon, Atwan has to leave in the hope that he can reach Bab az-Zawiya in Hebron, where he waits for a shared taxi.

“Maybe there’ll be a checkpoint for me, maybe there won’t be,” he said. It’s not so different from the conundrums his patients face. “When a patient gets sick, it’s his luck if the medicine’s there,” he said. “We’ve got no future. I swear: We’ve got no future.”

World.title: Sudan’s army claims dozens of RSF fighters killed in Nyala attack
World.content:
The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians.

The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement.

However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children.

The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres.

Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army.

Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”.

“In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.”

The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area.

This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control.



The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

World.title: IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
World.content:
Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.

Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.

“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”

Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.

Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.

“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.

The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.

“Escalating conflicts ‌and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).



The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.

Debt relief and regional support

Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.

Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.

“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.

Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.

“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

World.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
World.content:
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.

But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

World.title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
World.content:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.

The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.

The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.

He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.

Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.

He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".

"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.

Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.

"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".

The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.

Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.

World.title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico
World.content:
A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.

The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.

The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

World.title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
World.content:
Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off in which the rainforest's future is a key issue.

Left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off on 25 October, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

Satellite data shows that in the year to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.

The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.

World.title: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
World.content:
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.

US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".

Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.

The 42-year-old spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.

Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter.

"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said.

"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.

Hours later, she praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him.

As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.

"The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.

Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practise law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.

"When I was in China," she replied.

After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.

She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".

Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.

When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"

Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"

When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.

She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.

Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"

She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."

Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.

Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days during Trump's first term.

"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Prior to her appointment as press secretary, Zacharia was a frequent fixture on right-wing US networks such as Fox and Newsmax.

She had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and worked as a communications adviser for Trump's social media platform Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn.

In her early career, Zacharia worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.

World.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
World.content:
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.

The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand CondÃ©" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.

The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.

It will once again be on display in the CondÃ© Museum at the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly until 3 January.

The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.

While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.

The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (Â£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.

The exact origins of the Grand CondÃ© remain a mystery.

It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of CondÃ©, drawn up following his death, the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly said.

It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-AmÃ©lie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of OrlÃ©ans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the MusÃ©e CondÃ© collection.

World.title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
World.content:
US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight to New York.

A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and that there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting âmultiple sclerosis (MS), a statement read.

Blair's publicist said that the 54-year-old had a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".

The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board.

Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York had been "built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline".

They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.

The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement noted that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".

It added that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.

The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.

World.title: Pope's health should not be taken 'for granted', says top Vatican diplomat
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV's health should not be taken "for granted", a British senior Vatican official told the BBC.

Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, said the news of the Pope's ill health was "a bit of a game changer", adding "it's going to make things a bit different".

The Pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.

Speaking on Tuesday after the Pope's operation was announced, but before his cancer diagnosis, Archbishop Gallagher said: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted."

The 71-year-old had surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

Speaking to Radio 4's the Sunday Programme, due to air this weekend, the Archbishop said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair.

"And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out."

Asked how it will make things different going forward, the Archbishop said church figures might have assumed "that he was not quite like the rest of us who are very aware of our vulnerabilities and the ageing process".

He went on: "But lots of us have been through similar experiences at different times in our lives, and we've got through them, and so we hope it's going to be the same case with Pope Leo.

"I am concerned. I think we've got to ask the question: how was it discovered? What happened?"

World.title: INTERVIEW: How Johnvents is turning Nigeria’s cocoa challenges into a global agribusiness
World.content:
Over the years, Johnvents, a subsidiary of Capitalsage Holdings, has leveraged Nigeria’s agricultural potential to develop an integrated agribusiness spanning commodity trading, agro-processing. In this interview with PREMIUM TIMES, John Alamu, founder and group managing director of Capitalsage Holdings, discusses how Johnvents is transforming Nigeria’s agribusiness landscape through investments in cocoa and cashew processing, vegetable oil production, animal feed manufacturing and other value-added products.

Mr Alamu discusses the experiences that inspired his entrepreneurial journey, the challenges of accessing finance and markets, and the company’s efforts to improve cocoa quality through farmer training, sustainable practices, and access to improved seedlings. He also highlights the need to expand domestic cocoa production, replace ageing cocoa trees and strengthen agricultural processing to reduce Africa’s dependence on raw commodity exports.

Excerpt

PT: What motivated you to go into cocoa-product manufacturing?

Mr Alamu: I started my career at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan. I am also the proud son of a teacher who taught agriculture, and I graduated from the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta. So, when you look at my family background, education and career, you can see that agriculture has always been part of my journey. I began my career at IITA, a research institute, as a monitoring and evaluation specialist. This allowed me to work directly with farmers. At the time, we were not working specifically on cocoa. We worked with farmers cultivating cassava, maize and other crops.

Through our research, farmers repeatedly identified several challenges, but two consistently stood out: access to finance and access to markets. The response to these challenges was often more research, and the cycle continued. I decided not to see these two major problems in the agricultural sector merely as challenges. Instead, I saw them as opportunities to explore. I had several ideas about how to take advantage of these opportunities and turn them into viable businesses. I saw them as ventures I could pursue, and I believe that’s how the company name, Johnvents, came about. Our initial business focused on training farmers in good agronomic practices, buying their produce, and selling it to the market.

From there, we expanded into commodity trading. We supplied maize seedlings and grains to internally displaced persons’ camps to support food security efforts promoted by development finance institutions, the World Food Programme, Catholic Relief Services and other organisations. However, when I started my entrepreneurial journey, I did not limit myself to agriculture. I also established a financial services business called Credit Assistants Investment Limited, which has since grown into Capital State Technology Group.

At one point, I travelled to Akure to market a microfinance bank product. The visit took me to a site beside our current factory in Akure, owned by a cocoa cooperative conglomerate. The cooperative informed me that it had a distressed, moribund factory and was looking for investors. However, I knew nothing about the factory; bushes overgrown it, and the machinery needed attention. That experience sparked my interest. I told them I was willing to acquire the factory. I asked the cooperative for a flexible payment structure and help leveraging its brand. I also requested access to human resources, including engineers who could support the operation. One of the engineers recommended to us was Engineer Gomolu. He is still on our board today as the executive director, technical, at Johnvents Cocoa.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

That was how the story began.

We secured financing from the International Finance Corporation to refurbish the factory and acquire new machinery for our Akure operations. From there, we further acquired Premium Cocoa Products in Oyo State. The business became even more interesting as we diversified beyond cocoa.

Today, we process cashews at our Ondo State factory, with a capacity of 30,000 metric tonnes. We also have 10 plants in Ondo that process cashews into kernels and shells, process soybeans into soybean oil and soybean meal, and run an animal feed mill.

We have also expanded significantly into fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). We process cocoa into products such as Johnvents Choco Pops, Johnvents Choco Cubes, and Johnvents chocolate, including products for children. We also have our own bottled-water brand.

We operate across the agricultural value chain, including upstream, midstream, and downstream activities. Our vision is to become a truly global and inclusive agribusiness that facilitates global supply chains, particularly in food production and food security. We currently operate in 19 countries, and we plan to consolidate our presence in those markets by transitioning from commodity trading towards agricultural processing. Enough is enough. Africa has spent too much time talking about the need to stop exporting raw commodities. We do not want to join the chorus of complaints. We want to keep building factories and changing that narrative in a significant way.

PT: How do you ensure the quality of your raw materials, given concerns about the quality of cocoa beans sourced in Nigeria?

Mr Alamu: Quality products begin with primary production. It starts on the farm. Johnvents has invested significantly in a robust sustainability programme. I should mention that Johnvents is Rainforest Alliance-certified. This certification validates our sustainability efforts. What do we do for farmers? We link them with relevant agricultural research institutions, including the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria (CRIN), which provides access to improved, high-yielding varieties. Gone are the days when farmers had to wait five years for cocoa trees to mature. Some varieties now mature in less than three years, and some reportedly in as little as 18 months. The first step is giving farmers access to high-quality seedlings.

Secondly, through our sustainability programme, we connect them with appropriate financing partners to improve access to finance. We also train them in good agronomic practices.

Today, we have about 40,000 farmers under our programme, making it almost impossible to work with every farmer individually. To address this, we use different strategies. Some farmers are organised into cooperatives, through which we engage with them, while others are connected through our local buying agents. Our farmers and local buying agents are certified, and our factories are recertified as well. Because much of Nigerian cocoa is destined for Europe, we must comply with relevant European Union regulations and sustainability requirements. Our sustainability programme has helped us address these requirements.

A significant proportion of the cocoa we handle is now compliant with the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).

This involves addressing issues such as traceability and child labour, ensuring that children are not sent to farms when they should be in school. It also covers pesticide residues in crops. Through our training programmes, farmers learn which pesticides to use and the appropriate quantities. These issues previously made Nigerian cocoa less competitive in international markets.

We have a cocoa bean processing capacity of 48,000 metric tonnes. However, Nigeria’s cocoa production is declining, with annual output estimated at 300,000 metric tonnes. One challenge is that our competitors are not just other cocoa processors; they also include raw cocoa bean exporters. Raw bean exporters enjoy shorter business cycles because they don’t need to store large quantities of cocoa in warehouses for extended periods or commit the substantial working capital processors require.

As processors, we must hold stock and tie up capital while waiting to process and sell our products. This puts us at a disadvantage compared with raw bean exporters. We recognise that Nigeria’s cocoa supply may not meet our needs unless the country develops a deliberate agenda to increase cocoa production.

Beyond our sustainability programme, which addresses existing cocoa farms, we are also working to replace old cocoa trees, as many in production are ageing.

We have also developed our own agroforestry model, which we are currently implementing in Ondo and Cross River states. We appreciate the state governments’ support. Ondo State has provided us with approximately 1,000 hectares of land, where cocoa farmers can own plots and establish cocoa farms in line with prescribed quality standards. The Cross River State Government has provided us with approximately 7,000 hectares. We will continue to advocate for support from other cocoa-producing states. We have written to state governments and are awaiting their response. We are ready to work with them to make more land available for cocoa production. Nigeria needs to increase its output to compete with other major cocoa-producing countries. Côte d’Ivoire, for instance, produces more than 1.2 million metric tonnes of cocoa annually, while Ghana produces approximately 700,000 metric tonnes. Nigeria was once one of the world’s leading cocoa producers. I believe we can return to that position by investing in production, improving farm productivity, and expanding the country’s cocoa-growing capacity.

PT: With monthly electricity bills reportedly hitting ₦45 million, how close is Johnvents to transitioning into a fully self-sustained renewable energy model, and what timeline should investors expect for this switch?

Mr Alamu: Energy efficiency and the transition to cleaner energy are strategic priorities for strengthening Johnvents Group’s operational resilience, cost efficiency, and environmental performance. Given the energy-intensive nature of our processing facilities, we are taking a phased, site-specific approach to identifying viable renewable energy solutions.

As reported in our 2025 Sustainability Report, 39.41% of the Group’s energy consumption came from renewable and low-carbon sources. Building on this baseline, we are committed to assessing renewable energy opportunities across our facilities, identifying energy-efficiency improvements and evaluating the technical and commercial feasibility of solutions such as solar power and energy storage.

In parallel, we are strengthening our greenhouse gas accounting by calculating and monitoring our Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions to understand our emissions footprint better, identify key reduction opportunities, and track progress over time. These insights will help inform our energy transition priorities and support the development of a practical, data-driven decarbonisation roadmap. Our next steps will focus on assessing site-level energy demand, evaluating investment requirements and prioritising initiatives based on their potential to reduce grid dependence, energy costs and greenhouse gas emissions.

While we have not yet established a definitive timeline for achieving full renewable energy self-sufficiency, our immediate priority is to translate this ambition into a structured transition plan with measurable milestones, balancing emissions reductions and long-term cost savings with the reliability required to sustain our operations. Specific targets and timelines will be communicated as the assessments progress and the implementation roadmap is validated.

PT: Credit assessments have highlighted that a significant amount of working capital is tied up in inventory and advance deposits to aggregators. What steps are you taking to, free up cash flow and reduce liquidity pressures during the off-season?

Mr Alamu: Our working-capital requirements reflect the seasonal nature of agricultural procurement. During key crop windows, we strategically secure raw materials to support production and customer demand, with that inventory subsequently processed, sold, and converted into cash. Managing this cycle effectively is therefore a fundamental part of our operating model. Our focus is on maintaining strong discipline across the entire cash-conversion cycle, from procurement and inventory management to production, sales and collections. This includes strengthening demand and procurement forecasting, improving inventory turnover, aligning purchases with production and sales requirements, and maintaining close oversight of receivables.

Given the seasonality of the business, we also seek financing structures that are appropriately aligned with agricultural procurement cycles and the timing of customer and export receipts. Our cash-conversion cycle can extend to approximately 150 days during seasonal peaks, while customer collections typically occur within 25 to 40 days. This reflects the timing between procurement, processing, shipment,ment and collection rather than a uniform funding requirement throughout the year.

Our priority remains to manage this cycle prudently, maintain appropriate liquidity, meet our obligations as they fall due, and ensure that our operations are adequately funded to capture opportunities during critical procurement periods. Any specific financing or capital-management initiatives will be communicated in accordance with our approved financial disclosures.

PT: Insecurity and farmer displacement are major realities in your sourcing regions. How is Johnvents physically protecting its supply chain and ensuring a steady flow of raw materials if critical farming hubs face sudden lockdowns or disruptions?

Mr Alamu: Supply-chain resilience begins with understanding where our raw materials come from, maintaining strong relationships with suppliers and farmer groups, and avoiding unnecessary dependence on a single source or route. Our cocoa sourcing network spans several Nigerian states. This multi-origin approach gives us options to assess changes in local conditions, subject to crop availability, quality requirements, and commercial considerations. We also work through farmer associations, cooperatives and local buying agents, supported by sourcing and traceability processes. These relationships help us maintain visibility into supply conditions and respond when volumes, logistics or access are disrupted. At the operational level, security and emergency planning must be proportionate to the risk and coordinated with relevant authorities and local stakeholders.

We cannot eliminate the wider security risks affecting agricultural communities, and we would not claim that any sourcing model is immune to disruption. Our priority is to identify emerging risks early, assess alternative sourcing and logistics options where appropriate, and protect the safety of farmers, employees, suppliers and transport partners while maintaining responsible procurement.

PT: While your export-heavy model brings in foreign exchange, it also exposes you to intense global commodity-price shocks. What hedging strategies do you have in place to protect Johnvents if global cocoa or cashew prices fall unexpectedly?

Mr Alamu: Commodity-price volatility is a material risk for any processor or player operating in international agricultural markets. Our approach therefore combines disciplined procurement, close market monitoring, careful management of inventory and sales commitments, and a clear understanding of the price exposure at each stage of the trading and processing cycle.

Where export sales and input purchases are denominated in foreign currency, matching exposures and timing can help manage some risks. Still, it does not eliminate the impact of sharp movements in global commodity prices. The appropriate tools depend on the commodity, contract terms, market liquidity, and the group’s approved risk appetite. We assess exposures and commercial commitments to hedge risk, protect margins, and preserve our ability to meet customer and supplier obligations. Our broader priority is to manage exposure prudently, avoid taking risks that are not supported by our operating capacity, and build a resilient business across market cycles.

PT: Johnvents has set a target for 100 per cent traceability and certified sustainable sourcing by 2027. Given your reliance on fragmented independent aggregators, what is the biggest bottleneck holding you back from hitting this deadline?

Mr Alamu: Johnvents has achieved 100 per cent traceability and EUDR compliance across the relevant sourcing scope, representing a significant milestone in strengthening supply chain transparency and responsible sourcing. Our progress reflects continued investment in farm mapping and geolocation, supplier data management, farmer engagement, and monitoring systems. We now focus on sustaining this achievement as our sourcing network and volumes expand, while continuing to strengthen supplier oversight and certified sustainable sourcing across our supply chains. Working with independent aggregators requires consistent data management, verification, and adherence to responsible sourcing requirements across multiple actors and locations. Our published sustainability information also highlights progress in this area, including 122,916 hectares of farmland reported as verified deforestation-free and EUDR-ready in 2025.

Our priority is to maintain the integrity of our traceability systems, strengthen ongoing verification and advance certified sustainable sourcing in line with our 2027 commitment. This will help ensure that our sourcing practices remain transparent, reliable, and aligned with applicable regulatory and sustainability requirements.

PT: Fuel subsidy removal and food inflation have increased transportation costs for smallholder farmers. How is Johnvents ensuring these farmers don’t abandon your network for local buyers who may pay cash upfront without requiring strict compliance?

Mr Alamu: Farmer loyalty cannot be secured by asking farmers to absorb rising costs without support. It depends on whether the relationship offers a dependable market, transparent requirements and value over time. Our long-term cocoa programme aims to support 150,000 farmers by 2030, and our current published disclosures report more than 40,000 farmer partners across our sourcing network.

We are strengthening farmer relationships through training, access to seedlings, cooperative and aggregation structures, traceability support and links to markets. Training and clear communication about quality requirements can also reduce avoidable rejection, delays and costs.

Payment terms and transport arrangements are important to farmers’ decisions, so they must be commercially workable and communicated clearly. We should not promise universal farm-gate collection, transport subsidies or immediate cash payment unless those arrangements are available for the commodity and location. Our objective is to build relationships in which responsible sourcing requirements are matched by reliable engagement, transparent processes and a credible route to market.

PT: Large-scale cocoa processing faces growing scrutiny over deforestation and monocrop farming. Beyond providing macro-loans, how are you actively enforcing agroforestry practices among independent smallholders who lack the capital to shift to climate-smart farming?

Mr Alamu: Our approach is to make sustainable farming practical for smallholders, not simply to set requirements and expect farmers to meet them without support. Through our cocoa sustainability programme, we work with farmers on good agricultural practices, climate-smart methods, farm mapping and traceability. We have distributed more than 400,000 cocoa and shade trees since 2022, supporting efforts to improve farm resilience and encourage tree cover within cocoa landscapes.

We have trained more than 8,000 in climate-smart agriculture across Ondo State, and 122,916 hectares have been verified as deforestation-free and EUDR-ready. We use farm-level information and traceability systems to improve visibility of sourcing areas and help identify deforestation risks. These activities complement engagement with farmer groups and supply-chain partners on responsible sourcing.

Enforcement must be paired with practical support. Farmers need guidance on tree management, soil health, farm productivity and compliance, as well as access to seedlings and cooperative structures that can help them share knowledge and resources. We also need to monitor implementation and address non-compliance through our supplier and sustainability processes. We recognise that the transition takes time, particularly for farmers with limited capital, so our aim is to combine clear standards, monitoring and farmer support rather than rely on financing alone.

World.title: EFCC confirms custody of Maina’s son, speaks on next steps
World.content:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has confirmed that it has taken custody of Faisal Maina, son of former chairman of the defunct Pension Reform Task Team, Abdulrasheed Maina, following his arrest after six years on the run.

The commission’s spokesperson, Dele Oyewale, confirmed this to PREMIUM TIMES Saturday morning, saying a necessary court order would be needed to transfer him to a correctional centre to serve his prison sentence.

“Confirmed. The necessary court order will be obtained to take him to the Correctional Centre for him to serve his sentence,” Mr Oyewale wrote in response to a PREMIUM TIMES enquiry.

TheCable first reported that Faisal was arrested by operatives of the State Security Service (SSS) in the Karsana area of Abuja after intelligence indicated that he had secretly returned to Nigeria.

Full details about Faisal’s arrest remain sketchy. An SSS spokesperson in a terse message told our reporter that he was arrested on Thursday and subsequently handed over to the EFCC, which successfully prosecuted him, in absentia, in a money laundering case.

Faisal had been on the run since 2020 after he allegedly breached his bail conditions and fled the country while facing a three-count charge bordering on money laundering.

His trial continued in his absence, culminating in his conviction by the Federal High Court in Abuja in October 2021. The trial judge, Okon Abang, sentenced him to 14 years’ imprisonment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The court found that Faisal operated a fictitious account with United Bank for Africa (UBA), through which his father allegedly laundered N58.1 million.

The funds were deposited into an account operated in the name of “Alhaji Faisal Farm 2” and subsequently withdrawn by Faisal and his father between October 2013 and June 2019.

In November 2022, the Court of Appeal upheld his conviction but reduced his sentence from 14 years to seven years, ruling that the trial court should not have imposed the maximum sentence on a first-time offender.

Faisal’s father, Mr Maina, served an eight-year prison sentence at the Kuje Correctional Centre in Abuja after his conviction for laundering N2 billion in pension funds. He was released earlier in 2026 but has since been declared wanted over an alleged case of receiving stolen property.

World.title: CJID to launch Living Archives Initiative, unveil book honouring veteran journalist Lade Bonuola
World.content:
The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) is set to launch its new flagship project, the Living Archives Initiative, alongside a digital platform aimed at preserving Africa’s media history.

The launch, scheduled for 22nd October in Lagos, will also feature the unveiling of “Ladbone: A Life in Print”, an anthology of essays written in honour of veteran journalist Lade Bonuola.

The Living Archives Initiative is aimed at addressing a persistent gap in Africa’s journalistic memory, where important newspaper records, personal papers, photographs, broadcast recordings and first-hand accounts are often scattered, deteriorating or inaccessible.

CJID said the initiative would document, preserve and make accessible the lives and legacies of people whose work has shaped journalism, contributed to knowledge production and promoted public accountability and democratic development across the continent.

“Journalism cannot renew itself if it loses the memory of how earlier generations confronted power, defended standards and made difficult editorial choices,” CJID’s CEO, Dapo Olorunyomi, said.

“The Living Archives Initiative is an attempt to preserve that evidence as a resource that can help us gain the necessary context and think more clearly about journalism’s public purpose and future.”

The first edition of the project focuses on Lade Bonuola, popularly known as “Ladbone”, who is widely regarded as one of the most consequential editors in the history of the Nigerian press.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Bonuola began his journalism career at the Daily Times, where he authored the critically acclaimed “Caught-out by Ladbone” column. He later became the pioneer editor and managing director of The Guardian and co-founded The Comet in 1999.

He subsequently became the supervising chief consultant to Compass Newspapers before returning to The Guardian as chief consultant.

His career, which spanned more than five decades, took him through some of the most critical periods in Nigeria’s history, including military rule, democratic transitions and major changes in newsroom culture.

CJID said Mr Bonuola’s career offers an invaluable perspective to examine editorial independence, ethics and professional standards in Nigerian journalism.

The book, Ladbone: A Life in Print, draws on contributions from more than 80 editors, media managers, academics, political figures and industry experts.

“This book of essays provides a critical view and honest assessment of those formative years, offering readers a nuanced account of how Nigerian journalists navigated the perilous terrain of military repression while sustaining integrity, accountability, leadership and family,” Mr Olorunyomi said.

The digital archival platform being launched alongside the initiative is expected to serve journalists, newsrooms and fact-checkers, researchers, academics and students, policymakers, media and cultural institutions, and the general public.

CJID said the platform would also provide historical evidence for policy discussions on press freedom, governance and democratic resilience, while offering media and cultural institutions a model for similar archival efforts across Africa.

In Lagos, the launch will feature a panel discussion, a formal book review, the unveiling of the anthology and a reception to mark Bonuola’s 80th birthday.

Participants will receive an exclusive look at the digital archival platform and engage in discussions on media memory, professional standards and public trust.

CJID said the initiative builds on its work in accountability and information integrity by extending its focus to historical preservation and public access to credible records of Africa’s media history.

Members of the public, journalists and colleagues are invited to attend the virtual broadcast of the launch.

Registration is available via: https://us06web.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_XpWbhOGSQwicm_VPfB0QrQ

About CJID

The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) is a technology and knowledge-producing think tank that works to strengthen journalism and democratic accountability in Africa.

Founded in Nigeria in 2014, CJID works across research, media innovation, civic technology, accountability, verification, press freedom and capacity building.

Its mission is to strengthen West Africa’s journalism sector and promote democratic accountability for inclusive and sustainable development.

World.title: CAPPA, activists, labour group reject Lagos water privatisation, metering, demand public investment
World.content:
Community activists and a representative of labour organisations have urged the Lagos State Government to invest in public water infrastructure rather than rely on private operators, warning that long-term concessions and prepaid meters could make water less affordable for low-income households.

The groups spoke on Friday at a symposium in Ogba, Lagos, organised by the Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) and the Our Water Our Right Africa Coalition as part of the 2026 Africa Week of Action Against Water Privatisation.

The event was themed “No Illusions: Prepaid Water Meters and Water Privatisation Are Failed Models for Lagos, Nigeria.”

Speakers included Akinbode Oluwafemi, CAPPA’s executive director; Zikora Ibeh, the organisation’s assistant executive director; Rufus Olusesan, national president of the Precision, Electrical and Related Equipment Senior Staff Association (PERESSA); Dagar Tolar of the Movement for Socialist Alternative; and Favour John, founder and executive director of the Sustainable Futures Development Initiative (SUFDI).

Mr Oluwafemi warned that private-sector participation did not guarantee better services and could put water beyond the reach of poorer households.

“For profiteers, control of water is becoming the new petroleum,” he said.

He argued that access to water for drinking, cooking, washing and basic hygiene should not depend solely on a household’s ability to pay.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He argued that access to water for drinking, cooking, washing and basic hygiene should not depend solely on a household’s ability to pay.

Activists question 20-year concessions

Mr Oluwafemi called on the Lagos State Government to publish the terms of its proposed water concessions, including the financial obligations, tariff arrangements and protections available to investors.

According to information presented by CAPPA, the Lagos Water Corporation (LWC) has announced a framework for standardised 20-year concessions, with cost-reflective tariffs subject to periodic reviews, foreign-exchange protections for investors and a five per cent royalty structure.

The proposed concessions cover seven water facilities in Lekki, Akilo, Victoria Island Annex, Magodo, Abesan, Alexander and Apapa.

Speaking at the event, Ms Ibeh said the corporation reported receiving 23 bids across four project lots in May but had not identified preferred bidders or published the full proposed agreements.

CAPPA said it had requested the identities of bidders, evaluation criteria, feasibility studies and award decisions in March 2026.

The group also questioned the state government’s April 2025 agreement with Belstar Capital and ENKA for water infrastructure rehabilitation and expansion. It raised concerns about the selection process, financing obligations and possible effects on tariffs.

Ms Ibeh cited a one-year memorandum of understanding signed in 2026 with China Harbour Engineering Company and Naston Engineering Nigeria Limited for a proposed water infrastructure programme within the Lekki Concession Area.

The planned works include transmission infrastructure beneath the Lagos Lagoon, distribution networks, metering and household connections.

The Lagos State Government had presented public-private partnerships as a way to attract investment, rehabilitate water infrastructure and expand access to reliable supply.

At a stakeholder engagement in August 2025, the Lagos Water Corporation said the initiative was intended to bring together public authorities, investors and development partners to improve service delivery.

Activists call for rehabilitation of waterworks

Mr Tolar said the government should address the condition of existing water infrastructure rather than rely on private-sector participation to resolve the state’s water shortages.

He stated that Lagos had major waterworks and 48 mini and micro waterworks, but their combined output was inadequate to meet demand.

Citing figures he presented at the symposium, Mr Tolar put the combined production capacity of the facilities, including the Adiyan waterworks serving Lagos and Ogun states, at about 200 million gallons daily. He estimated that Lagos needed at least 500 million gallons a day.

The figures and operational rates he cited could not be independently established from the information provided at the event.

Mr Tolar called for a comprehensive “Water for All” plan that would include rehabilitating existing facilities, building additional waterworks and using modern technology to increase production.

He said the plan should account for future population growth. He also questioned how much successive administrations had invested in water infrastructure since Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1999.

“No form or version of privatisation will fix the water problem in Lagos or Nigeria,” he said.

He cited electricity privatisation and private-sector participation in waste collection as examples of reforms he believed had failed to deliver the expected benefits.

Communities bear the cost of water shortages

Mr John said research into community water infrastructure in Lagos showed that residents often had to provide and maintain facilities that should serve the public.

Presenting findings from a research project on strengthening resilient public water services, he said many communities relied on water points donated by councillors, religious institutions and individuals because government facilities were unavailable or poorly maintained.

He explained that community development associations (CDAs) sometimes pooled money to buy water from tankers, pay electricity bills and repair pumps.

“In your community, for example, there’s no public water. There’s a situation whereby the CDA even organises to fund a water tanker sometimes,” he said.

Mr John cited a community where residents reportedly spent about N85,000 weekly on water, yet the supply remained insufficient.

He proposed public-community partnerships that would give residents a role in managing facilities. Women and young people, who often bear much of the burden of fetching water, should also be represented in community-level decisions.

“Water should be accessible and should be available and should be safe for every human consumption,” she said.

Labour warns of job losses

Mr Olusesan said workers had a direct stake in the proposed reforms, warning that restructuring and private-sector concessions could lead to retrenchment, casualisation and the loss of employment benefits.

He urged the government to protect workers’ rights, regularise casual staff and give trade unions representation on the boards of public water corporations.

CAPPA said the restructuring of the Lagos Water Corporation led to the disengagement of 425 contract workers in December 2023 and the dismissal of 391 permanent staff on grounds of redundancy on 15 April 2024.

The organisation and labour groups challenged the decisions, arguing that the workforce reductions weakened the capacity of a public institution responsible for providing an essential service.

The corporation, however, attributed the restructuring to a personnel audit and operational requirements, according to Ms Ibeh.

Mr Olusesan criticised what he described as the promotion of market-oriented water reforms by international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

He argued that policies centred on cost recovery, commercialisation and public-private partnerships could shift more of the cost of water provision to households.

Citing experiences in Ghana, Senegal and other African countries, he said private-sector management had not guaranteed affordable water for poorer communities.

The PERESSA president also proposed community water-monitoring committees to report leaks, monitor public taps and hold water authorities accountable. He advocated public-public partnerships, through which established public utilities could help improve other public water systems.

Prepaid meters raise affordability concerns

Mr Oluwafemi noted that prepaid water meters could cut off households when their credit ran out, regardless of their circumstances.

“When a meter cuts off supply because credit has expired, it cannot distinguish between leaking pipes or a family waiting for daily wages,” he said.

He stated that households facing unemployment, illness or emergencies could lose access to water when they were least able to cope with the consequences.

“A policy that recognises purchasing power but disregards essential need is discriminatory in its effects,” he noted.

Ms Ibeh said CAPPA had documented complaints from residents in Akilo and Baruwa about unreliable supply, delays in activating purchased units, low water pressure and discrepancies between payments and the water received.

She stressed that the complaints raised questions about whether advance payment necessarily guaranteed reliable service or greater accountability.

CAPPA argued that prepaid metering could not be separated from the wider debate over private-sector participation. It said residents needed to know who would control distribution, how services would be funded and whether revenue protection would take precedence over their needs.

CAPPA questions public consultation

Ms Ibeh said the Lagos State Government’s move towards private-sector participation in water provision predated the current management of the Lagos Water Corporation but had gathered momentum through restructuring, procurement exercises and investment agreements.

She stated that CAPPA had challenged the direction since at least April 2023, when it questioned the privatisation implications of a December 2021 memorandum of understanding between the corporation and the United States Agency for International Development.

She also cited partnerships involving the Resilient Water Accelerator, WaterAid, Arup and the Global Development Incubator as part of efforts to attract investment into the state’s water sector.

Ms Ibeh questioned a stakeholder workshop convened by the corporation in August 2025 to discuss private investment in water supply.

According to her, the corporation had already invited proposals under procurement reference LSWC/BFOT/001/2025 for the rehabilitation, upgrading, operation and maintenance of mini and micro waterworks under a Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

The submission deadline was 28 August 2025.

CAPPA described the workshop as a sham consultation, arguing that residents were being asked to discuss a policy that had already advanced through procurement rather than being given a meaningful opportunity to influence the choice of service-delivery model.

The organisation called for greater transparency in procurement and meaningful consultation with affected communities before decisions with long-term consequences were made.

World.title: Luddites as gatekeepers of literature, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
The Luddites were a movement of skilled textile workers in England who rebelled against industrial machinery between 1811 and 1816. Having spent years mastering their crafts, they watched machines produce textiles faster and more cheaply, threatening their livelihoods and diminishing the value of skills painstakingly acquired over generations. Some, invoking the legendary General Ned Ludd, responded by smashing the machines. The British government retaliated with military force, executions and harsh punishments. Ultimately, mechanised production prevailed, and the traditional methods the Luddites sought to preserve gradually gave way.

Their story offers a useful lens through which to examine today’s anxieties about artificial intelligence and literary creation. As machines become increasingly capable of producing fluent, sophisticated prose, a familiar battle is unfolding between those who embrace technological change and those who fear it threatens the very foundations of their craft. The question is whether we are witnessing a legitimate defence of literary integrity or the emergence of a new class of Luddites determined to police how writers create.

Recently, there was a controversy surrounding Jerry Falade’s highly anticipated debut crime novel, Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body. The manuscript reportedly attracted an offer exceeding $2 million from Minotaur, a Macmillan imprint, in a 14-way auction, with British publishers also making substantial bids. Publication was planned for 2028. Yet the deal collapsed after concerns emerged about possible AI involvement in the writing.

According to the author’s agent, the manuscript had initially impressed its readers, and the agency had declined to use AI-detection software because the author’s explanation appeared credible. Doubts reportedly intensified after a meeting in which aspects of that explanation appeared to change. The agency subsequently withdrew the manuscript, although the full circumstances remain unclear.

The case raises important questions about authorship, honesty and the limits of technological detection. It also illustrates how quickly an emerging literary career can become entangled in a dispute over the provenance of words.

Falade is not alone in facing controversy. Jason Arday, Mia Ballard and HM Wolfe, all black, have encountered scrutiny or backlash over allegations involving plagiarism, AI use or questions of authorship, although the circumstances differ considerably. Controversies involving these Black writers and academics have unfolded amid a wider political climate in which anti-woke campaigns have sought to discredit individuals and institutions associated with progressive causes. These cases should not be conflated, nor should criticism of an author’s conduct automatically be dismissed as politically motivated. But neither should technological suspicion become a convenient instrument for discrediting writers without adequate evidence.

AI-detection platforms such as Pangram have entered this contested terrain, promising to distinguish human-written prose from machine-generated text. For sure, such tools may be useful in identifying passages that warrant further examination. But a detector does not have privileged access to an author’s mind or creative process. It identifies patterns associated with AI-generated language; it cannot, by that fact alone, establish plagiarism, dishonesty or literary worth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A human writer may produce prose that a detector mistakenly flags as artificial.

My concern, however, extends beyond the racial politics surrounding some of these controversies. The more fundamental question is how we should use a transformative technology without surrendering the values that make literature worth reading.

We need to stop treating AI as some evil spirit destined to possess and destroy the creative mind. The more useful question is not whether writers should use AI, but to what extent, under what conditions and with what obligations of disclosure. We need rules that distinguish legitimate assistance from wholesale substitution, intellectual collaboration from misrepresentation, and editing from the outsourcing of authorship.

Demanding that writers reject AI altogether is like asking a man to prove his manhood by walking 200 miles through the unforgiving desert sun when an aeroplane can take him to the same destination in less than an hour. The analogy is imperfect, because literary creation is not simply a journey from one point to another. The struggle, the choices and the craftsmanship may be integral to the destination. Nevertheless, insisting that every task must be performed the old-fashioned way merely because it once was is not a convincing defence of artistic excellence.

A writer may develop an original argument, conduct the research, determine the structure, supply the examples, and decide what the work should communicate. The writer then uses AI to improve sentence construction, eliminate repetition, or clarify a difficult passage. Has the writer committed a sin? Not inherently. Has the writer surrendered literary integrity? Not necessarily. Many of us still run our writing through Microsoft Word to identify spelling and grammatical errors.

We must also distinguish AI assistance from plagiarism. Plagiarism involves presenting another person’s words, ideas or creative work as one’s own without appropriate acknowledgment. AI-generated text does not automatically constitute plagiarism, although AI can reproduce material from existing works without attribution. That is a genuine concern, but it is not the same as declaring every use of generative AI an offence against literary creation.

Two writers described childhood poverty in a Nigerian village. One grew up hungry, watched classmates arrive at school with money while he had none, and learned early that poverty determines not only what a child owns but also how the world treats him. Years later, he transforms those memories into a novel. The other has never experienced such deprivation but uses AI to produce an eloquent, emotionally compelling account of the same experience.

Both passages might be beautiful. Both might move readers. Yet their literary authority may differ. The first draws upon lived experience, memory and personal reflection; the second may depend more heavily on the writer’s ability to direct and refine a machine’s output.

But we should not romanticise suffering or human authorship. Having endured hardship does not automatically make someone a great writer, and a novelist need not personally experience every circumstance described in a book. Imagination has always allowed writers to inhabit lives beyond their own. What matters is the intelligence, insight, judgment and artistic choices brought to the work.

Photography did not abolish painting, nor did the arrival of digital cameras make every photograph a work of art. Technology changed how art could be produced without eliminating the need for artistic judgment. AI may similarly transform literary production without making originality irrelevant.

The danger is that, in the absence of agreed standards, we have begun using AI as both the alleged offender and the judge. There is no universally accepted framework governing how much AI assistance a literary work may receive, when disclosure is necessary or how accusations should be investigated. Publishers, universities and literary competitions need transparent policies proportionate to their purposes. A competition may reasonably demand unaided writing, while a publisher may permit AI-assisted editing provided the author remains responsible for the work and complies with disclosure requirements.

The Luddites might have achieved more by demanding protections against exploitation and a fairer distribution of the gains from industrialisation than by trying to destroy machinery they could not ultimately stop. Their struggle was not simply against technology; it was against the economic power technology placed in the hands of those who controlled it.
