World.title: Africa: Ebola Spread Raises Fresh Urgency for Africa's Domestic Health Funding
World.content:
Bulawayo — An Ebola death last week in Kenya is highlighting the urgency of Africa's public health emergency preparedness and how the continent's governments are committing their national budgets to the health sector.

The Kenya case is serving as a call to arms in the fight against Africa's public health emergencies and how locally coordinated efforts are adequately equipped to contain the spread of communicable diseases.

"Health emergency preparedness gives us a head start, and Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place," Janabi said in a 6 October media brief, which was in stark contrast to concerns raised in the DRC that life-saving medical supplies only arrived ten days later from neighbouring countries, effectively allowing Ebola to leave a trail of death.

As the disease surges at its north Kivu epicentre in the Democratic Republic of Congo, questions have returned about how the shuttering of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has devastated public health emergency responses across Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Last week, Doctors Without Borders warned that the current Ebola strain was spreading so fast for emergency health workers "it was like fighting a megafire," further raising concerns over how the DRC and neighbouring countries will tackle the crisis amid increasingly limited resources.

Despite being often cited as having vast mineral wealth, the DRC's Ebola response has been plagued by an under-funded health sector where international humanitarian agencies are struggling to provide basic medical care.

As the new Ebola strain took root in the DRC's east, Amadou Bocoum, CARE International's DRC Country Director, lamented that "with proper funding, we would have had prepositioned stock and begun distributing critical supplies like PPE from day one, but instead, we started with nothing and lost 10 days."

These funding concerns would be raised weeks later by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) at the 76th Session of the WHO Regional Committee for Africa in Addis Ababa in August.

UNECA noted that "Africa's health financing model remains structurally fragile," with governments failing to allocate adequate budgets for the health sector.

African governments and other health sector players have already raised alarm over the Trump Administration's decision to ice the USAID, which triggered a continent-wide shortage of anything from condoms to malaria and HIV/AIDS drugs.

At the WHO Regional Committee conference, UNECA raised concerns that "external health assistance was down almost 30 per cent," and as Ebola spreads, the effects of that deficit are being felt with catastrophic consequences.

The impact of the reliance on overseas development assistance was made clear by Aboubakri Diaw, who leads UNECA's Sustainable Financing Initiative, who told the gathering that "Africa does not have a reform deficit. It has a sustainable financed-reform deficit."

"Health financing strategies sit on shelves. Insurance schemes are legislated but struggling to be capitalised. Benefit packages are defined but not costed into medium-term expenditure frameworks. A reform without a budget line does not constitute a policy," Diaw said.

Yet it is a commitment African governments made in 2001 at the Abuja Declaration to allocate 15 percent of national budgets to health, but countries have fallen short, with some allocations ranging between as little as 2 percent and 12 percent, according to the World Health Organisation.

To address the public health funding crisis, UNECA says what remains crucial is "a fundamental reset in how African governments and their finance ministries fund health systems" in a continent where millions lack access to and cannot afford basic medical care.

"External aid covered more than 30 per cent of health expenditure, and in some 13 countries the ECA has looked at, households pay more for health than their own governments do," Diaw said, adding that "many countries on the continent now spend more on servicing debt than on public health."

Amid these challenges and competing public spending priorities, it is not yet clear how governments will navigate these new public health funding realities, as pressure from international lending institutions for African countries to repay billions of loans still remains.

Close 

Analysts however see the funding crisis as part of Africa's broader political architecture where short-term planning by sitting governments prioritises projects closely linked to the election cycle.

"Governments have to balance health against infrastructure, security, education, social protection and other priorities," said Pakhani Mhazo, a public health researcher based in South Africa.

"However, health preparedness often produces benefits that are not immediately visible to voters. For example, if you invest in disease surveillance, laboratories and emergency systems and successfully prevent an outbreak from becoming a crisis, there is no obvious event that voters can see as the result of that investment," Mhazo told IPS.

Meanwhile, without any clear or immediate sources to fill the funding gaps left by international aid, African governments have their work cut out, and as Claver Gatete, UNECA Executive Secretary, reminded African ministers during the High-Level Forum on Sustainable Health Financing in April this year, "Health is not expenditure; it is investment - in people, in productivity and in prosperity."

IPS UN Bureau Report

World.title: Kenya: Image of Kenyan Senator Edwin Sifuna Asleep At Public Event Is Doctored
World.content:
Image of Kenyan senator Edwin Sifuna asleep at public event is doctored

IN SHORT: An image posted on Facebook purportedly shows the Nairobi senator drunk and asleep alongside veteran broadcaster Fred Machoka. But inconsistencies between the image and footage from the event suggest it was manipulated.

A Facebook post claims that Edwin Sifuna, the senator for Kenya's capital Nairobi, became drunk at a public event. It includes an image appearing to show him asleep in a chair next to veteran broadcaster Fred Machoka, who also appears to be asleep.

The image shows Sifuna wearing a white shirt and black trousers, sitting next to Machoka, with several bottles of alcohol and glasses on a table in front of them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Another image shows Sifuna awake, sitting with his arms folded.

One image is labelled "Mlevi Sifuna", Kiswahili for "Sifuna the drunkard". The post describes him as "drunk and disorderly" and a "fake" presidential candidate.

Sifuna, an opposition politician who has declared his intention to run for president in Kenya's 2027 elections, launched the Equitable Party on 4 October 2026.

The image circulated shortly after Machoka celebrated 50 years in broadcasting at an event in Nairobi on 10 October. Sifuna attended the celebration, which featured performances by several musicians, including Congolese star Koffi Olomide.

On 14 October, president William Ruto mocked Sifuna's new party and referred to his appearance at the celebration, where bottles of alcohol were visible on a table. Ruto also questioned Sifuna's presidential ambitions.

The image has also been posted here, here and here.

But does it really show Sifuna and Machoka asleep after drinking too much? We checked.

Doctored photo

Royal Media Services, Machoka's longtime employer, published a video of the celebration. We examined it and compared it with the circulating image.

Both men appear in the footage, but neither is shown asleep.

We also found several inconsistencies. Videos from the event show Sifuna wearing a black wristwatch, which is missing from the circulating image.

Additionally, the man presented as Machoka in the image also has different facial features from those seen in the event footage. His red outfit lacks the black shoulder detailing visible in the video.

Close 

These differences suggest the image was manipulated.

We also analysed the image using Hive Moderation's AI content detector, which returned a 99.8% likelihood of AI-generated content. Such tools are not conclusive, but the result adds to the evidence that the image is inauthentic.

Sifuna attended Machoka's anniversary celebration, but the circulating image purporting to show the two men asleep appears to have been doctored.

World.title: Africa: No, Spain Did Not Introduce Visa-Free Travel for Eight African Countries in April 2026
World.content:
No, Spain did not introduce visa-free travel for eight African countries in April 2026

IN SHORT: A Facebook post claims Spain introduced visa-free travel for citizens of eight African countries in April 2026. But European Union regulations show that six of these countries still require visas for short visits, while the other two already enjoy visa-free access.

A Facebook post claims Spain introduced visa-free travel for citizens of eight African countries in April 2026.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The post lists Botswana, Namibia, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mauritius, Seychelles, Cape Verde and Rwanda. It claims holders of ordinary passports from these countries can visit Spain for up to 90 days within any 180-day period without a visa.

Visa-free travel makes international trips easier and cheaper by removing visa application requirements and fees. However, travellers must still meet other entry requirements, and visa-free access does not automatically allow them to work or settle permanently.

The post has also been posted here, here, here, here, here and here.

But is this true? We checked.

No new visa exemption

Spain has not announced a new visa exemption for these eight countries. It follows common European Union rules governing short visits to the Schengen area, a group of European countries that generally allow travel between them without internal border checks.

We reviewed the European Union's official visa regulations, which list countries whose citizens must obtain a visa to enter the Schengen area and those whose citizens are exempt for short stays.

The regulations show that Botswana, Namibia, Eswatini, Lesotho, Cape Verde and Rwanda remain on the list of countries whose citizens generally require visas for short visits.

Mauritius and Seychelles are already exempt, allowing their citizens to visit for up to 90 days within any 180-day period without a visa, provided they meet other entry requirements.

Spain's foreign affairs ministry confirms that visitors must comply with Schengen entry requirements, including obtaining a visa where necessary.

The claim is false. Spain has not introduced visa-free travel for the eight African countries. Only citizens of Mauritius and Seychelles already qualify for visa-free short visits.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Food Problem Doesn't End at the Farm
World.content:
guest column

Walk through Nairobi’s Kangemi Market, Mile 12 Market in Lagos or Makola Market in Accra, and you will see stalls filled with fresh produce. Yet behind this abundance lies a difficult reality. Farmers struggle to earn enough from what they grow, traders lose produce before it reaches consumers, and many families cannot afford a nutritious meal.

This is one of the biggest problems facing Africa's food system. Food can be available in the market and still be out of reach for those who need it. According to the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report , 309 million Africans experienced hunger in 2025. The same report found that 66.6% of people on the continent could not afford a healthy diet. That means roughly two in every three Africans struggled to afford the food needed for a balanced diet.

There is some encouraging news. The share of Africans experiencing hunger fell slightly from 20.3% in 2024 to 20% in 2025 . But progress remains slow, and millions of families still face difficult choices about what they can afford to eat.

Recently, I had the opportunity to help plan the plenary sessions for the 2026 Africa Food Systems Forum (AFSF) in Kigali, Rwanda. As I worked on the programme, bringing together discussions on investment, jobs, nutrition and climate resilience, I kept returning to one question: what needs to change for the millions of Africans whose livelihoods and daily meals depend on agriculture?



The discussions we planned went well beyond increasing food production. We looked at how Africa could create more jobs through agriculture, attract investment, improve nutrition and help farmers deal with changing weather patterns. What became clear to me was that these issues cannot be addressed separately. A farmer can produce a good harvest and still make a loss. A country can grow more food while families continue to struggle to afford it.

Consider what happens after harvest. In Kenya, farmers growing tomatoes, potatoes and other fresh produce often face problems with storage, transport and access to markets. When several farmers harvest at the same time, prices can fall sharply. Without proper storage, they may have little choice but to sell at whatever price is offered or risk losing their produce altogether.

In Nigeria, traders face similar problems. Fresh produce travels long distances from farming areas to markets such as Mile 12 in Lagos. Poor roads, high transport costs and unreliable electricity make it harder to keep food fresh. By the time it reaches consumers, some of it may have spoiled, while the cost of transporting what remains is passed on to buyers.

These are problems that can be addressed. Better roads, affordable cold storage, irrigation and local food processing would help farmers protect their harvests and reach more buyers. Innovation does not always have to mean introducing a new app or expensive technology. Sometimes it means making sure a farmer can store tomatoes for a few more days or transport vegetables to the market without losing part of the harvest.

There are examples of progress across the continent. At this year’s AFSF, the African Development Bank shared results from its African Emergency Food Production Facility, which had reached nearly 15 million farmers across 34 African countries and helped produce an additional 45 million metric tonnes of food . The programme has helped improve access to seeds, fertilisers and other support needed to increase production. It shows what can happen when investment reaches farmers and responds to the challenges they face.

But producing more food is not enough. We must also think about the quality of food people eat. In many households, having enough maize flour, rice or another staple does not necessarily mean having a nutritious meal. Vegetables, fruits, eggs, milk and other foods remain too expensive for many families. This is particularly worrying for children, pregnant women and other people who need a balanced diet to stay healthy.

Conflict, disease outbreaks and changing weather patterns are making food security even harder. In Sudan, war has disrupted farming and food markets, while the recent Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has raised concerns about cross-border trade and livelihoods. Across the continent, droughts, floods and unpredictable rainfall continue to affect harvests, making it harder for families to access affordable food. These challenges show why improving food security must also involve protecting livelihoods and helping communities prepare for difficult seasons.

There is also an opportunity to create more jobs, especially for young people. Too often, discussions about youth in agriculture focus on encouraging them to take up farming. Yet there are opportunities in food processing, transport, storage, packaging and selling agricultural products. Supporting young people to build businesses in these areas would create jobs while helping food move more easily from farms to consumers.

Close 

Governments have an important role to play. Agricultural investment must go beyond distributing seeds and fertilisers. Farmers also need reliable roads, water, storage facilities, affordable loans and access to markets where they can earn fair prices. Businesses, too, need to develop services that smallholder farmers can afford, rather than solutions designed only for large commercial farms.

Planning the Forum's plenaries gave me a better appreciation of how much work is already happening across Africa to improve agriculture and nutrition. It also reminded me that we must judge progress by what changes in people's lives. For farmers, that means earning enough to support their families. For parents, it means being able to buy nutritious food without giving up other basic needs.

Africa's food problem does not end when crops leave the farm. It ends when farmers can make a decent living from what they grow and families can afford good food throughout the year. That is where our attention, investment and efforts should be directed.

Kingsley Ochieng is a strategic communications professional who advises organisations working across development, agriculture, health and sustainability in Africa.

World.title: Bears star Caleb Williams could reinjure hamstring by returning too soon, surgeon says
World.content:
Caleb Williams is listed as questionable for the Chicago Bears' game on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons as he looks to return from his hamstring injury. Should he play, though?

Former college football quarterback-turned-foot-and-ankle surgeon Dr. Drew Burdi isn’t sure if the juice is worth the squeeze. Burdi dealt with a hamstring injury during his playing days at Western Michigan and knows how tough they are to manage.

"I think he could reinjure it," Burdi told OutKick in a recent interview. "I had, when I was playing, I had a hamstring, I pulled my hamstring. It felt the same way. I remember looking around, I was running and I felt like somebody came up and hit me in the back of my leg, and then I realized there was no one around me, and I knew exactly what happened."

Burdi said that when the hamstring is injured, it's actually partially torn. If it's not given time to heal properly, it becomes more susceptible to tearing again.

"Then that just puts stress on other parts of the body, you could be running differently. It can put him in a compromising positions that he just normally wouldn't be in when he's 100%," Burdi said.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Williams refused to disclose the medical grade of his hamstring injury but called it "pretty serious."

"I felt a pop," Williams said. "That's why I looked back. I looked back just like everybody else does when you feel a pop. Think somebody grabbed you and nobody grabbed me."

The Bears' star quarterback also said he wasn't sure whether he would play against the Falcons. Burdi said that if Williams has any trepidation, he should sit out another week.

"'Cause they really look good (without him), except for the Packers (game). But I mean, without that game, I don't know. I'd probably say take more time because I think that they could. It depends on their schedule too. If their schedule is good enough where they can get out of it at .500 and have him come back healthy, I think it's better than trying to push himself, win a game, maybe this week, but then he injures it further, and then he might be out longer. It's one of those injuries where you can try to push it, but you really have to know yourself. If it feels like you're still not 100%, it's probably worth just holding off on it," Burdi said.

Without Williams, the Bears have gone 2-1. They beat the Philadelphia Eagles with Case Keenum, beat the New York Jets with Tyson Bagent, and then lost to the Green Bay Packers. Bagent started against the Packers but was replaced by Keenum late in the blowout loss.

If the Bears heed Burdi's advice and sit Williams for one more week if he doesn't feel 100% and lose to the Falcons on Sunday, they will still have managed to go .500 without their star quarterback for a month.

The last thing the Bears need is for Williams to hustle back only to reinjure himself and miss more time.

World.title: The Cignetti effect is real: Indiana football sparks an unbelievable 'revival' in Bloomington
World.content:
The crowd inside the "Upstairs Pub" started to grow as the clock turned toward Friday night on the campus of Indiana, with students getting out of class and heading towards to local drinking establishments for what was going to be a wild 24 hours.

Obviously, the mood has shifted around this college town thanks to the Hoosiers winning last year's CFP title, along with having a head coach in Curt Cignetti who has turned this program into a football juggernaut in just two years.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOULD TO BE BECOME AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH 24-TEAM EXPANSION

Whether it was the apparel stores that had fans waiting in lines for their chance to purchase Indiana gear, or the restaurants that were already filling up early Friday afternoon, it's obvious that the attitude has changed around this college town that once glossed over the football season in anticipation for basketball.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Later today, it will be No. 4 Ohio State visiting No. 5 Indiana in what will be the most electric atmosphere Bloomington has seen in decades.

You can call it a "revival," or the Cignetti effect, but it's not hard to notice the culture change in Bloomington.

"We're a football school now, and I hate to say that about the basketball program," Edward, from just outside Indianapolis noted. "We spent years praying for some type of revival of college football within this fan base, and we finally have it during one of the craziest times in sports.

"A lot of schools are trying to pull off the Indiana magic of rebuilding a program in such a short time period. And those expectations are truly centered around what transpired here in Bloomington. That part is wild to me. We expect to win football games now, which is a wonderful feeling to have.

So, about Indiana beating Ohio State at home

The last time a Hoosiers' football team defeated the Buckeyes in Bloomington was in 1988.

It took thirty years for Indiana to snap a losing streak to Ohio State, which finally came to an end last season inside Lucas Oil Stadium in the Big Ten championship game.

Also, this will be the first time a top-five college football matchup has taken place inside Memorial Stadium since 1960, as Indiana rises a 22-game winning streak into their showdown with the Buckeyes on Saturday.

Essentially, there are a lot of firsts that could end up coming to fruition for an Indiana team that has defied the odds over the past two seasons, against plenty of odds and fans who might still be under the impression this was all just a fluke.

I'm here to tell you that nothing Curt Cignetti is doing on this campus, and opposing ones, is centered around some magical voodoo that the Hoosiers head coach has placed on the Big Ten.

CURT CIGNETTI WAS SO FOCUSED THIS OFFSEASON, HE TURNED DOWN ALL EXTERNAL REQUESTS: 'I'M 95% FOOTBALL'

Whether or not folks outside Bloomington believe Indiana can do it again this season is not the point.

The supporters who are lining Kirkwood avenue, or the thousands who made their way into town on Friday evening, are the true barometer of where this program has been taken in such a short time period that has other college athletic directors trying to replicate the Cignetti magic.

"I don't think folks truly understood what we were going through as a fan base," Thomas, longtime season ticket holder told OutKick. "I've been coming to games for thirty years, and I've never seen this type of excitement, and it's hard to correlate it with basketball. Sure, we're not oblivious to the narrative that followed our football program like a black cloud.

"But, why do you think we're not taking these moments for granted? We've earned this sh-t, and I promise you this fan base isn’t cocky. We just expect to win now, which clearly wasn’t the case just a few years ago. So yea, I expect us to beat Ohio State."

If Indiana can do it, so can others around college football

I've been around plenty of college campuses during my career, and the resurgent joy that you see in Bloomington is contagious.

This is no longer a loyal group of fans waiting for November to roll around so they can walk into Assembly Hall to watch the basketball program, which has also had its problems over the years.

But what Indiana football did for the school is provide hope that everything that has transpired over the last two years in one sport, can be done again across multiple venues across campus.

Curt Cignetti has not just provided a championship mindset for the passionate fans that were sitting through days of blowouts and small glimmers of hope in past years.

The man who told you all to 'google' him has reignited an athletic department and fan base that will make Saturday's atmosphere on Indiana's campus feel more like a cinematic backdrop that will host college football's premier matchup of the day.

World.title: Hasan Piker's influence tests breaking point of Democratic Party
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ahead of the midterm elections, one name has repeatedly surfaced in conversations about the future of the Democratic Party: Hasan Piker.

The political commentator streams for hours each day on Twitch, promoting socialism, criticizing Israel and the U.S. and discussing the news of the day from his far-left perspective. But as Piker has gone from a niche online commentator to a real-life player in Democratic politics, his growing involvement has raised questions about what his influence could mean for the future of the party.

While Piker's Twitch streams are viewed by tens of thousands daily, his online reach is not what has drawn the questions about the future of the party; rather, it is how engaged his followers are.

"It's very clear to me that the people who do love and support him, really love and support him. So, the followers that he has are super loyal and I think they're really active, and they're very engaged," Isaac Saul, founder of the non-partisan politics newsletter Tangle, told Fox News Digital.

OCASIO-CORTEZ CALLS FOCUS ON HASAN PIKER 'ABSOLUTELY LUDICROUS' AS SOME DEMOCRATS DEMAND DISTANCE

Piker's followers are mostly young people, a demographic Saul called a "prized possession for the Democratic Party." He explained that Democrats were eager to hold onto young voters "because if they can turn out younger voters, that's going to increase their odds of winning in all manner of elections that happen in American politics."

Mark Penn, a longtime Democratic pollster who served as an adviser to former President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, similarly pointed to Piker's appeal to young voters, describing him as almost a "Pied Piper." However, Penn questioned how closely those voters actually align with the streamer's views.

"Nobody could possibly agree with the garbage that Hasan Piker says. It's anti-American, it's antisemitic, it's anti virtually anything, it's anti-having any decorum, sensibility, or intellectual component beyond kind of throwing everything and everyone overboard. So, the whole thing is nihilistic," Penn told Fox News Digital.

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Saul recently outlined his positions on Piker in a piece titled, "My honest thoughts on Hasan Piker." He told Fox News Digital that readers asked him repeatedly, "What's your beef with Hasan Piker?," prompting him to explain his position fully. Saul started his piece by stating that he believes "Piker is a bad guy" and said that he doesn't "trust" the Twitch streamer.

Saul sees Piker as a "big pariah" within the Democratic establishment, even as he gains prominence. The Tangle founder believes, however, that the 2026 midterm elections could shift the party's perspective on Piker and the influence of the far left.

HASAN PIKER VOWS HE WILL PRESSURE JAMES TALARICO TO GOVERN AS A LEFTIST, NOT A MODERATE

"I still view him as kind of an outsider-y person trying to throw his weight around. I think the 2026 midterm has the potential to change that because Piker has endorsed some of the more progressive kind of DSA-type candidates, and if we see them win in House or Senate races, he said, 'We're gonna hold them accountable,'" Saul told Fox News Digital.

Penn also sees the midterms as a potential test of Piker's influence, specifically in the Michigan U.S. Senate race where he was involved with Abdul El-Sayed's campaign. Beyond Piker, Penn sees the midterms as an evaluation of the effectiveness of socialist movements.

"Obviously, I think the Michigan race is a big test case on all of this. I think that if El-Sayed wins in Michigan, then that will be a huge boost to these movements, to people like Piker and all of the outlandishness that they stand for because it wins elections," Penn told Fox News Digital. "If there's a setback here and a setback on the headline elections in Maine, Michigan, and Texas, then maybe the Democrat party is going to come much more to its senses and say these 'movements really didn't work.'"

KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY

While Saul and Penn see the midterms as a test of whether Piker can leverage his online popularity into real-world results, others argue that the shift is already happening, pointing to the growing number of candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Julian Epstein, a former chief counsel for Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee, told Fox News Digital that he believes mainstream Democrats are underestimating the influence of Piker and the left-leaning movement behind him.

"I think that the lie a lot of moderate Democrats are telling themselves is that you're only going to see 10, 12 members of Congress that fall under the DSA banner, and I think that's delusion," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "I think what you're increasingly seeing is that the socialist movement and the far-left movement is becoming the beating heart of the Democratic Party. Why? Because that's where all the activist energy is, and we saw that with the primaries."

Mainstream and moderate Democrats, according to Epstein, are "scared of this movement" and that they are not willing to fight against it.

"Democrats are increasingly scared to take this movement on because they fear the flying monkeys of the online left," he said.

Epstein also argues that establishment Democrats have lost control of the party. He said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and other establishment Democrats have ceased being leaders and are increasingly turning into "marionettes of the far-left."

While Epstein believes Piker appeals to "very frustrated" voters who "want to burn down the system," Saul sees some of the streamer's more mainstream views as part of the key to his popularity.

INSIDE HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL VIEWS ON AMERICA, ISRAEL AND SOCIALISM

"Hasan Piker supports Medicare for all. He wants to abolish cash bail. He thinks big agriculture needs to be broken up. He wants to renegotiate our relationship with Saudi Arabia. I mean, I think those ideas are not just broadly popular with progressives, but popular probably with some people in the populist MAGA right," Saul told Fox News Digital. "I think he could become an influential figure. If there was more momentum in Congress to make some of those policy prescriptions law."

As some Democrats attempt to reach Piker's young audience, they could risk losing voters who already feel that the party has gone too far to the left.

JAMES CARVILLE VOWS TO ABANDON DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF FAR-LEFT HASAN PIKER BECOMES LEADING VOICE

Penn noted that political parties could have much more to gain by saying no to extreme movements than going along with them.

"So much time is spent on turnout and base and not enough realization that if I said no to the extremes, I could get a lot of those voters in the middle to switch. And those are twice as powerful as getting those extreme movements," Penn said.

Tanya Tsikanovsky, a former Democrat who worked to elect Hillary Clinton in 2016 before later leaving the party, told Fox News Digital that she believes the Democratic Party's shift to the left is leaving voters like her politically "homeless."

"I think that we need to stop focusing on how bad or how maybe salvageable the Democratic Party is and not think about them at all, and instead focus on the independents or on the moderate Democrats, like I once was, that feel completely homeless," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "Because there are a ton of [Sen. John] Fettermans and Bill Mahers that are gonna really not have anywhere to go soon. Their party is going to be completely eaten up by the DSA."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Tsikanovsky agreed with Epstein's assessment that moderates in the Democratic Party have been left without power amid the rise of DSA candidates across the country.

"The DSA candidates and people like Hasan Piker are the ones that are being platformed by that party and the moderate ones don't really have power anymore at all," Tsikanovsky said.

The debate over Piker's role in the Democratic Party is at the heart of a larger question about how far left the party is willing to shift in order to gain voters, and how much that change could cost or benefit them.

Saul argued that Piker's influence is best understood by viewing his ability to shape the national conversation, rather than seeing him as a politician or activist.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think when you consume his content, or you think about him as a player in the space, you should think about them as a kind of provocateur, a pundit. Not a journalist, not even an activist. Not a politician, but somebody who is just trying to change the conversation culturally that people are having. And I think, when you do that, he makes a lot more sense," Saul said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hasan Piker and the DSA for comment.

World.title: Serial killer's ex-wife slept beside murderer for 8 years, never suspected his deadly double life

For years, Bonnie Lou Gower shared a bed with a man she thought she knew better than anyone. She had no idea the man sleeping beside her was capable of murder.

Her husband, Richard "Marc" Evonitz, was leading a double life, one that would ultimately expose him as a serial killer who preyed on young girls.

His victims included a 16-year-old who lost her life while Evonitz was still married to Gower.

SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED

Decades after Evonitz’s crimes came to light, Gower is revisiting the warning signs she didn't recognize — alongside the young woman who survived him.

In Investigation Discovery’s true crime docuseries "The Serial Killer Connection," Gower meets with Kara Robinson Chamberlain, who endured 18 hours of captivity and torture before escaping Evonitz, as they investigate whether he may be linked to other unsolved cases.

For Gower, one question has followed her since learning the truth about the man she married.

"When I initially learned about [his crimes] and I told people, honestly their first response is, ‘Well, obviously you knew. How could you not have known?’" Gower told Fox News Digital.

"That was my very first question to the FBI. ‘How could I not know this? How could I not know I was sleeping next to somebody for eight and a half years that was doing this?’ And of course, they assured me that there’s no way I could have known."

Looking back, Gower admitted there were things she didn’t question at the time.

Whenever she left town to visit family, Evonitz insisted on staying behind, claiming he had to work. Only later did Gower discover that he had actually taken time off while she was away.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"One of the reasons he never came with me was because he said he was working," said Gower.

"And then, I come to find out, he had actually taken off work on the days that I was out of town. But at the time, I wasn’t at all concerned about leaving him behind. I was just going and visiting my family. It definitely makes you look at everybody and everything now, whether you can trust someone’s words or actions."

Gower met Evonitz, who was eight years her senior, in South Carolina. He was the older brother of one of her friends and would come home whenever he was on leave from the U.S. Navy. She quickly developed a crush on him as she got to know him and, at age 16, Evonitz asked her out on a date.

They married in August 1988 when she was 17 and he was 25.

"You think you know who you are when you’re 17, but I really don’t think I did," said Gower. "I don’t think I had a handle on that. And I was relatively sheltered. I was very naïve, very trusting, taking everything at face value. I think he knew that."

During the marriage, there were moments when Gower suspected Evonitz was being unfaithful. Whenever she questioned him, Evonitz told her it was all in her head. She believed him. But as the relationship progressed, Evonitz began isolating her from friends and family as they moved around the country, from Maine to San Diego to Virginia.

SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER

"No one ever thinks that their significant other is going to be a serial killer," Chamberlain told Fox News Digital. "I think worst case, and this is something that she expressed to me, he was having an affair. No one ever thinks your spouse is out murdering someone."

"He kept that part of himself very tightly controlled and didn’t show it to the people he was closest to."

The marriage began to unravel after Evonitz left the Navy. Gower said financial pressures fueled growing tensions between the couple, while Evonitz became prone to mood swings and what she described as "rages." He also frequently criticized her weight. Behind closed doors, Gower was also uncomfortable with his interest in bondage, according to the docuseries.

Even as the marriage reached its breaking point, Gower said she still didn’t see Evonitz as someone capable of hurting her. Walking away, she said, was a decision that came after years of mounting unhappiness.

When Gower made the decision to leave the marriage, Gower said her fear was for him, not herself.

"I was concerned for his safety when he said he was going to take the gun and kill himself," Gower recalled. "I never feared for my own life."

SEND US A TIP

Even after she finally walked away, Gower said Evonitz had left her questioning whether she had any justification for doing so.

"When I left, I felt like I was leaving for no real good reason," she said. "[But] I wasn’t happy."

According to Gower's TikTok, she and Evonitz were married from August 1988 until January 1997. Multiple reports indicate that their divorce was finalized in 1998. Years later, Gower would learn just how much she hadn’t known about the man she left behind.

On June 24, 2002, 15-year-old Chamberlain was at a friend’s home in South Carolina when Evonitz pulled into the driveway. The stranger approached her with pamphlets and asked if her parents were home. Then, he held a gun to her neck and threatened to shoot her if she screamed. He forced Chamberlain into a dark storage container in his car.

At Evonitz’s apartment, Chamberlain was repeatedly sexually assaulted. He restrained her to a bed. After hours of torture, Chamberlain managed to free one of her hands from a pair of handcuffs with her teeth, unclip a leather leg restraint and quietly bolt out the door as Evonitz slept. As she took off, Chamberlain encountered two men who took her to a police station.

Chamberlain led officers back to her captor’s apartment. But when investigators arrived, Evonitz had escaped. Police tracked Evonitz to Sarasota, Florida, but as they closed in on him, Evonitz died by suicide. He was 38.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Once investigators began digging into Evonitz’s past, Chamberlain’s abduction proved to be only part of the story. Evidence recovered from Evonitz’s South Carolina apartment, former Virginia residence and vehicle linked him to three unsolved murders.

On Sept. 9, 1996, Evonitz abducted 16-year-old Sofia Silva from the front steps of her home in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, where he and Gower had been living. Her body was discovered about five weeks later in neighboring King George County.

Then, on May 1, 1997, sisters Kristin "Kristi" Lisk, 15, and Kathryn "Kati" Lisk, 12, vanished after returning home from school. Both girls had been sexually assaulted and strangled. Their bodies were discovered five days later in the South Anna River.

Notes discovered by investigators indicated that Evonitz already had his eye on other potential victims, Fox News Digital previously reported.

It would be months after Chamberlain’s abduction that Gower learned of her ex-husband’s other victims.

"It felt like it wasn’t real at all," Gower admitted. "It felt like this was something that happens in the movies. This wasn’t real life. It was very hard to believe that he could hurt anybody. He had never hit me or physically abused me."

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Now, Gower and Chamberlain are looking to Evonitz’s past for answers about whether there could be other victims.

Gower has helped piece together a timeline of Evonitz’s movements during their marriage, providing investigators with dates, locations and old calendars as potential cold cases are examined.

"Of course, he wasn’t always where I thought he was," said Gower.

Chamberlain, meanwhile, has been investigating whether Evonitz could be responsible for other unsolved crimes, examining cases dating back to the 1980s and tracing his movements during his years in the Navy and in the decades before her own abduction.

"I genuinely think that there is a level of escalation that we see between an indecent exposure [incident] and then three homicides in approximately nine months and then a break before me that is unexplainable to me," she said.

"Everything’s possible and nothing has been confirmed," Chamberlain stressed. "It’s a frustrating place to be, but I will not stop searching."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

One potential key to finding answers is DNA.

While investigating cases for the docuseries, Chamberlain said she learned that Evonitz’s DNA profile was not in CODIS, the FBI’s national DNA database. However, she said authorities in Spotsylvania County still have a blood sample that can be provided to law enforcement agencies seeking to compare his DNA with evidence from other cases.

Chamberlain said she hopes Evonitz’s DNA can ultimately be entered into CODIS, allowing for broader comparisons with evidence from unsolved crimes.

"I genuinely believe that there’s no way he only murdered three girls and kidnapped me," she said. "I don’t think that there’s a world in which that’s true."

While making the docuseries, Gower learned that Evonitz had kept a photograph of her when she was just 11 years old — years before they began dating — hidden behind another framed picture of her. Gower said it was not a photograph she had taken with her when she left home and that she never knew Evonitz possessed it.

"It’s disturbing enough that he would have 11-year-old me in a picture behind something," she said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Decades after learning the truth about the man she married, Gower said she is still trying to make sense of it.

"I don’t think you ever make sense of it," she said. "There’s no tidy little box to put it in to make it make sense."

"I’m still grappling with it. I’m still processing."

World.title: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

It was a week of legal turmoil for one of America's most recognizable members of Congress.

Early Monday morning, federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

The raid was part of an ongoing criminal probe into Omar's immigration status, with sources telling Fox News Digital that authorities are scrutinizing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out paperwork for her to become a U.S. citizen.

A day later, U.S. Attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., Jeannine Pirro, announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities.

FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Fox News Digital breaks down what we know so far about each investigation:

Financial Disclosure Investigation:

In May 2025, Omar filed financial disclosure forms for the year 2024, a required for every member of Congress to complete every year. I showed that she had between $6 million and $30 million in assets connected to two businesses run by her husband, Tim Mynett. One was was a venture capital firm, and the other a California winery.

Her financial disclosures from the year prior, covering 2023, said those assets were only valued at between $15,000 and $51,000 total.

The now-defunct winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year.

The massive reported spike in net worth over the one-year span raised eyebrows, leading a watchdog group called the National Legal and Policy Center to file a complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct in February of this year.

'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP

Less than a month after the complaint was filed, Omar amended her 2025 disclosure form. The new filing reduced the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000, and said the businesses had zero value after accounting for liabilities.

ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT

Omar blamed an accounting error, and has since repeatedly insisted that she is not a millionaire.

In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures.

But the hubbub caught the eye of Pirro, who confirmed on Fox News' "America Reports" Tuesday that her office is investigating the discrepancies.

Further details about the investigation have not yet been released.

Criminal Immigration Probe:

Monday's judicially authorized raid of Omar's Washington, D.C. home sent shockwaves through the political world, with many critics calling it politically motivated because it occurred three weeks before November's general elections.

The Trump administration has denied those accusations.

DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’

HSI agents spent several hours at Omar's home, and the Wall Street Journal reported that the lawmaker's personal cell phone, computers and passport were seized during the search. She has not been seen publicly since before the raid.

Sources told Fox News Digital that investigators are scrutinizing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork when Omar was become a U.S. citizen decades ago. The Journal also reported that the goal of the probe is to strip Omar of her citizenship.

A dozen people, including family members, were subpoenaed in relation to the investigation.

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

"Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully," President Donald Trump said Monday of the raid. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me."

"I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is ... a non-country, and then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution," he continued. "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it."

On Tuesday in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital after rallying for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, Vice President JD Vance echoed a similar sentiment.

"We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," Vance said. "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this. And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."

ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Vance made it clear taking that unprecedented step of denaturalizing a sitting member of Congress is possible, but only if the law requires it based on the facts of the case.

"And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," Vance said.

"We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime."

"But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law."

A spokesperson for Omar did not return multiple requests for comment throughout the week.

However, Omar has responded on social media.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said.

World.title: Income inequality at Obama Foundation, as brass thrives and rank and file seeks union
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: The beleaguered Obama Foundation has an income inequality problem: While half of its employees earn six-figure salaries, led by CEO Valerie Jarrett at $771,000, dozens at the other end of the scale are fighting for union representation.

The workplace disparity comes to light just as Fox News Digital reported that the long-delayed Obama Presidential Center's price tag hit $1 billion — nearly triple the original estimate for the Chicago facility. The Obama Foundation, former President Barack Obama's private nonprofit, reported 172 employees receiving more than $100,000 in salary in its 2025 tax filing — roughly half its 342 reported employees.

Jarrett, one of former President Barack Obama's closest advisors and a former senior White House official, has led the Obama Foundation since 2021, overseeing the final years of construction of the Presidential Center on Chicago's South Side.

OBAMA'S BILLION-DOLLAR BABY: CHICAGO CENTER'S PRICE TAG HITS MONUMENTAL MILESTONE, TRIPLING ORIGINAL ESTIMATE

Her total pay rose by around $15,500 from 2024 and she is one of at least four of the nonprofit's 10 highest-paid executives with previous ties to the Obama White House or campaign.

"The Foundation pays our employees rates that are competitive with the market," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "We have more than 500 employees worldwide, roughly 300 of whom are based at the Center."

The current workforce of more than 500 is substantially larger than the 342 employees reported in the Obama Foundation's 2025 tax filing, which covers the year ending nearly six months before the Presidential Center opened in June. The nonprofit did not provide an updated payroll breakdown.

The Obama Foundation saw its annual payroll and benefits bill come in at $50.4 million in 2025, soaring from $18.5 million in 2018. The nonprofit brought in approximately $159 million in revenue last year, of which nearly $151 million consisted of contributions and grants.

The spending surge came as the Obama Foundation expanded its leadership and civic programs at home and abroad while racing to finish the beleaguered Presidential Center. The sprawling 19.3-acre campus sits on publicly owned parkland in Chicago's Jackson Park.

WATCH: Professor breaks down Obama Foundation's finances amid $1B Presidential Center costs

Expert view

Brian Mittendorf, an accounting professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit finances, said the proportion of Obama Foundation employees earning more than $100,000 stood out compared with a typical nonprofit, but noted that the organization relies heavily on specialized staff.

"That's clearly higher percentage than your average nonprofit," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "But here we're dealing with a nonprofit that's probably very expertise heavy. It's very heavy on like the think tank side. And as you look at a think tank, it would look very differently than say a local food bank."

Mittendorf said the Obama Foundation's employees likely possess specialized skills that could command substantial pay elsewhere.

"So it does reflect that a lot of their employees are ones that they would consider having an outside opportunity that would justify them getting paid at that level," he said. "Like I said, it is atypical for a standard nonprofit, but probably not that unusual for a nonprofit of its type."

The Obama Foundation also reported a higher proportion of employees receiving more than $100,000 than five other presidential nonprofits examined by Fox News Digital.

Roughly half its reported workforce exceeded that threshold in 2025, compared with 37% at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, 29% at the Carter Center, 23% at the Clinton Foundation, 13% at the Reagan Foundation and 10% at the George & Barbara Bush Foundation, according to their respective 2024 tax filings, the most recent available for the review.

OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER'S $470M SAFETY NET UNDER SCRUTINY AS SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY'RE OWED MILLIONS

Executive pay

Jarrett's salary rose from approximately $581,000 when she took over as CEO in 2021 to $740,000 in 2022, remaining at that level through 2024 before climbing to nearly $755,000 in 2025.

For comparison, Fox News Digital reviewed the latest available tax filings from five other major presidential foundations, all of which reported lower CEO salaries than Jarrett's $771,000 in 2025.

The Reagan Foundation paid its CEO approximately $735,000 and the Carter Center $531,000 for fiscal years ending in 2025, while the George W. Bush Presidential Center paid its top officer $661,000, the George & Barbara Bush Foundation $426,600 and the Clinton Foundation $425,000 for 2024.

Beyond Jarrett, several former Obama administration officials continued to collect hefty six-figure paychecks at the Obama Foundation.

Christina Tchen, former chief of staff to first lady Michelle Obama, received approximately $431,000 in salary in 2025, while Michael Strautmanis, a former Obama campaign and White House aide, collected approximately $404,000. Laura Lucas Magnuson, a former White House communications official, received approximately $396,000.

Other top earners included Robbin Cohen, who received approximately $666,000. Cohen previously led Pritzker Realty Group, founded by billionaire Democratic donor and former Obama commerce secretary Penny Pritzker, a cousin of Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.

Former Cook County chief financial officer Ammar Rizki received approximately $400,000.

The Obama Foundation defended its executive salary practices.

"The Board of Directors uses comparability data and a compensation consultant to review and approve the compensation of the CEO, officers and key employees on an annual basis," Bittner told Fox News Digital.

OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25

The nonprofit also pointed to higher pay for top executives at other major charitable institutions, including approximately $2 million for the Getty Trust's president and CEO, $1.7 million for the Rockefeller Foundation's president and $1.5 million for the Mellon Foundation's president, citing figures from their recent tax filings.

The Getty Trust, however, operates on a vastly different financial scale, with a multibillion-dollar endowment compared with the Obama Foundation's approximately $14.2 million in reported endowment funds at the end of 2025.

Asked whether Jarrett's pay was excessive, Mittendorf said the answer was subjective, particularly given the Obama Foundation's size and financial resources.

"This is not an unusual amount that to see for a highest paid employee for a director or a CEO," he said, noting the nonprofit's net assets exceeded $1 billion.

Mittendorf acknowledged, however, that substantial executive pay at charitable organizations can attract criticism.

"So I think you see criticism from time to time of executive directors that get paid at this level, not that they could not get paid similar amounts in the private sector, but that there is a belief that in the nonprofit sector, the pay should not just reflect what you would get in the public sector, but something more modest," he said.

"It's quite common, though, for an organization of this size."

Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan, a longtime critic of the Obama Foundation's use of public parkland for the private organization, accused the nonprofit of enriching Obama's inner circle at taxpayers' expense.

"The Obama Center is another far-left political operation that acts as a non-profit while using taxpayer dollars to make Barack Obama's inner circle rich," Grogan told Fox News Digital.

The Obama Foundation maintains that construction of the Presidential Center was privately funded and that its operating costs are covered by revenues and private donations. Public funds have also supported infrastructure improvements surrounding the campus.

Workers push to unionize

The hefty executive paychecks come as rank-and-file Obama Foundation employees push to unionize, alleging rolled-back benefits and mounting workloads. Workers also claim deteriorating conditions have driven experienced colleagues to leave, taking valuable institutional knowledge with them and piling more work onto those who remain.

The employees, organized under Obama Workers United with AFSCME Council 31, include visitor services and cleaning staff, museum and technology workers, and employees involved in the nonprofit's educational and global programs.

"Amidst increasing workloads we have seen our benefits rolled back and support from leadership to be minimal," the workers wrote in a public letter.

SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY’RE OWED MILLIONS, FACE FINANCIAL RUIN, AFTER HELPING BUILD OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The workers also urged Obama Foundation leadership to respect their right to organize and refrain from spending money on anti-union lawyers, messaging or meetings.

The Obama Foundation said it supports employees' right to organize.

"We are deeply committed to the fundamental right of workers to organize and make their voices heard," the nonprofit said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "As members of our staff explore union representation, we approach this process with immense gratitude for their contributions, deep respect for unions, and a sincere commitment to working collaboratively with our partners in labor."

World.title: Oregon school shooting victims include 5-year-old whose family is ‘broken and lost’
World.content:
The victims killed in a special needs classroom at an Oregon elementary school Thursday included a 5-year-old boy whose family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting and a young teacher working her “dream job.”

The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. Officials said an armed bystander fatally shot the teen gunman, putting an end to the shooting spree.

“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen,” Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said Thursday.

Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old with long, curly hair, was identified as one of the victims by a family member.

Rhoam Summer. Swan Amity

Rhoam’s mother, Kelik Summer, posted to a Facebook group last night, saying Thursday was “the worst day of my life. My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting.”

“We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe,” Summer wrote.

Officials did not identify the other slain children, ages 8 and 11, at the request of their families.

Rhoam’s family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting. Swan Amity

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said that when officers arrived, two boys and a teacher were dead at the scene. Officers and medics attempted lifesaving care on another boy, he said.

A 7-year-old injured in the shooting was stabilized in serious condition at a hospital, Krantz said. Another teacher, Becky Drury, 54, had “serious but non-life-threatening injuries,” police said.

Megan Lambert, 25, a central Oregon native and Boise State University graduate. Bend Police Dept.

The family of the teacher killed in the attack identified her on Friday as Megan Lambert, 25, a central Oregon native and Boise State University graduate who dedicated her life to both teaching and coaching girls in the Central Oregon Volleyball Club.

She was a substitute teacher before getting her position as a full-time teacher, the family said in a statement read during an afternoon news conference.

“She loved Silver Rail,” the family said. “This was her dream job.”

She also loved volleyball and rejected a salary during her first year as a coach so girls whose families couldn’t afford the costs of participating could play, the family said.

“She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs,” it said.

Rebecca Drury was injured in the shooting. Bend Police Dept.

In a statement, Drury’s husband thanked people for their support.

“The kindness and concern shown to our family and everyone affected mean more than we can express,” her husband wrote.

“Right now, our focus is on my wife, Becky, and her recovery, and on supporting our family through an unimaginably difficult time,” he wrote. “We respectfully ask for privacy and space as we navigate the days ahead.”

The attack began just before 1 p.m. Thursday, police said, as the shooter scaled a perimeter fence at the school, shot at and breached a set of double doors, and entered Lambert’s special needs classroom, where he opened fire.

Krantz said another teacher, who was not named, threw a cellphone at the shooter during the attack and tackled him. “She almost certainly help prevent more bloodshed,” he said. That teacher was uninjured.

The bystander who shot the attacker entered a classroom in which a teacher and the gunman were in the middle of a physical altercation, Krantz said.

The shooter had been a special needs student at the school, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said at the news conference. A possible motive remained under investigation.

Kaylub Giamanco. via Facebook

Kyle Giamanco identified the person who took down the gunman as his brother, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a father of two children who attend the elementary school.

Kaylub Giamanco is a hero, his brother told NBC News, but doesn’t feel like one. He can’t get the children out of his head and feels guilty he didn’t save more people, Kyle Giamanco said.

Kyle Giamanco also said he is friends with the family of the 7-year-old child who is in the hospital. The child, who is in a wheelchair and was shot in the face, is recovering from surgery.

World.title: Zelenskyy says Trump is ‘rewarding Putin’ as he waives new Russia sanctions passed by Congress
World.content:
President Donald Trump waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, arguing in an executive order Friday that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.”

Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.

Passed with bipartisan support, the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline.

Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.

Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that lifting sanctions was “wrong” and “only helps the Russians.”

In a Telegram post, he decried what he called an “American sanctions blackout,” adding that a “weakening of pressure on the aggressor, effectively serving as a financial reward for Putin—only encourages him to continue his attacks.”

“It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin,” he later told journalists in WhatsApp messages. “On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support.”

The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement.

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally who is not seeking re-election next month, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X.

Zelenskyy thanked both Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, and praised the late Graham for his prolonged vocal support for Ukraine.

“He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible. It’s difficult without him, I’ll say frankly,” Zelenskyy said. “And I am grateful to his friends who supported him.”

Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions.

Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers.

The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.

World.title: Pope Leo to be discharged from the hospital after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous nodule from his right lung, the Vatican said, and will make an appearance to lead prayer on Sunday.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement.

“He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican,” it added.

He was expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”

So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.

Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

A drawing of Pope Leo XIV is laid at the statue of John Paul II outside the Gemelli University Hospital, where Pope Leo XIV is recovering after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty Images

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.

His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.

“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.

Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.

Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.

This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.

Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.

The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

World.title: Federal investigation of letters with suspicious substances widens
World.content:
A federal investigation of letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to elected officials’ offices has expanded as some Republicans have been identified as targets of the mailings, a person with direct knowledge of the investigation told NBC News on Friday.

Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, Ted Cruz of Texas and Mike Rounds of South Dakota confirmed that they were among the GOP lawmakers targeted by the mailings.

Two letters were sent to Collins, including one to her Portland office and another to her office in Washington, D.C., Collins’ chief of staff, Katie Brown, said in a statement Friday. Brown said that the letters were intercepted before they arrived and that no one was injured by them.

Ricketts wrote in a post on X that his Omaha office “received a letter with a powdery substance” that matched the description of those sent to other offices.

“Our team worked closely with Omaha PD, FBI, and Capitol Police. They confirmed the substance was not harmful,” Ricketts wrote. “We are grateful for our law enforcement.”

Cruz described a similar letter sent to his Houston office, writing in a post on X, “This incident is deeply concerning. Attempts to intimidate your political opponents have no place in our country.”

In his own post, Rounds wrote that his Sioux Falls office had received a suspicious piece of mail. He said that his team alerted the Sioux Falls Police Department after seeing guidance from the U.S. Capitol Police regarding other letters they had intercepted.

“This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members. This has no place in our nation. America is better than this,” Rounds wrote.

The names of the other targeted Republicans have not been revealed, though they are members of the Senate, the source said. Rep. Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans, said that his district office in California had also received a letter.

“No one should have to worry for their safety simply because they go to work for the American people,” Kiley wrote. “This incident highlights — once again — why we need to bring down the temperature in our politics and embrace a return to civility and commonsense.”

Those lawmakers join a growing list of identified targets including at least 26 state election offices and at least 22 offices of congressional Democrats. Seven of those Democrats are senators, including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York.

On Friday, Reps. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts; Maxwell Frost and Darren Soto of Florida; Zoe Lofgren, Jimmy Panetta, Linda Sanchez, Laura Friedman and Gil Cisneros of California; Ritchie Torres of New York; Bonnie Watson Coleman, Rob Menendez and Analilia Mejia of New Jersey; Eugene Vindman of Virginia; Pramila Jayapal of Washington; Jan Schakowsky, Robin Kelly, Brad Schneider and Mike Quigley of Illinois; Rep. Hillary Scholten of Michigan; Gwen Moore of Wisconsin, Kelly Morrison of Minnesota and Sarah Elfreth of Maryland also said offices in their home states received such letters.

Democratic Sens. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Alex Padilla of California, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Chris Coons of Delaware, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota have also reported that their offices received suspicious letters.

It is not yet clear just how many offices have been targeted by the mailings, though it appears that federal officials are approaching the incidents as being connected.

Two other sources familiar with the investigation into the suspicious letters, which contain an unknown white powder substance, said law enforcement has yet to trace the exact origins of the letters or the person or persons responsible for sending them.

According to one of the sources, “dozens and dozens” of letters have been sent out nationwide matching the same description.

“Everyone is at a loss at the scope of this, and no one knows where this is coming from,” another source told NBC News. “Most of the letters have been addressed to state offices but some to D.C.”

The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are leading the investigation. Most, if not all, the letters sent to the senators were intercepted before they were delivered.

One of the sources said preliminary field testing continued through the night on the unknown substance and that so far, all the powder tested has been determined to not be hazardous.

Further testing will take place at law enforcement laboratories, the source added.

Senate and House staffers received notices Thursday with warnings about the suspicious packages as officials began to investigate the letters.

As of Friday afternoon, state election offices in Alabama, Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming have also received packages.

The mailings come less than three weeks before Election Day and after threats against election workers have increased in recent years. Incidents of suspicious substances being mailed to election workers were reported both in 2023 and just weeks before the 2024 presidential election.

World.title: On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around"
World.content:
As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.

"I'll be the first person to tell you that just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around," Vance said during a town hall in Michigan that will air Saturday evening.

Vance was responding to a question from a woman who said her small business is struggling. Polls show that most Americans are dissatisfied with the state of the economy and frustrated with inflation, and the majority of voters blame the Trump administration's policies.

President Trump is more positive, giving his administration an "A+" on the economy.

Asked about Mr. Trump's characterization of the economy by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, Vance said: "I think that what the president is saying is that we are seeing all of these massive new investments come into our country. But he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first, before you can employ the workers working in those factories."

"I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around," the vice president continued.

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.
