World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Bolsonaro and Lula head into the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign in a statistical tie
World.content:
Bolsonaro and Lula head into the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign in a statistical tie

17th Saturday, October 2026 - 06:23 UTC Full article

Both polls were conducted before the Senate approved on Wednesday a cut in the working week from 44 to 40 hours, one of the flagships of Lula’s campaign

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are heading into the final days of the campaign for the October 25 runoff in a statistical tie, according to two new polls. A Datafolha survey released on Thursday night gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, compared with 52% and 48% a week earlier, with a margin of error of two points.

A Quaest poll published on Wednesday puts Bolsonaro on 46% of voting intentions and Lula on 44%, also within the margin of error. Some 9% will vote blank or spoil their ballot and just 1% are undecided. Rejection rates are similar: 54% say they would never vote for Bolsonaro and 53% would never vote for Lula. Asked which they fear more, Lula’s re-election or the Bolsonaro family’s return to power, respondents split evenly at 43% each. Lula leads in the northeast and among recipients of the Bolsa Família programme; Bolsonaro in the south and among evangelicals.

Both polls were conducted before the Senate approved on Wednesday a cut in the working week from 44 to 40 hours, one of the flagships of Lula’s campaign, which Bolsonaro also voted for.

In an interview with TV Globo, Lula said he supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for the most serious crimes, a proposal until now championed by his rival, who wants to reduce it from 18 to 16. “My opinion, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any heinous crime I am in favour of lowering the age of majority,” he said. The president also took responsibility for his high rejection rate: “If I failed to make people understand the government I formed, I cannot blame anyone, the fault is mine.”

Bolsonaro, who won 47.03% of the first-round vote against Lula’s 45.16%, has secured the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties, and has promised to maintain the current government’s social programmes and create a Ministry of Prosperity. The two candidates will face each other on Sunday in their first debate, on the Band network.

World.title: Brent touches US$110 for the first time since May on Middle East tensions
World.content:
Brent touches US$110 for the first time since May on Middle East tensions

17th Saturday, October 2026 - 06:17 UTC Full article

Attacks around Hormuz have intensified over the past ten days, with Iran saying it is responding to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month

Brent crude reached US$110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, driven by fears that escalation in the Middle East could further tighten supplies and by doubts over how much diesel Russia can supply to the market. Brent settled 3.7% higher at US$109.86, its highest since May 19, while US benchmark WTI rose 3.5% to US$101.41.

Over the week, Brent has gained 4.9% and WTI 10.4%. Prices rebounded after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Yanbu, the Red Sea port the kingdom uses to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Initial reports indicated no damage to its facilities.

Attacks around Hormuz have intensified over the past ten days, with Iran saying it is responding to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month. “Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower,” consultancy Kpler said, forecasting a slow and uneven recovery in the absence of a political deal.

The war in Ukraine is adding to the pressure. President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire on energy sites announced on Sunday by US President Donald Trump, and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow. A day later, a drone attack forced the suspension of a distillation unit at Russia’s Ryazan refinery. “It’s questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets,” said Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial. Trump announced last week a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply some 4.8 million tonnes of diesel.

To ease the market, the International Energy Agency agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of fuel, and the US Department of Energy offered an exchange of up to 17 million barrels from its strategic reserve. According to the International Monetary Fund, higher energy prices benefit Latin America’s commodity exporters and hurt importers.

World.title: Trump drops his new press secretary after a week of controversy
World.content:
Trump drops his new press secretary after a week of controversy

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

She admitted that, although she graduated in law, she had not passed the bar exam, despite presenting herself as a lawyer for years

Katie Zacharia will leave her post as White House press secretary just five days after taking it up, according to advisers to President Donald Trump quoted by several US media outlets, following a widely criticised first briefing and the revelation that she had presented herself as a lawyer without passing the bar exam.

A White House official said Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role. Before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia, Trump told reporters he had suggested she reconsider staying on: “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. Katie, do you need this?” The president said she had been treated “very unfairly” by the media and that many people wanted the job.

Zacharia, appointed on October 9 to succeed Karoline Leavitt, held her first and only briefing on Tuesday, lasting 14 minutes, in which she was unable to answer a question about whether the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Days later she admitted that, although she graduated in law, she had not passed the bar exam, despite presenting herself as a lawyer for years.

Her tenure is shorter than the 11 days Anthony Scaramucci spent as Trump’s communications director in 2017.

World.title: Rodrigues-Birkett, UN leadership hopeful: “Not choosing a woman would send a very negative message”
World.content:
Rodrigues-Birkett, UN leadership hopeful: “Not choosing a woman would send a very negative message”

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

Guyana’s ambassador to the UN, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, one of the best-placed candidates to succeed António Guterres at the head of the organisation, has warned that not choosing a woman “would send a very negative message to the world”, in an interview with the newspaper El País published on the day the Security Council holds its first informal colour-coded straw poll, which reveals whether any of the five permanent members opposes each candidate.

“I am not running because I am a woman; I am running on the basis of my ability and my competence. But if there is one place that should set an example on equality between men and women, it is the UN,” said the former Guyanese foreign minister, 53, who is of Arawak Indigenous descent. “The women taking part in this process have stepped forward. I do not believe that, at this stage, the world has concluded that none of us has the right profile.”

Rodrigues-Birkett called for respect for the principle of rotation, under which it is now the turn of a candidate from Latin America and the Caribbean, and for any new contender to be subjected to “the same level of scrutiny” as the current ones. She also warned that reaching January 1 without a successor “would be one of the best ways to undermine the credibility of the UN”.

The candidate slipped to third place in the last informal poll, on October 7, after articles recalled her criticism of Israel over the war in Gaza. “If defending the Charter and international law is going to work against me in this race, I choose that without hesitation,” she said, adding that she was aware of “other efforts” against her that she would discuss “at the right time”.

According to leaked results of that poll, Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan received 9 encourage and 6 discourage votes; Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, 6 encourage, 7 discourage and 2 no opinion; and Rodrigues-Birkett 5 encourage, 9 discourage and 1 no opinion. To be recommended to the General Assembly, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour and no opposition from a permanent member. According to the specialist outlet PassBlue, the United Kingdom would oppose Grossi because of Argentina’s claim over the Falklands.

Seven candidates remain in the race, four of them Latin American. No woman has led the UN in its more than 80-year history.

World.title: Kast and Paz open the way in La Paz to normalising Chile-Bolivia relations
World.content:
Kast and Paz open the way in La Paz to normalising Chile-Bolivia relations

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

“President Paz, today we stop turning our backs on each other. We did not come just for a gesture, we came to begin making history,” Kast said after the bilateral meetings

Chilean President José Antonio Kast and his Bolivian counterpart Rodrigo Paz pledged on Friday in La Paz to move towards normalising diplomatic relations “at the highest level”, broken off since 1978, during a visit the Chilean government described as historic as the first official bilateral visit by a Chilean president to Bolivia in more than seven decades. The two governments signed economic integration and border security agreements, although they did not announce the restoration of embassies.

“President Paz, today we stop turning our backs on each other. We did not come just for a gesture, we came to begin making history,” Kast said after the bilateral meetings. Paz replied that the two countries have “historical differences” and that the claim to sea access is enshrined in Bolivia’s Constitution, “but Bolivia understands that this history cannot hold back its development. Problems of the past must be resolved.” Kast invited Paz on a state visit to Chile in 2027.

Ministers from both countries signed agreements on mining integration, electricity interconnection, bi-oceanic corridors, border security and the migration status of Bolivians living in Chile. They also discussed reviving the Arica-La Paz railway, provided for in the 1904 treaty between Bolivia and Chile, 24-hour operation at the Tambo Quemado-Chungará border crossing and the fight against smuggling. According to the Oruro customs post, more than 76% of Bolivia’s foreign trade passes through the Chilean ports of Arica and Iquique.

Bolivia’s claim to sovereign access to the sea, which it lost at the International Court of Justice in 2018, was not on the agenda. “We are not going to renounce our historical claim, but it is also clear that we have to address a fundamental agenda,” said Bolivia’s Minister of the Presidency, Fernando Aramayo.

The rapprochement comes at a time of alignment between the two governments, which this year joined the Shield of the Americas, the US-backed regional security alliance. The Bolivian opposition, however, criticised the visit over the destruction in Chile of part of a seized shipment of Bolivian timber over alleged traces of drugs. “The situation is tense, we cannot be hypocrites,” said deputy Elena Pachacute of the Unidad alliance.

World.title: Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector
World.content:
Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector

16th Friday, October 2026 - 13:59 UTC Full article

HMS Protector role helped to maintain a sovereign, reassuring, and versatile presence in the South Atlantic and the British Antarctic Territory

The Royal Navy's only ice patrol vessel has been towed into Devonport, reportedly with a double engine failure, raising fresh concerns over how the news will be interpreted by Argentina. HMS Protector fulfils an icebreaking role to monitor the demilitarized Antarctic and support safe navigation for scientific research in challenging conditions.

According to the UK’s Defense Investment Plan and the Royal Navy, she is due to be replaced by a more modern variant.

However, the document also highlighted the importance of the military's now-missing ice patrol capability to “maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory”.

Speaking to BFBS Forces News, retired Royal Navy Commodore Steve Prest assessed the geopolitical significance of the vessel's woes given Argentina's continued claim to the Falkland Islands.

“In those territories down in the South Atlantic, there is still some contestation over their sovereignty, and we've seen a resurgence of some of those claims from Argentina in recent weeks and months, emboldened by the political situation in America,” he said.

“Let's not forget that it was the withdrawal of one of the previous ice patrol ships that was down there, HMS Endurance that was one of the precipitating factors of the invasion of the Falklands in 1982.

”It was seen as a signal that the British weren't interested in the South Atlantic in quite the way they previously had been. So these things are important, not only in terms of the work that they do, but also the signaling that they send geo-strategically.“

Considering the international discourse, the timing of HMS Protector's defect, as described by the Royal Navy, demands new context applied to any concern over South Atlantic security.

The withdrawal of the previous icebreaker in the 1980s was seen as a retreat of the UK from some of its overseas territories and interests, Cder. Prest explained.

”I don't think we're in that situation at all now,“ he said. ”I think we're absolutely crystal clear in terms of the UK Government's policy around the sovereignty of the British South Atlantic territories, the Falkland Islands and so on.

“We have significant military assets down there, not least fast jets and air defense teams and infantry companies. So the Islands are well defended, far better defended than they were in 1982.”

He added: “I don't think we should be too alarmed. The diplomatic and Foreign Office signaling is unambiguous with regard to sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. So I don't think there's going to be the same miscalculations.

”I don't think we need to worry about that. But these ships, HMS Protector and her predecessors, had a job of work to do down there. And that job of work will need to be done.

“And we should, in my view, both for reasons of doing that job of work, but also signaling that we still take our maritime responsibilities in that part of the world seriously, replace the ship as quickly as possible.”

A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place.

”As part of the Defense Investment Plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability. She remains part of the fleet, and any decisions on her immediate future will be made in due course.”

World.title: The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact
World.content:
The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact

16th Friday, October 2026 - 10:07 UTC Full article

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue

The escalating dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands has spilled into trade: London, a member of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, has not ruled out using its position to stall Argentina’s bid to join the pact, which requires the consensus of all its members. The British government says Buenos Aires’s conduct raises “very serious questions about its reliability as a partner”.

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran replied that the UK does not comment publicly on accession discussions and does not speculate on possible sanctions, though it will continue to consider “all appropriate measures”. She added that Argentine attempts to obstruct economic activity in the archipelago “damage legal certainty”.

Argentina submitted its accession request on June 2. The pact brings together Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, Vietnam and the United Kingdom, the only country to have joined since its creation. Opening accession talks and issuing the final invitation both require the consensus of all members, so any one of them can block the process. Uruguay, which applied in December 2022, has been in formal negotiations since November 2025 in a working group chaired by Chile.

According to Argentina’s foreign ministry, the country’s exports to the bloc’s members reached US$16.329 billion in 2025, with a surplus of US$8.93 billion. Staying out would not halt that trade but would deprive exporters of the pact’s tariff preferences and common rules. The separate bids by Argentina and Uruguay have also caused friction in Mercosur, where Brazil has questioned their departure from joint negotiations with third countries.

The warning caps a week of escalation. On Tuesday, Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion, after the United Kingdom on October 11 rejected its claims and refused to adopt the measures it had demanded. The tribunal has yet to set a hearing date. The same day, London announced it would use its protection of trading interests legislation to prevent British companies and citizens from having to comply with Argentine sanctions; according to the British press, the measures would be in force before the end of the year. Navitas Petroleum, the project’s operator, welcomed the British backing and has said it is replacing two contractors that withdrew under Argentine pressure.

The Argentine government rejects the reliability argument. “Reliability is shown by honouring the international commitments one has undertaken,” Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said earlier this month, arguing that the United Kingdom is exploiting disputed resources in breach of UN resolutions calling on both countries to negotiate.

World.title: Inter-American Court hears case over the April 11, 2002 killings in Caracas
World.content:
Inter-American Court hears case over the April 11, 2002 killings in Caracas

16th Friday, October 2026 - 09:59 UTC Full article

The only people convicted over the events were Metropolitan Police officers, released this year, and police commissioner Iván Simonovis, who escaped house arrest in 2019 and lives in exile

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held this week in San José, Costa Rica, the first public hearing in the case over the killings of April 11, 2002 in Caracas, when an opposition march came under gunfire near the Miraflores Palace. Nineteen people died and dozens were wounded that day, in the run-up to the coup that removed then-president Hugo Chávez from power for two days.

The case, known as Trujillo et al. v. Venezuela, was brought before the inter-American system that same year by lawyers Alfredo Romero and Gonzalo Himiob of the NGO Foro Penal. The Inter-American Commission referred it to the Court on July 9, 2024, after concluding that the Venezuelan state had violated the rights to life, personal integrity, assembly, and judicial guarantees and protection, and had not shown that the use of lethal force was legitimate, necessary or proportionate. The Court has yet to rule.

Testifying before the court, journalist Delvalle Canelón, who witnessed the shooting from a rooftop and was a witness at the trial held in Venezuela, said she had been threatened during that process by two of the men who fired from the Llaguno bridge and who were later acquitted. “There has been no investigation in Venezuela into these events. There is total impunity that persists to this day,” Romero said. Mohamed Merhi, father of Jesús Capote, an 18-year-old shot in the head, said impunity “is the result of a system that has protected those responsible”.

The only people convicted over the events were Metropolitan Police officers, released this year, and police commissioner Iván Simonovis, who escaped house arrest in 2019 and lives in exile. Although Venezuela denounced the American Convention on Human Rights in 2013, the Court retains jurisdiction over events that occurred before that date.

The parties have until November 13 to submit their final written arguments, which may include alleged victims left out of the initial file and the request for reparations.

World.title: Shirley Manson’s Garbage to headline free Zócalo show next month
World.content:
Garbage in the Zócalo! And for free?

No, we’re not talking about a sanitation worker’s revolt or some weird twist to recycling and reusing household waste.

The American rock band Garbage will play a free concert in the Zócalo on Saturday, Nov. 14, the final show of their North America tour which kicked off back in September 2025.

Lead singer Shirley Manson, aka “The Godmother of Rock,” said the show will mark the close of 30 years of traditional, continuous bus-touring for the band, saying long-term heavy touring has become economically and personally unsustainable.

Shortly after the Mexico City mayor’s office jumped the gun (officials shared the announcement through the government’s official X account before deleting the post), Garbage confirmed the gig on Instagram.

“Well. The news got leaked so here we are — a little off balance and rushing to catch up,” the band wrote. “We were going to announce this show tomorrow, but someone has beaten us to it.”

Overcoming the spilled beans, Garbage — which has sold 17 million albums worldwide — declared they were enthusiastic about the invitation.

“We are so immensely proud and deeply honoured to have been invited by the Mexican Government to play in Mexico City on the 14th of November at Mexico City’s most prestigious venue – The Zócalo,” the band said.

Manson also heaped praise on the band’s Mexican fans for supporting the group since their first visit in 1996. Since then, Garbage has played in Mexico 16 times, including three shows last year (April 4 in Zapopan, Jalisco; April 6 in Monterrey and Nov. 14 in Mexico City).

“We are one of the most fortunate bands in the world to have enjoyed playing in Mexico since we first arrived on the scene but this is the absolute cherry on the top of what has been a passionate and 30 year long love affair,” the Instagram post said.

Formed in 1993 in Madison, Wisconsin, the band’s four-member line-up has remained unchanged: the Scottish lead singer Manson and American musicians Duke Erikson (guitar, bass, keyboards), Steve Marker (guitar, keyboards) and Butch Vig (drums, percussion).

With reports from El Financiero, Consequence, Chilango and Billboard

World.title: Mexico reduces fishing restriction area by 86% to focus on vaquitas’ known habitat
World.content:
Mexico has reduced the zone where gillnets are banned by 86%, saying the smaller area will ease restrictions on fishermen while focusing conservation efforts on protecting the nearly extinct vaquita.

The new rules, which went into effect Thursday, shrink the restricted area in the Upper Gulf of California from 11,106 square kilometers (roughly the size of Jamaica) to 1,562 square kilometers (slightly larger than Mexico City).

Last year, scientists estimated that just seven to 10 vaquitas remained in the Upper Gulf of California — the species’ only habitat across the globe. The vaquita is the world’s smallest porpoise.

President Claudia Sheinbaum praised the change as a way to protect biodiversity while supporting fishing communities whose livelihoods have been constrained by the restrictions.

The Environment and Natural Resources Ministry (Semarnat) said the boundaries follow recommendations from the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita, based on sightings and monitoring over the past two decades — such as a 2019 count showing 22 remaining vaquitas.

The population collapse from about 600 in 1997 has been driven by vaquitas becoming entangled and drowning in gillnets, large mesh nets that are often set illegally for totoaba, a fish whose swim bladder is prized in China.

Within the newly revised zone, fishermen may use only approved gear — no gillnets.

Within the larger area, a 225-square-kilometer Zero Tolerance Zone will retain its boundaries and total ban on fishing, but the new decree authorizes a transit channel for qualifying, small fishing boats. Gillnet fishing remains prohibited along that route.

The agreement also requires boat monitoring systems and identification markings for gillnets used outside the prohibition zone.

Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a marine biologist and senior adviser at the San Diego–based National Marine Mammal Foundation, said that concentrating enforcement could help save the species.

“It is difficult to enforce a ban over a very large area, which includes vast areas with no recent records of vaquitas,” he told Reuters. “If you lose a ring, you don’t search your entire house. You focus on where you lost it.”

However, another scientist, biologist Gerardo Ceballos of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), told Reuters that authorities lacked the technical and logistical capacity to enforce even the smaller zone.

The changes come after a July meeting in which UNESCO gave Mexico six months — until Feb. 1, 2027 — to report on concrete steps to protect its Gulf of California World Heritage site, including the vaquita, and address threats from proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects.

However, the new decree does not cite UNESCO as its impetus.

It explicitly links the revisions to Mexico’s commitments under CITES, an international treaty intended to ensure wildlife trade does not threaten species’ survival. The document cites a Feb. 5 decision for Mexico to pursue the revisions, before UNESCO’s July meeting.

Adult vaquitas grow to roughly 1.5 meters (5 feet) and weigh about 30 to 55 kilograms (65 to 120 pounds).

A training expedition in May recorded sightings and acoustic detections; however, the next full observation survey isn’t planned until May 2027.

With reports from Reuters, Reforma and SDP Noticias

World.title: Rotting meat stench from US-backed screwworm fly plant triggers protests in Chiapas
World.content:
Residents of a small Chiapas town took to the streets again on Thursday to demand the relocation of the sterile fly production plant used to control the New World Screwworm (NWS).

Protesters in Metapa de Domínguez have complained about the smell emanating from the plant since it began operating in June. Locals describe the foul odor as akin to rotting meat and say the plant’s proximity to homes and schools poses a health risk.

En #Metapa, #Chiapas, pobladores protestan y exigen la reubicación de la planta de moscas contra el gusano barrenador, construida por #México y #EUA. Acusan grave contaminación, daños a la salud y afectaciones a la vida cotidiana. https://t.co/F2lzS8yvcH — Cheché Torres (@Chechetc) October 15, 2026

They ended a three-day sit-in in early September after government officials agreed to address their complaints.

Residents told Reuters that the smell now regularly wafts across the town, even disrupting classes at nearby schools.

Mercedes Becerra de la Cruz, a local truck driver, said protesters want the plant relocated.

“We don’t care about the investment; we want this plant moved, because the smell is overwhelming,” Becerra told Reuters.

The protest comes less than four months after President Claudia Sheinbaum and U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins inaugurated the US $51 million facility, a key part of the bilateral effort to ​halt a screwworm outbreak that has disrupted the cross-border cattle trade since November 2024.

The Mexican government described the sterile fly plant as critical to protecting Mexico’s livestock industry, public health, the environment and the food sovereignty of both nations.

Millions of pest flies are raised inside the controlled, biosecure laboratory, where their larvae are fed a nutrient-rich mixture (e.g., eggs, milk and powdered hemoglobin) that mimics an animal’s open wound. The pupae, or adult flies, are treated with radiation to make them sterile.

Because female screwworm flies mate only once, mating with a sterile male results in no offspring, eventually crashing the wild population.

Sterile flies are the main defense against screwworm, a parasite that burrows into the flesh of warm-blooded animals and can be fatal if untreated.

As the smell has worsened, reaching ranches several kilometers away, residents said the government has not kept its September promises leaving them no choice but to protest again.

“We hope the commitment to reduce the fetid odors will be fulfilled no later than Dec. 16, otherwise we might be forced to undertake road blockades and other pressure tactics,” one resident told Diario del Sur newspaper.

With reports from Reuters, Diario del Sur and Forbes México

World.title: Mexico’s telecom sector shifts again as Televisa buys AT&T for US $2 billion
World.content:
In a major, though expected, telecom shake-up, Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings have agreed to acquire AT&T’s mobile telephony business in Mexico for US $2 billion.

The announcement was made on Oct. 13, though the deal is subject to regulatory approval. However, the parties expect to finalize the transaction during the first quarter of 2027.

When they do, a consortium will be formed in which Televisa and Fintech — the latter an investment firm owned by Mexican businessman David Martínez — will each hold a 50% stake.

The move had already been anticipated by industry members. For a year, the U.S. subsidiary had signaled its intention to sell its Mexican franchise as part of a broader strategy to concentrate its investments in the United States, where it seeks to expand its fiber-optic and 5G mobile networks.

According to Televisa, AT&T will receive the payment in cash upon the closing of the transaction, subject to adjustments and other contractual and contingent benefits. The buyers will finance the acquisition through a combination of their own funds and secured debt, with no recourse against the consortium.

For Televisa, the transaction represents an opportunity to incorporate a large-scale mobile operation into its existing portfolio of fixed-line connectivity and pay-TV services. AT&T Mexico has approximately 24.7 million subscribers and ranks as the second-largest mobile operator in the country.

The deal could turn the media giant into the first company to achieve a setup known as “quadruple play,” meaning it would offer bundled internet, television, fixed-line, and mobile services. The aim would be to strengthen its competitive position against Telcel, which is part of América Móvil, owned by business tycoon Carlos Slim.

“[Televisa’s] position is significantly strengthened by this transaction, with a view to the coming years,” head of Spectrum Intelligence Rolando Alamilla told the newspaper El País.

The telecommunications market in Mexico is now concentrated among a handful of companies. More than half of all mobile phone users are served by Telcel, followed by AT&T, Movistar and Grupo Walmart (Bait).

During her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum said she viewed the transaction as “a good thing,” and explained that the acquisition of AT&T by Televisa and Fintech Holdings will help competition and improve internet services in the country.

“What we want is for there to be competition, for investment to take place, and for the internet to be better,” added Sheinbaum.

With reports from El País and Forbes

World.title: El Jalapeño: Foreigner who opens message with ‘buenas tardes’ accidentally gains three aunts
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

SAN MIGUEL DE ALLENDE, Guanajuato — A recently arrived resident of San Miguel de Allende who attempted to adhere to local etiquette by opening a WhatsApp message to his neighbor with a proper “buenas tardes” found himself fully integrated into a local family structure, added to a multi-generational group chat and assigned three distinct aunts within two hours.

Arthur Pendleton, 38, had originally intended to send a brief text asking for the phone number of a reliable plumber to look at a slow-draining sink. Remembering advice from an online guide to Mexican social norms, Pendleton typed “Buenas tardes, Don Héctor, espero que se encuentre muy bien” before posing his question.

“I expected a phone number or a quick thumbs-up,” Pendleton said Monday, adjusting to the rapid expansion of his domestic commitments. “Instead, Don Héctor called immediately, invited me to Sunday lunch, introduced me to his sister Doña Rosa, and within 20 minutes she had brought over a container of caldo and called me mijo.”

By 3 p.m., Pendleton had been added to a WhatsApp group titled “Familia García y Amigos 2026,” which generates roughly 140 messages a day consisting primarily of animated morning greetings and detailed updates regarding regional weather patterns.

According to family members, the transition was a direct consequence of basic civil protocol.

“If someone sends a message that simply says ‘Send plumber number,’ you give them a number,” explained Doña Rosa, who confirmed she considers Pendleton family despite having only interacted with him once prior when he was standing near a gas truck. “If someone takes the time to say buenas tardes, that is family; and you cannot let family fix a sink on an empty stomach.”

Sociologists who study diplomatic integration note that while foreign residents often fear social isolation upon moving abroad, the primary hazard in Mexico is accidentally agreeing to attend a child’s first communion within 45 minutes of asking for directions.

At press time, Pendleton confirmed he had been assigned to bring extra ice to Christmas dinner, with Doña Rosa reassuring him that he only needed to show up “si se puede, no te preocupes,” an expression that legal scholars confirm leaves zero grounds for absence.

World.title: US commerce secretary’s resistance to cutting tariffs stalls trade talks with Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s trade talks with the United States have stalled as a direct result of U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s opposition to tariff cuts, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

Citing people familiar with the negotiations, the Journal said talks were at an impasse due to disagreements ​over the U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum from Mexico.

The report said Lutnick has opposed significant cuts to the 25% tariff on Mexican cars and the 50% tariff on steel, aluminum and derived manufactures (finished products made of steel and aluminum). Such levies were imposed by the Trump administration for what it called national security reasons and are administered by Lutnick’s department.

Mexico is on record as citing tariff relief as its top priority in trade negotiations with the U.S.

The Journal traces Lutnick’s intransigence to pressure from U.S. domestic industry, which has told the Trump administration that reducing tariffs would harm businesses and lead to layoffs.

Lutnick is not leading the negotiations with Mexico, but according to the Journal his presence is creating tension with the man who is — U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

It is the second time Lutnick has disrupted advanced negotiations with a North American partner, the report said, apparently referring to Canada. But he has now re-inserted himself into Trump’s trade agenda after being sidelined through most of 2026 as Greer gained more prominence.

Sources told the newspaper that the two countries appeared close to finalizing a deal that would have reduced the U.S. tariffs in exchange for a series of concessions from Mexico.

Mexico had already agreed to suspend for five years the 10% tariff it applied to imports of parts and components intended for vehicle assembly. This concession also seeks to reduce assembly costs, attract investment in new production lines and strengthen supply chains, especially as the automotive industry has been contracting.

Finalizing this bilateral deal would pave the way for further talks on renewing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which is currently under review.

Officials from both countries denied that the bilateral talks had stalled. Mexican officials and numerous business executives had expressed optimism about an imminent agreement.

On Wednesday, Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard updated federal deputies about the perceived progress in the bilateral trade talks.

During his meeting with members of the Social Economy and Cooperativism Promotion Committee and the Economy, Commerce and Competitiveness Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, Ebrard told the lawmakers that President Claudia Sheinbaum’s leadership had helped Mexico consolidate itself as the country with the best conditions for accessing the U.S. market.

Just two weeks earlier, after meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer at the National Palace, Ebrard declared that “Mexico is ever closer to reaching new trade agreements with the United States and does not expect to lose the favorable position it maintains with other Washington partners.”

Ebrard was scheduled to meet with the same two legislative committees on Friday.

With reports from The Wall Street Journal, El Universal, Reuters, El Economista, LopezDoriga.com, La Silla Rota and The Latin Times

World.title: Officials urge caution as Category 3 Hurricane Trudy approaches Pacific coast: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, said the Category 3 storm will pass about 65 kilometers off the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday. Why today’s mañanera matters

According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Trudy was about 380 kilometers southwest of Acapulco, Guerrero, at 9 a.m. Mexico City time on Friday. Trudy — a Category 3 hurricane at 9 a.m. — is forecast to approach the coast of western Mexico this weekend.

Meanwhile, the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) is working on a plan to respond to the grievances of healthcare workers, who protested across Mexico on Tuesday to demand higher pay, better work conditions, increased funding for healthcare and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

Sheinbaum indicated that IMSS would improve its pay offer, but didn’t say whether it would agree to the 10% raise workers are seeking.

Late in the press conference, she offered an upbeat assessment of Mexico’s export sector, which is a significant contributor to GDP.

Hurricane Trudy to approach Mexico’s Pacific coast this weekend

Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, reported that Hurricane Trudy was “relatively far” from Mexico’s Pacific coast on Friday morning.

However, Trudy will approach the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday as a Category 3 hurricane, he said.

“It’s going to be very close, it’s going to be 65 kilometers from the coast,” Vázquez said.

“We have to be very careful because any movement [of the hurricane] to the right or the left can change meteorological conditions a lot,” he said, warning of strong winds and large swells.

Vázquez called on residents of coastal areas of Colima and Jalisco to take care and stay alert over the weekend “because on Sunday there could be a major hurricane off the coast.”

Sheinbaum: IMSS is working on a ‘comprehensive program’ to respond to healthcare workers’ demands

A reporter asked the president whether she was confident that the government could soon reach an agreement with IMSS employees, who, in a vote on Wednesday, formally rejected an offer of a 2.9% pay rise coupled with a 3.9% increase in benefits.

Sheinbaum noted that IMSS and the National Social Security Workers Union (SNTSS) held talks on Thursday, adding that IMSS director Zoé Robledo is “evaluating” a “comprehensive program” in response to the demands of workers.

She said the IMSS proposal would include not only a bigger salary increase, “within the limits of what’s possible,” but also “the regularization of positions” — i.e. making temporary jobs permanent — and measures to address other worker demands.

In a video message on Thursday morning, Robledo said that IMSS and the SNTSS would “analyze alternatives to develop a better proposal within the framework of what’s possible.”

Sheinbaum predicts that Mexico’s tech exports will continue to grow

A reporter noted that the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean is forecasting that Mexico’s export revenue will increase 26% in 2026, the second highest projected growth among 33 countries in the region. She asked Sheinbaum what the growth in exports means for the Mexican economy, which recorded 1.2% annual growth in the first six months of 2026.

“The export of electronics has increased a lot and plants in Mexico are being expanded due to the demand from data centers in the United States,” Sheinbaum said without explicitly answering the reporter’s question.

“And [electronics exports] will probably keep growing,” she added.

Sheinbaum also said that “a part of the [Mexican] automotive industry” had “recovered” in terms of export revenue, “despite [U.S.] tariffs” on vehicles.

She highlighted that Mexico isn’t just exporting to the United States, but also to European countries and Japan, among other nations.

Mexico exported goods worth a record US $549.4 billion in the first eight months of 2026, a year-over-year increase of 29.3%.

Mexico News Daily reported last month that, despite the record performance, analysts point out two concerns: the predominance of the U.S. as Mexico’s main buyer and the country’s reliance on Asia as an indispensable supplier for the fast-growing computer industry.

World.title: MND Local San Miguel de Allende: New forum, migrant aid and local honors
World.content:
Collaboration is on the agenda for a new community organization, a local NGO recommends ways to help migrant children, a photography exhibit from Cervantino is in town, and the city and a local Red Cross team recently won major awards.

Here’s the latest on some of the many community activities happening in and around San Miguel de Allende.

San Miguel Forum aims to link philanthropy, NGOs

A new community organization focused on addressing challenging social issues by enhancing collaborative efforts held its bilingual inaugural event Oct. 6-9 at the Instituto Allende in San Miguel.

The San Miguel Forum drew 88 invited attendees evenly split between foreigners and Mexicans, said Larry Cooley, one of the group’s cofounders. Participants included international philanthropists, implementers and policy-makers interested in scaling solutions to societal challenges in six areas.

These areas — dropout prevention, hospice/palliative care, girls’ empowerment, youth employment, and water and watersheds — were joined by the overarching issue of community cohesion, which Cooley said turned out to be the most popular theme.

“It seemed important (due to) the gentrification of San Miguel, so some sense of belonging and some sense of community identity didn’t get lost in the shuffle,” he said. “It has different manifestations in different places. With people from outside, it was different than within San Miguel.”

According to a media release issued after the inaugural event, the forum’s goal “is not simply to identify problems, but to connect people and resources around solutions that can grow to match the scale of the need while remaining locally appropriate and sustainable.”

Cooley said foreigners who attended the inaugural event had an interest in scaling efforts, as well as an interest in Mexico, and that organizers wanted to focus on issues that were “really topical for Mexico now.”

Private philanthropy is being called upon to do a lot more these days, he said, and it needs to find ways to collaborate with government and the private sector to solve societal problems at scale.

“Mexico is ahead on many, many things but is behind on that part,” Cooley said. “Philanthropy’s role at scale is trying to find ways to influence what governments are doing but doing it better and include people who are not being included.”

The San Miguel Forum is planning a second gathering in San Miguel in November 2027. For more information, contact info@sanmiguelforum.org.

Ways to help migrant children, courtesy of local NGO

The San Miguel-based Latin American Relief Fund (LARF) is recommending a number of ways to assist migrant children in both Mexico and the United States. As the group’s October newsletter discusses, thousands of children have been separated from their families when parents are either detained or deported from the U.S.

LARF recommends supporting the ABBA migrant shelter in Celaya, which will celebrate its 11th anniversary next month. ABBA provides children with education, rehabilitation and therapy, while helping them acquire the documents required to enroll in school or access other services in Mexico.

LARF also recommends these U.S. organizations that help migrant children:

The Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, which supplies trained staff and volunteers to act as independent child advocates.

The Acacia Center for Justice , which provides lawyers for unaccompanied children.

Each Step Home , which funnels donations to a commissary account for families held in a Dilley, Texas, detention camp.

Centro gallery hosts photography exhibit from Cervantino

The 54th annual Cervantino Festival in Guanajuato, held Oct. 3-18, is again sharing artistic offerings with other cities in Mexico. Last year, San Miguel was a host city for live music performances and film screenings from the festival’s Cervantino Circuit schedule.

This time, a photography exhibit called “Habitando la imagen” (“Inhabiting the Image”) features the work of Yolanda Andrade Salas. Her photography reveals “the complexity of urban life, popular culture, diverse identities, and the everyday gestures that construct collective memory.”

The exhibit will be shown through Jan. 10, 2027, at Galería Meridiana 101º inside the Instituto Allende, Ancha de San Antonio 22 in Centro.

Condé Nast Traveler readers rate San Miguel 4th-best city

The 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards from Condé Nast Traveler magazine ranked San Miguel No. 4 on the list of the 10 Best Small Cities in the World. It was rated No. 5 last year.

Victoria, Canada, was No. 1 on this year’s list, followed by Puerto Vallarta; Florence, Italy; San Miguel; Lucerne, Switzerland; Dubrovnik, Croatia; Porto, Portugal; Amalfi, Italy; Venice, Italy; and San Sebastian, Spain.

San Miguel did much better in Travel + Leisure magazine’s 2026 World’s Best Awards, coming in at No. 1 for the second year in a row.

Local Red Cross team shines in national competition

Cruz Roja Mexicana, the local Mexican Red Cross organization in San Miguel, was recently named No. 7 across the country in a National Vehicular Rescue Competition. The competition tested emergency rescue team members on their rapid response, technical skill and preparedness.

Team members were challenged with a timed simulated motor vehicle accident and had to use extraction equipment, apply patient care techniques and work together to achieve the desired results. They were congratulated by municipal and community leaders for the impressive national achievement.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: Guinea Declassifies 2 Conakry Land Reserves
World.content:
GUINEA · LAND

Key Facts — What is happening A presidential decree read on Friday, 16 October 2026, declassifies the land reserves of the Simbayah Wanindara industrial zone and Kassa island in Conakry, which are to be restructured and regularised for their occupants.

— Why it matters It opens the way to put land in order for people already living and working on two Conakry sites, though leased plots, public facilities and security installations stay outside the decree.

— The numbers Simbayah Wanindara covers 315 hectares, 38 ares and 35 centiares (about 779 acres), and one report puts Kassa island at 435 hectares (about 1,076 acres), so more than 750 hectares in total.

— Who is who Mamadi Doumbouya, who took power in a 2021 coup and was inaugurated as elected president in January 2026, is named as the signatory; four ministers apply the decree.

— What to watch Ministry notices on surveys, the registration of occupants and a timetable, none of which has been announced, plus publication of the full decree text.

— What it means for you Americans with a land claim or property plans in Conakry should read the full decree before acting, since it carries no US measure and no change to travel rules.

Guinea has declassified the Simbayah Wanindara industrial zone and Kassa island in Conakry, a decree read on Friday shows. Both sites are to be restructured and regularised for the people who occupy them.

A presidential decree read on Friday, 16 October 2026, declassifies the Guinea land reserves of Simbayah Wanindara and Kassa island. Both sites lie in Conakry, the capital, and are to be restructured for their occupants.

Guineenews, a Guinean news site, reported the decree on Friday, and Mosaïque Guinée, another Guinean outlet, carried it the same night. Both outlets cite the decree, whose full text was not on an official website on Saturday.

What the Decree Says About the Guinea Land Reserves

The Simbayah Wanindara reserve is held under title deed number 23-190-2018-TF of Conakry. It measures 315 hectares, 38 ares and 35 centiares, or about 779 acres.

Guineenews says decree number 211-PRG-SGG-89 of 23 November 1989 had earlier covered the reserve. A hectare is 10,000 square metres, so the site is about 3.15 square kilometres.

The Kassa island reserve is registered under title deed number 23-267-2018-TF of Conakry, Guineenews reports. Mosaïque Guinée alone gives its area, and Guineenews gives none.

Mosaïque Guinée puts the Kassa area at 435 hectares, 49 ares and 30.85 centiares (about 1,076 acres). It says the two sites together exceed 750 hectares, about 1,855 acres.

That is roughly 2.2 times the size of New York’s Central Park, which covers 843 acres. The Kassa figure rests on one outlet, so treat the combined total with the same caution.

Article 2 says both sites will be restructured, regularised and developed under the Urban Planning Code and the Land Code. Mosaïque Guinée adds that the decree cites article 113 of the Land and State Property Code, the Code foncier et domanial.

Guineenews says only that “the President of the Republic” issued the decree. Mosaïque Guinée names him as President Mamadi Doumbouya and says he signed it on Friday.

Plots and Facilities the Decree Leaves Out

The decree excludes plots under emphyteutic leases or building leases. An emphyteutic lease is a long-term land lease, and a building lease lets a tenant construct on land owned by someone else.

Public facilities are also excluded, including schools, health centres, sports grounds, green spaces and cemeteries. So are places of worship and installations of the defence and security forces.

Easements, meaning legal rights of way across land, are excluded as well. So are the road corridors of the Leprince road, the cross streets and the secondary roads.

Who Applies the Decree and Who Signed It

Guineenews says four ministers apply the decree, each within their own remit. They are the ministers for Urban Planning and Land Development, National Defence, Territorial Administration and Security.

Mamadi Doumbouya has led Guinea since a 2021 coup, and he was inaugurated as elected president in January 2026. Only Mosaïque Guinée names him as the signatory of this decree.

Residents of Wanindara Celebrate the Decision

Mosaïque Guinée reports that residents of Simbayah Wanindara, in the Lambanyi commune, took to the streets on Friday to show their satisfaction. Reflet Guinée, another Guinean outlet, describes a festive mood and quotes residents who call the decision historic.

Elhadj Fafa M’Bira Mané, former head of Lambanyi’s special delegation, a local administrative body, called it an answer to a long wait. Mosaïque Guinée says he told Reflet Guinée that his reaction was positive and thanked the President.

These are the reactions of supporters, and the reports quote no critic of the decree. The views of people living on Kassa island have not been reported.

What It Means for US Readers

No US government measure is attached to the decree, and none of the reports mention foreign investors, mining or bauxite. Guinea is better known to US readers for bauxite and the Simandou rail tunnel at Kindia, which are separate stories.

Anyone with a land claim in these areas should read the full decree before acting, because status can change by decree. The reports do not say whether foreign owners or lessees are affected.

Travel rules for Americans are unchanged by the decree. Other recent Guinea business news includes the first refined gold export on 9 October.

What Is Not Known

The full decree text was not on the presidency, government secretariat or state broadcaster websites checked on Saturday, 17 October. The details therefore rest on Guineenews and Mosaïque Guinée.

Only Mosaïque Guinée gives the Kassa area, the article 113 reference and the name of the signatory. Only Guineenews gives the title deed numbers and the 1989 decree, and the 2026 decree number is stated by neither.

No report says how many households, businesses or buildings stand on the two sites. The cost, the timetable and the body that will run the regularisation have not been announced.

It is not stated what title or compensation occupants will receive, or how competing claims will be settled. Whether holders of excluded leases face any change is also unreported.

What Comes Next

The four named ministers must now apply the decree within their remits. No dates for surveys or the registration of occupants have been announced.

Mosaïque Guinée says carrying out the restructuring programmes will be the decisive step for the people concerned. The reports describe a framework and do not say when occupants will receive documents.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Guinea declassify on 16 October 2026?

A presidential decree declassified the land reserves of the Simbayah Wanindara industrial zone and Kassa island in Conakry. Both sites are to be restructured, regularised and developed for their occupants.

Where are Simbayah Wanindara and Kassa island?

Both reserves are registered under title deeds of Conakry, Guinea’s capital on the Atlantic coast. Simbayah Wanindara is an industrial zone, and the reports give no further location detail for either site.

What does declassification mean in this decree?

The land is no longer held as a state reserve, and Article 2 says it will be restructured, regularised and developed. One outlet says the land leaves the state’s public domain.

Which plots does the decree exclude?

It excludes plots under emphyteutic or building leases, public facilities, places of worship, defence and security installations, easements and road corridors. Schools, health centres, sports grounds, green spaces and cemeteries are named among the public facilities.

Does the decree change anything for American investors or travellers?

None of the reports mention foreign investors, mining or travel rules, and no US measure is attached. Anyone with a land claim in these areas should read the full decree text once it is published.

Sources: Guineenews, Guinée : les réserves foncières de Simbayah Wanindara et de Kassa déclassées (décret); Mosaïque Guinée, Décret : déclassement des réserves foncières de Simbaya-Wanindara et de l’île de Kassa; Mosaïque Guinée, residents of Simbaya-Wanindara welcome the decision; Reflet Guinée, Déclassement de Wanindara : les habitants expriment leur joie; Eyewitness News, Guinea’s Doumbouya to be sworn in as president on 17 January; Presidency of Guinea and General Secretariat of the Government (checked, no decree text found) (all accessed 17 October 2026).

World.title: Tanzania’s State Miner Plans 3 New Mines
World.content:
TANZANIA · MINING

Key Facts — What is happening STAMICO, Tanzania’s State Mining Corporation, said on Friday 16 October that it plans three new mines, two for gold and one for graphite, after 2025/26 revenue reached TZS 147.8 billion (about US$56.2 million).

— Why it matters Revenue is about 114 times the 2018/19 level, and the state firm now wants a bigger role in mineral exploration, extraction, processing, value addition and trading.

— The numbers Revenue was TZS 147.8 billion (about US$56.2 million) against TZS 1.3 billion (about US$0.5 million) in 2018/19, with three mines planned, three fully owned today and 18 drilling rigs bought.

— Who is who STAMICO is the state mining firm that explores, mines and trades minerals, led by managing director Dr Venance Mwasse, and South Africa’s Plantcor is its partner on the Kigosi gold licences.

— What to watch A larger coal briquette plant is due to be inaugurated towards the end of October, and a stock exchange listing is a long term goal with no date set.

— What it means for you No US company is named in the plans, but STAMICO says it is seeking investment partners for its large projects, which could interest foreign funds buying into Tanzanian gold and graphite.

STAMICO plans two gold mines and one graphite mine. Its revenue rose from TZS 1.3 billion (about US$0.5 million) to TZS 147.8 billion (about US$56.2 million).

STAMICO plans three new mines, two for gold and one for graphite. STAMICO is Tanzania’s State Mining Corporation, and its revenue reached TZS 147.8 billion (about US$56.2 million) in 2025/26.

Managing director Dr Venance Mwasse outlined the plan to media editors in Dar es Salaam on Friday 16 October. The Citizen and the Daily News both reported the briefing, which the Treasury Registrar helped organise, The Citizen says.

The Treasury Registrar is the government office that oversees state-owned companies and agencies. It has run a series of such briefings for public bodies, and a similar one for STAMICO took place in August 2023.

What STAMICO Plans Three New Mines Involves

The Daily News quotes Dr Mwasse saying the corporation has planned three major mines, two gold and one graphite. Work on the gold side is under way at Kigosi, where exploration is in its third month of completion.

Kigosi lies in Bukombe District, Geita Region, in north-western Tanzania. STAMICO signed a cooperation agreement there with South Africa’s Plantcor Mining and Plant Hire in February 2026, TanzaniaInvest reported.

The Citizen says the graphite mine would be 100 percent owned by the corporation. It adds that the gold projects are expected to draw wider investment, but neither outlet names the second gold site.

The Citizen also reports that STAMICO has acquired 20 licences for strategic minerals, including some used in industrial and technological applications. The corporation is seeking partners with the capital and technology for projects that need heavy funding.
