World.title: Man accused of torching Hotchandani family’s $485,000 vehicles still without attorney as arson case heads to High Court
World.content:
Man accused of torching Hotchandani family’s $485,000 vehicles still without attorney as arson case heads to High Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly two years after three luxury vehicles belonging to businessman Bob Hotchandani and his son were destroyed in a suspected arson attack, the man accused of setting them ablaze is still without an attorney as his case moves toward trial in the High Court.

Twenty-four-year-old Manuel Anthony Moralez appeared unrepresented before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday for a case management conference involving three counts of arson.

When questioned about legal representation, Moralez told the court that he intended to secure an attorney and would try his best to do so if granted additional time.

Justice Nanton agreed to adjourn the matter until March 15, 2027, giving Moralez approximately five months to obtain legal representation. However, she warned that if he remains unrepresented by then, the court will have to proceed with setting a trial date.

Moralez, a construction worker from Sandhill Village, was charged with three counts of arson in December 2024 following a fire that destroyed three vehicles parked outside the Hotchandani family residence on Barrack Road in Belize City.

The vehicles included a 2022 Cadillac Escalade valued at $250,000 and a 2023 Audi Q7 valued at $150,000, both belonging to 75-year-old businessman Bob Hotchandani. A Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck valued at $85,000, belonging to his son, Sunjay Hotchandani, was also destroyed.

According to earlier reporting by 7News, police said three men arrived at the property by boat shortly before 5:00 a.m. on December 22, 2024, poured a flammable substance on the vehicles and set them on fire before escaping by boat.

Surveillance cameras reportedly captured the attack, and police subsequently identified Moralez as one of the alleged perpetrators.

At his initial arraignment, prosecutors opposed bail, citing the substantial value of the destroyed vehicles, the surveillance evidence and concerns that Moralez could interfere with the investigation or face retaliation from other persons allegedly involved. He was subsequently remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

The case has since been committed to the High Court for trial, but proceedings remain stalled while Moralez attempts to secure legal representation.

Moralez’s next court appearance is scheduled for March 15, 2027.

World.title: BTB leads Belizean tour operators to FCCA Cruise Conference
World.content:
BTB leads Belizean tour operators to FCCA Cruise Conference

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Tourism Board led a delegation of Belizean tour operators to the Florida Caribbean Cruise Association’s 32nd Annual Cruise Conference, held October 12 to 16 in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The conference is one of the region’s largest cruise tourism events, bringing together more than 700 delegates, including cruise line executives, destination leaders and government representatives from across the Caribbean and the Americas.

Belizean operators met one on one with cruise line executives to showcase their tours and explore opportunities to secure direct contracts for the upcoming cruise season.

The delegation also connected with tour operators from across the region to share best practices and discuss ways to improve the cruise guest experience.

The BTB says it remains committed to supporting local tour operators and strengthening Belize’s position as a competitive, premier cruise destination. It thanked the participating operators for representing Belize with professionalism and pride.

World.title: Two years without Court-ordered psychiatric reviews: Shedrack White’s murder case remains in limbo
World.content:
Two years without Court-ordered psychiatric reviews: Shedrack White’s murder case remains in limbo

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The High Court is still grappling with the case of Shedrack White, a man accused of murder who was declared mentally unfit to stand trial more than two years ago, after it emerged that court-ordered psychiatric evaluations were never conducted as required.

White appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, represented by attorney Norman Rodriguez, as the court sought to determine his current mental fitness and whether he should remain at the Belize Central Prison or be placed elsewhere.

In February 2024, Justice Nanton ruled that White was unfit to stand trial after he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. The court ordered that he receive appropriate treatment at the Kolbe Foundation and undergo psychiatric evaluations every six months, with the results submitted to the court.

However, Justice Nanton noted on Friday that those periodic reviews had not been carried out as ordered, raising questions about why the court’s instructions were not followed.

Although a psychiatric assessment was conducted in June 2026, the judge found it insufficient because it failed to address whether White was currently fit to enter a plea or stand trial.

A further evaluation has now been ordered, with the psychiatrist given until October 20 to complete the assessment and until October 27 for the report to be filed with the court.

Justice Nanton acknowledged that several difficult questions remain, particularly if White continues to be found unfit to stand trial. These include whether he should remain at the Belize Central Prison, be transferred to another suitable facility or be released into the care of his family.

During an earlier hearing in September, White’s sister, Priscilla White, expressed willingness to accommodate him at the family home and ensure he receives his medication. However, the court must also consider his safety, access to treatment and any potential risk to the public.

White is accused of the July 29, 2020 murder of William Rubio, who was fatally stabbed during an altercation near the Pound Yard Bridge in Belize City.

During the original competency proceedings in 2024, government psychiatrist Dr. Alejandro Matus testified that White had undergone four psychiatric assessments and was diagnosed with schizophrenia. The doctor indicated that White would require lifelong treatment and was unlikely to become fit to stand trial.

Justice Nanton has ordered Crown Counsel Glenfield Dennison to file the prosecution’s written submissions by November 5, while the defense must file its submissions by November 12.

The matter has been adjourned to November 16, 2026, when the court is expected to consider the psychiatric findings and arguments from both sides before determining the way forward.

White has not been convicted of Rubio’s murder, and his fitness to stand trial remains unresolved.

World.title: Jamie Young’s murder trial pushed to 2027 as Court offers sentencing indication following failed plea talks
World.content:
Jamie Young’s murder trial pushed to 2027 as Court offers sentencing indication following failed plea talks

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder trial of Jamie Caesar Young, accused of fatally shooting his former girlfriend’s new partner during a highway pursuit in 2024, has been pushed back to 2027 after plea discussions between the defense and prosecution failed to produce an agreement.

Young appeared before High Court Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, where his attorney, Dr. Lynden Jones, informed the court that discussions with the Crown had not reached a successful conclusion and that the matter would therefore proceed to trial.

However, with the court’s calendar already fully booked for the remainder of 2026, Justice Nanton informed the parties that a new trial date would have to be scheduled for next year.

In an unusual development, Justice Nanton invited the defense to consider a Maximum Sentence Indication (MSI), a procedure through which the court would indicate the maximum sentence Young could face if he entered a guilty plea under the circumstances presented. Jones accepted the court’s offer on his client’s behalf.

The defense has been ordered to file its submissions and agreed facts of the case by 4:00 p.m. on Monday, October 19. Justice Nanton is expected to deliver the sentencing indication at 1:00 p.m. on Friday, October 23.

The judge made clear that Young is not obligated to accept the indication and that declining it would not prejudice his right to proceed to trial.

Young is charged with the March 16, 2024 murder of 30-year-old Damion Dominique Baptist, a bus driver and former Belize Defence Force soldier from Burrell Boom Village.

According to earlier reports by Breaking Belize News, Baptist was driving a red Ford Fusion along the Philip Goldson Highway with Young’s former girlfriend, Laneedrah Dawson, when Young allegedly pursued them in a grey pickup truck.

Investigators allege that Young repeatedly pulled alongside their vehicle and opened fire. Baptist was eventually struck in the head near Our Lady of the Way RC School in Ladyville, causing him to lose control of the vehicle and crash into a lamppost. He was pronounced dead after being transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Young subsequently surrendered to police and was charged with murder and aggravated assault against Dawson.

During pre-trial proceedings in May, prosecutors indicated that they intended to rely on surveillance footage, photographs and material allegedly extracted from a phone, while the defense disclosed plans to call an alibi witness.

The trial has since suffered several postponements, including an October 5 adjournment after Jones reportedly fell ill and another postponement on Thursday.

The latest development leaves open the possibility of resolving the case without a trial, depending on the sentencing indication and Young’s decision. If no agreement is reached, the murder trial will proceed in 2027.

World.title: Police recover stolen SUV following Burrell Boom home invasion; two detained
World.content:
Police recover stolen SUV following Burrell Boom home invasion; two detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have recovered a stolen Toyota SUV and detained two persons of interest following an aggravated burglary in Burrell Boom Village, Belize District, early Wednesday morning.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith said the incident occurred around 3:30 a.m. on October 14, when a resident was awakened by noises inside his home. Upon investigating, he was confronted and assaulted by an intruder before being restrained.

The victim reportedly observed three other men inside the residence. The assailants ransacked the property and escaped with an undisclosed amount of cash, jewellery, a cellphone and his Toyota SUV.

Smith said police subsequently issued an alert for the stolen vehicle, which was spotted by officers patrolling Santa Familia Village in the Cayo District. A pursuit followed, during which the occupants abandoned the SUV and fled.

The vehicle was recovered and processed for forensic evidence, including fingerprints, as investigators worked to identify those responsible.

Smith confirmed that two persons of interest have been detained, while another individual is being sought in connection with the burglary.

The stolen vehicle was previously reported to be a burgundy 2017 Toyota Rush taken from a residence in Burrell Boom.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Fernando Jones, Esau Perez shot dead at wake in Cotton Tree Village; police suspect ongoing feud
World.content:
Fernando Jones, Esau Perez shot dead at wake in Cotton Tree Village; police suspect ongoing feud

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a double murder in Cotton Tree Village, Cayo District, where 27-year-old Fernando Jones and 21-year-old Esau Perez were shot and killed early Friday morning following a wake.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, officers on patrol heard gunshots at approximately 3:57 a.m. and responded to the area, where they discovered both men with apparent gunshot wounds.

Investigators believe Jones was the intended target. Smith explained that Jones was leaving the wake when an armed man emerged and fired several shots at him. As the gunman fled, he also fired in the direction of Perez, fatally wounding him.

Smith said investigators believe the shooting is connected to an ongoing dispute between rival factions operating in the village. Two persons of interest have been detained as investigations continue.

Police are also preparing for possible retaliation. Smith confirmed that operational efforts in the village have been adjusted, particularly with another wake or gathering reportedly scheduled for Friday night.

She acknowledged that police had already stationed a patrol in Cotton Tree because of previous violent incidents but revealed that Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado identified a lapse in patrol operations on the night of the murders.

Smith said corrective action would be taken and those responsible for the lapse would be held accountable.

Cotton Tree has experienced previous incidents of gun violence, including a double murder in 2024 and another fatal shooting in August 2026. However, police have not established any connection between those incidents and Friday’s killings.

World.title: DIRTY COWARDS
World.content:
THE police have identified one of three men killed in a firefight in the Five Miles area off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine, Friday morning, during which gunmen used a child to draw cops closer before opening fire, killing one law enforcer.

He is Malique Hussey, otherwise called Mal Boss, from Spanish Town, St Catherine, with connections in Five Miles.

According to the police, Hussey was a known associate of a high-risk target identified as Kenroy Willis, who operates out of the St Andrew North Police Division and is wanted for four murders.

Up to news time the police had not determined the identities of the other two men who were fatally shot in the gun battle which also resulted in the death of Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was assigned to the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations Unit, and the injury to a constable who, up to press time, was in hospital in critical condition.

A third cop suffered minor injuries, not gunshot-related, during the incident.

A 10-year-old child was also shot in what Jamaica Observer sources say was a deliberate attack by Hussey, who was her father.

According to the police, about 5:15 Friday morning members of its Special Operations Unit went in search of Willis, Hussey, and their cronies.

On arrival, the police were met with gunfire by men who had barricaded themselves in a house with a woman and three children, including a monthsold baby.

During the stand-off the men indicated that they wanted to surrender, and used one of the children to signal their willingness to lay down their illegal firearms.

“I can confirm that a child was held out the door, and it was declared that they were willing to surrender, and when the police approached, seeking to retrieve the child, fire was opened upon those policemen,” senior communications strategist at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Dennis Brooks told journalists metres from the shooting scene.

“The gunmen shot from behind the child, which placed the police in a precarious position, even in accessing the building, because of the presence of children,” Brooks said.

He explained that they were met by heavily armed men, and a woman declared from inside the building that she and two children were inside.

The woman, the injured 10-year-old, and the baby were allowed to leave the building by the gunmen, who kept a child inside the house as they continued to fire at the cops who were supported by members of the Jamaica Defence Force.

According to Brooks, the men manipulated the presence of the children in the house and the police’s willingness to accept their surrender, pretending to wave the ‘white flag’ multiple times.

“It is the intention of the police on every operation to bring persons to justice, place them before the court, and so it is not our intention to proceed marauding into a building — whether or not there are children and women in there.

And if there is an indication, even the slightest indication, that they are willing to surrender then we are going to engage that possibility,” Brooks said.

He lamented the death of the corporal who was trying to retrieve the child, describing it as heartbreaking.

“I left several policemen and women in tears in Kingston because they knew him well… He was promoted to the rank of corporal about a month ago, which speaks to his own dedication and the recognition of his work.

“I mean, imagine at this time he is just enjoying this new development in his career, and he is [the] pride of his family in this moment, and for his life, his light to be put out in such a manner in seeking to make this country a safer place — it is heartbreaking,” Brooks said.

The pain of Shaw’s colleagues was palpable at Spanish Town Hospital as news spread that two of their colleagues had been rushed there with gunshot wounds.

It became worse when it was confirmed that he had died while the constable had been rushed into surgery.

Shortly after 10:00 am a policeman was seen leaving the hospital’s Accident and Emergency Department (A&E), with sources indicating that he was the person who had suffered the non-gunshot-related injury.

The cop appeared to be in some discomfort as he limped towards a police vehicle parked on the grounds of the hospital.

The vehicle was quickly surrounded by other cops.

Shortly after 11:00 am, people who appeared to be related to the shot cops stormed onto the facility, with cries of grief, as they sought to enter the A&E Department seeking answers.

About five minutes later a black police vehicle raced onto the compound, with cops carrying what appeared to be the bodies of the three slain criminals.

For a minute chaos unfolded as several people hurried to the van to observe what was happening.

But this curiosity was stopped in its tracks by police personnel, who chased away civilians trying to capture videos or photos.

In his immediate reaction to the attack on the men and women under his command, Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake, who visited the scene, described the gunmen as murderous.

He said while death is always a possibility for a cop, “We prepare, we equip, so that every single member after an operation goes home to his or her family safe and injury-free.

Unfortunately this morning, that hope and that preparation was shattered.” Blake told the police on the scene that the best way to honour their fallen comrade would be to remain relentless.

“Because we are who we are, because we would rather take them in to face the court, we lost a member… let not that define how we operate going forward,” said Blake.

“I know it is a tough time, and for the colleagues of the officer killed and the officer injured, I understand,” added Blake.

The attack on the police was condemned by political representatives during Friday’s sitting of the Senate, human rights group Jamaicans For Justice, and several other organisations

World.title: Market Bag: Farmers hopeful that rains will cool prices
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Farmers in Mandeville are optimistic that recent rainfall will boost agricultural production and bring much-needed relief to consumers, as produce prices remain high amid an extended period of drought.

During this week’s visit to the Mandeville Market, lettuce was among the most expensive items, selling for $1,400 per pound. Sweet peppers were priced at $600 per pound, while tomatoes and carrots were each selling for $500 per pound.

Sweet potatoes were going for $450 per pound, escallion for $400 per pound and onions and Irish potatoes for $300 per pound. Scotch bonnet peppers were being sold for $200 per bag.

Despite the high prices, farmers told Market Bag host Carlysia Ramdeen that improving weather conditions have renewed hopes for increased production and a possible reduction in prices in the coming weeks.

One farmer, who only identified himself as ‘Stone’, explained that the return of rainfall, coupled with cooler temperatures, is encouraging more farmers to resume planting.

“Now everybody is going to go out and plant because we getting back little rain, the temperature are dropping, so more farmers are going out and planting now, so prices gonna come down for a while,” Stone shared.

However, he cautioned that any relief could be short-lived, noting that excessive rainfall could also disrupt production and drive prices higher.

“That vary on how the weather keep up. If we get too much rain, production is going to go down, so that is going to surge the prices,” he added.

Fellow farmer Orando White echoed those sentiments, noting that it remains too early to determine how the recent rainfall would affect produce prices.

“Even if there is a price decrease, I believe that it will be stable enough where customers and sellers likewise and farmers can be happy at the same time,” White said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: ‘Deeply troubling’: JTA alarmed as 15 Kingston High teachers get termination letters
World.content:
LaSonja Harrison, JTA President

More than a dozen teachers at Kingston High School have been issued termination letters by the institution’s Board of Management, a move described by Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) president La Sonja Harrison as “deeply troubling” and “extremely egregious”.

Observer Online understands that 15 teachers, some of whom have been employed at the institution for more than a year, received the letters following a recent board meeting. The letters were signed by the chairman of the school board, Carlton Samuels and Acting Principal Sashauna Gordon.

Samuels told Observer Online that the separations were based on assessments and the performance of the teachers.

“We had a situation where we did have some separations based on assessments, outcomes, and performance, and it’s not fully completed yet. That’s as much as I can say right now,” he said.

However, the school’s principal, Jermaine Loutin, described the affected educators as excellent teachers who deserved permanent appointments, also pointing to the performance of one teacher whose subject area, he said, recorded a 100 per cent pass rate over the past three years.

Loutin, who is currently on vacation leave, said he had recommended that approximately 32 teachers be granted permanent appointments at the board’s last meeting in June. He said he subsequently learnt that the board had met and issued termination letters to some teachers.

“Most of these teachers, when I say most, 99 per cent of them are excellent teachers who are due their permanent appointment,” Loutin said. “I have seen some of the letters that teachers have sent to me, but I would have expressed to them that I have nothing to do with this.

“My recommendation for them was for them to be made permanent, so I cannot say why the board would have made that decision,” the principal said.

He further alleged an ongoing challenge of recommendations submitted by the principal to the board being disregarded.

“I cannot say why the board would have made that decision. But I know that the matter has been reported to the JTA, and the matter has also been reported to the Ministry of Education, and they are conducting their investigation,” Loutin shared.

Termination letters seen by Observer Online were all dated October 6, 2026 and stated that the teachers’ employment would end on October 21.

The letters, issued by the school’s Board of Management, said the decision followed a review of the teachers’ personnel file, appraisal records, attendance and punctuality, as well as assessment outcomes for classes taught between December 2025 and June 2026.

The board said the school’s administration would discuss arrangements for ending the teachers’ employment, including outstanding compensation, applicable benefits and the return of school property.

JTA president La Sonja Harrison said the association became aware of the matter last Friday after the affected teachers lodged complaints with its South-East Regional Office.

She said the association has since raised the issue at its monthly meeting with the Ministry of Education and is awaiting the outcome of a meeting between the ministry and the school’s board chairman scheduled for next Wednesday.

“To our understanding, the teachers would have been engaged for more than a year, and so, having received the letter, the situation is very concerning, egregious to our mind in some case, but as we said, we are awaiting to see what are the outcomes, deliberations, talks, what is coming out of those conversations with the board, and then the association will take it further,” she said.

“It is a very deeply troubling matter, extremely egregious if you ask me, but we are awaiting since the ministry assured us that they will be having a meeting on Wednesday concerning the same,” she continued.

The JTA president further pointed to provisions under the Code of Regulations for Teachers governing the termination of teachers’ services.

“Just as when persons complain that the teachers leave and should give at least three months’ notice. The teachers should receive notice, and the teachers have to receive notice at a particular time because the code tells you that the teacher is engaged and, over a period of a year, three terms, we would carry out the necessary supervisory matters and then engage in an appraisal and terming before the end of the third term, if it is that the school will continue with the services of the teacher or not,” Harrison said.

Minister of Education and Youth Senator Dana Morris Dixon told Observer Online that she had been informed of the matter and has since instructed Permanent Secretary Dr Kasan Troupe to investigate the development.

She said an update will be provided after receiving the investigation report.

World.title: JCF will not be intimidated, Blake declares after deadly Sligoville attack
World.content:
Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — Commissioner of Police Dr Kevin Blake has vowed that the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) will not retreat in its fight against criminal gangs following Friday morning’s deadly gun attack on police personnel in Sligoville, St Catherine, which left one officer dead and another critically injured.

In a strongly worded statement, Blake condemned the attack, declaring that the police would intensify their efforts to dismantle criminal networks responsible for violence across the island.

“Let there be no misunderstanding. The Jamaica Constabulary Force will not be intimidated. We will not retreat and we will not relent,” Blake declared.

“Those responsible and the criminal networks that enable them will be pursued, dismantled and be brought to justice. There can be no community ceded to gunmen, no safe haven for gangs, no territory beyond the reach of the law,” he added.

The deceased officer has been identified as Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was attached to the JCF’s Special Operations unit.

Another policeman, who sustained gunshot wounds to the head, is undergoing surgery, while several other police personnel and a young girl were also injured during the confrontation.

The girl is reportedly in serious but stable condition.

READ: UPDATE: Two men killed after gun battle with police in Sligoville

Reports are that about 5:15 am, a team from the JCF’s Special Operations unit was conducting an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The officers were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under heavy gunfire from two men who had barricaded themselves inside a house with other occupants.

Both gunmen were subsequently killed during the confrontation.

According to Blake, the officers were pursuing a high-risk target linked to violent crime when they came under sustained gunfire.

“This tragedy lays bare the brutal conditions our officers confront daily, pursuing the most violent elements in our society, so that Jamaicans can live without fear,” the commissioner said.

“We expect every officer we deploy to return home safely. Today, that expectation was shattered,” he added.

Blake also expressed condolences to the family of the fallen corporal and pledged the force’s support for the injured officer and his relatives.

“We mourn with the family of our fallen colleague and stand firmly with the family of our injured member,” he said.

Despite the tragedy, the police commissioner maintained that the JCF remains resolute in its efforts to confront violent criminals.

“Our resolve is undiminished, our duty unchanged. We grieve, but we will act,” Blake declared.

World.title: Court injunction blocks PNP bid to take control of Clarendon Municipal Corporation
World.content:
CLARENDON, Jamaica — An interim injunction has blocked the People’s National Party’s (PNP) bid to take control of the Clarendon Municipal Corporation, following a Supreme Court order presented during a special meeting of the council on Friday.

The court order barred the council from debating or voting on key agenda items relating to the proposed removal of Mayor Joel Williams and Deputy Mayor Clivalee Mundle.

The development comes amid political tensions at the municipal corporation following the announcement by Councillor for the May Pen North Division, Tanya-Lee Williams that she intends to leave the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) and join the PNP.

Williams reportedly attempted to cross the floor during Thursday’s sitting of the municipal corporation. However, the move was ruled inadmissible after she failed to follow the correct procedure under the council’s standing orders, resulting in the adjournment of the meeting.

In a statement on Thursday, the JLP said it had taken note of Williams’ announcement but had not received a formal resignation letter from the councillor.

The party said processes had been activated to facilitate her expulsion.

READ: JLP moves to expel councillor after announced defection to PNP

World.title: No final for JC as ISSA upholds Walker Cup ban
World.content:
Jamone Lyle (second right) and his Jamaica College teammates celebrate a goal in their Walker Cup semi-final against Mona High on Saturday, October 10, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) has upheld its ban on Jamaica College (JC), rejecting the school’s appeal after it was removed from the Walker Cup for using an ineligible player.

ISSA imposed the sanctions over the eligibility of footballer Jamone Lyle on October 13, days before the Walker Cup final set for Friday, October 16.

The decision was shared via press release Friday morning, with ISSA indicating the Executive Committee has upheld all decisions made by the disciplinary committee.

JC Board of Management Chairman Lance Hylton said the appeal had been lodged within 24 hours of the ruling, describing the penalties as “unsupportable, extreme and excessive”.

READ: JC appeals ISSA sanctions over Jamone Lyle, says procedure was unfair

The sanctions followed a ruling that JC fielded an ineligible player after Lyle was found to have a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

JC was subsequently removed from the Walker Cup, banned from next year’s competition and ordered to forfeit its Manning Cup second-round match against St Catherine, which it had won 3-2. The game result was reversed to a 3-0 victory for St Catherine.

The decision also paved the way for Kingston College (KC) to face Mona High in Friday’s Walker Cup final, after Mona lost to JC in the semi-final on penalties.

World.title: UPDATE: Two men killed after gun battle with police in Sligoville
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — The two men who barricaded themselves inside a house with other occupants and engaged policemen in a gun battle in Sligoville, St Catherine, on Friday have been killed.

The morning shoot-out left one policeman dead and several other police personnel and a young girl injured.

The deceased officer has been identified as Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was attached to the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations unit.

Another policeman, who sustained gunshot wounds to the head, is undergoing surgery. The injured girl is reported to be in serious but stable condition.

The confrontation began about 5:15 am when a team from the JCF’s Special Operations unit carried out an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The cops were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under gunfire from the two men, who had barricaded themselves inside the house with other occupants.

A strong police presence remains in the area as investigations continue.

READ: Cop killed, others injured in Sligoville gun battle

— Llewellyn Wynter

World.title: Cop killed, others injured in Sligoville gun battle
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — An ongoing gun battle in Sligoville, St Catherine, has left several cops injured and at least one lawman killed, according to reports reaching Observer Online.

The Observer understands that the incident began about 5:15 am on Friday when a team from the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations unit was conducting an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The cops were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under gunfire from two men who had barricaded themselves inside the house among other occupants.

During the exchange, a young girl who was inside the building reportedly sustained gunshot injuries. It is understood that she managed to escape from the house and was taken to hospital by a police team.

Sources described her condition as serious but stable.

Members of the JCF’s SWAT Team, Area 5 Area Fugitive Apprehension Team (AFAT), the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) and other police personnel are on the scene as the operation continues.

More information to come.

— Llewellyn Wynter

World.title: Police, protesters clash ahead of mass demonstrations in France
World.content:
Students, farmers and members of the Yellow Jacket movement, among others, are slated to take to the streets on Saturday in a “convergence of struggles” to protest raising living costs, sluggish wages and deep disagreements with the government.

The government expects “a fairly large turnout,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday.

Saturday’s demonstrations originated in the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better studying conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.

The government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.

The government has also defended the law enforcement response to the student protests despite numerous allegations of police brutality, including incidents that left one teenager with a severed hand and another blind in one eye. Nuñez said the use of “stun grenades” was authorized on Saturday, after a temporary ban on their use against students.

While far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is backing protesters, far-right leader Jordan Bardella pledged support for the police.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
World.content:
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.

Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.

The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.

“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

World.title: EU leaders clash over migration, Ukraine and budget in Brussels — but delay big decisions
World.content:
Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU.

Luc Frieden and Emmanuel Macron speak ahead of a round table during the EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels.

But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.”

“In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded.

World.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
World.content:
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.

Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.

Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.

"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.

He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
World.content:
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

World.title: Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
World.content:
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.

That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”

The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.

While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.

SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.

The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
World.content:
The stark warning comes as Kyiv heads into a brutal winter and faces a cash crunch.

BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia.

“Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.”

In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat.

Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.

The Ukrainian president traveled to Brussels to meet with European leaders and shore up financial support for his embattled country. While the EU is Ukraine’s staunchest backer, the bloc’s list of priorities is stacked with rising energy costs, looming elections, geopolitical crises and an impasse over its €2 trillion budget.

World.title: Hungarian PM Péter Magyar says Zelenskyy unlikely to visit Budapest later this month
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he did not expect Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to visit Budapest later this month, despite having extended an invitation to Kyiv.

 

More than 100 politicians have been invited to state ceremonies on 23 October to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

However, in an interview with 444.hu published on Saturday, Magyar said he thought Zelenskyy's attendance was unlikely, even though Russian President Vladimir Putin had not been invited.

It comes after Magyar and Zelenskyy said at the EU summit in Brussels on Friday that they could meet again later this year.

"Either I will travel to Kyiv and from there we will go together to Beregszász, or the president will come to Budapest and from there we will go to Beregszász," Magyar said.

In post on X following their Brussels meeting, the Hungarian PM said he had expressed his "full solidarity" with Ukraine as it continues to battle Russia’s ongoing invasion.

He added that the pair had agreed to "continue talks at ministerial level, with a special focus on improving the situation of minorities in both countries" and that they believed it was "in both countries’ interests to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations."

Zelenskyy's deputy chief of staff had told Euronews earlier this week that the Ukrainian leader had been invited to Budapest for the 23 October commemorations amid efforts to reset relations between Kyiv and Budapest after years of diplomatic disputes that have repeatedly obstructed Ukraine's path towards EU membership.

"We have received an invitation. On 23 October, an event will be held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution," Zhovkva said. "The President of Ukraine has received an invitation to attend. We shall see."

World.title: Pope Leo XIV cleared for discharge from hospital, Vatican says
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been cleared for discharge from hospital following surgery to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, the Vatican announced on Saturday.

 

"Following the doctors’ assessment this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Hospital, where he was hospitalised for surgery on his right lung," a statement from the Vatican press office said.

"He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow, he will lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment," it added.

Doctors said the decision had been made after blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed he was fit to be discharged.

The 71-year-old pontiff has been recovering in Rome's Gemelli hospital since undergoing the operation on Tuesday.

The Vatican said earlier this week that the "lower lobe of the right lung was removed" during the procedure, whilst also confirming a diagnosis of a "pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests."

"The Holy Father was in the operating room for about 3 hours, and the duration of the operation itself was around 90 minutes. The surgery was successful and there were no complications," it added.

On Thursday, doctors said a chest X-ray had shown "good recovery" of the affected lung.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 17th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Super tanker ablaze after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, IRGC says
World.content:
A super tanker has caught fire after striking a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday.

 

In a statement shared via Iranian state media, the IRGC's navy said a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a mine whilst "attempting to pass through an unauthorised route" in the Strait, causing a "massive explosion" and a "fierce fire." It is unclear exactly where the incident took place.

Iran's Fars news agency posted a video appearing to show the vessel ablaze.

The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the consequence of defying Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz is burning in the fire of trust in the terrorist US army," the IRGC navy added in its statement.

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial gas and oil transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.

Iran effectively cut off the passage, which usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade, following US and Israeli strikes on the country, prompting the US to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The US military has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the IRGC has control of the Strait, saying commercial vessels have continued to transit the region "despite unwarranted IRGC aggression."

Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), said in an update on Friday that US forces were working with regional allies and partners in the shipping industry to help protect vessels navigating the Strait.

"Let me be clear, the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran," he said. "It remains open for business."

World.title: North Korea says it tested new AI-powered torpedo system
World.content:
North Korea said on Saturday that it had tested a new AI-powered torpedo system as it continues a wave of recent weapons demonstrations.

 

The country's KCNA state news agency reported that the test involved the "super-speed, precisely guided" Zam-2.0 torpedo system, which it said uses artificial intelligence to aid with target detection and guidance.

The report said the test had verified the weapon's propulsion systems.

It comes after North Korea also tested two types of underwater-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday as part of what is believed to be a push to bolster its naval capabilities. The missiles are thought to have been fired from a submarine.

North Korea has also carried out a number of ballistic missile tests in recent weeks as it seeks to build up its arsenal amid growing tensions with neighbouring South Korea.

In August, US President Donald Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.

"You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.

Trump said at the time that he intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan.

The president also claimed earlier this month that he was preventing a war between North and South Korea "on a constant basis."

World.title: No money for Ukraine and EU budget cuts: What could a Le Pen victory mean for the EU?
World.content:
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.

 

On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.

“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.

Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”

He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.

Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.

Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.

Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.

Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.

“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”

‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’

“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.

He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.

These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.

Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.

“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”

According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.

Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.

Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget

With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.

Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.

Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.

Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.

“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.

Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.

On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.

Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.

Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.

“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.

EU budget for 2028-2034

Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."

She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.

Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.

Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.

She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.

Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.

“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.

Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.

“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.

The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.

Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.

“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

Maria Tadeo contributed to this report

World.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions package
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive a new package of sanctions and tariffs on Russia shortly before it was due to take effect, telling Congress it was in the US' national interest.

 

Trump had signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" into law in September in a push to increase pressure on the Kremlin and the Russian economy.

The legislation - named in honour of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the measures - had sought to impose sanctions on Russian government and military officials, major banks, and vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. It also provided for duties on Russian goods and goods from certain countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has called the decision to put the sanctions on hold a "significant and truly historic moment," adding that the package could have "brought economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a complete standstill."

Trump's move comes amid his increasing criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

It also follows a controversial announcement from Trump, who is gearing up for the US' midterm elections, earlier this month on a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to release large flows of diesel into global markets in an effort to bring down fuel prices.

"It was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."

Zelenskyy in Brussels

The Ukrainian leader has been in Brussels this week, where he has been meeting with European leaders to discuss the ongoing war.

Taking questions from the media on Friday, Zelenskyy was asked whether he felt he had been made a "scapegoat" for Trump's "own problems" ahead of November's midterms.

He gave a wry smile and said: "This is my answer."

Addressing the US-Russia diesel deal, Zelenskyy added that Ukraine "can’t accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next."

"I’m absolutely sure of that," he said. "After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don’t defend that through diplomacy – who will do it for us?"

World.title: Video shows Norwegian teenager arrested over UK contract killing plot
World.content:
A Norwegian teenager who travelled to the UK to carry out a gangland killing has been sentenced to 20 years in detention.

 

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, in March 2025. Newly released police footage shows Natland's arrest at the Huddersfield hotel.

Police found two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition, a court previously heard.

During his retrial, jurors heard that Natland had been recruited by Sweden's Foxtrot Network, an organised crime group described in court as being backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland had admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder. He was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court, in London, on Friday.

The intended target has not been identified publicly.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for Vladimir Putin.

Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.

His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

Overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man Image: Daria Nazarova/AFP

What did Zelenskyy say?

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.

"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.

Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.

He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​

Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks

The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.

Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.

However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.

Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.

Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

Russia's overnight attacks hit numerous civilian sites Image: REUTERS

Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.

On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.

The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."

"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.

Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."

Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Germany news: Merz faces conservative youth wing in Bonn
World.content:
10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Merz pushes reform agenda

Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Saturday acknowledged that his administration's reform plans "shake up the country, shake up our party," but insisted that they are the only choice for the CDU going forward.

Speaking of his plan for a fundamental overhaul of Germany's retirement, nursing care and health insurance systems, Merz said: "If we can't show that we've gotten our economy growing sustainably again before the next parliamentary election, that we've sustainably reformed and future-proofed our welfare system by the next parliamentary election, we won't stand a chance in the next parliamentary election."

Merz insisted that his Cabinet should sign off on the reforms by the end of the year.

Among these is a controversial reform that would raise Germany's retirement age.

Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners in the federal government are against the move, as are three CDU state premiers in eastern Germany.

World.title: Mexico sentences killers of US, Australian surfers to 158 years each in prison
World.content:
Three Mexican men were found guilty last week of murdering foreign surfers in 2024. The case had drawn global condemnation, particularly in Australia, where two of the victims were from.

A court in Mexico sentenced three men to more than 158 years each in prison on Friday for murdering two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.

The court also ordered the ​defendants to pay compensation to the victims' families, an official said.

The three defendants, Jesus Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were convicted a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.

What was the case about?

In 2024, the three victims were on a surfing trip to Mexico's Pacific coast.

Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their American friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were shot dead in Baja California state during an attempted robbery.

The three were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on April 27, 2024.

The murders of the three tourists in Mexico drew global condemnation Image: Karen Castaneda/AP Photo/picture alliance

Days later, their search, assisted by the FBI, led to their bodies dumped in a cliff-top well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Their killings sent shockwaves through Ensenada, the hotspot for surfing that attracts people from around the world.

While Mexico has long struggled with widespread insecurity, the area where the murders were committed was considered safe for tourists.

What did the families of the victims say?

"There will ​never be justice for the loss of a child, but these men will never hurt anyone else again,” said ​Page Rhoad, mother of the slain ‌American, via Zoom after the sentencing.

The Robinsons' parents traveled to Mexico from Australia for the month-long trial and left after the initial guilty verdict.

"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said.

Debra Robinson said what hurt the most was that her sons "were treated with such cruelty" in their final hours.

Callum and Jake Robinson's parents were in court to hear the guilty verdict Image: Guillermo Arias/AFP
