World.title: With a fall and a horse’s death, this day at Caulfield became racing’s worst nightmare
World.content:
Updated SportRacingCaulfield Cup With a fall and a horse’s death, this day at Caulfield became racing’s worst nightmare Andrew Wu and Danny Russell Updated October 17, 2026 — 8:26pm ,first published 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This was the racing industry’s worst nightmare. The death of a horse in full view of a sellout crowd cast a pall over a day that was meant to honour the history of one of the turf’s great races. As connections of the ghostly grey Kingswood celebrated an unlikely win in the 150th running of the Caulfield Cup, hundreds of metres away a green tarp was erected around one of the runners. A riderless Half Yours after the fall. Getty Images This year’s Australian Oaks winner Ohope Wins lay stricken on the track after a sickening two-horse fall involving last year’s champion Half Yours.



The mounting yard was sent into shock as medical staff raced to treat the fallen jockeys Mark Zahra (Half Yours) and Jye McNeil (Ohope Wins). Concerned hoops peered from the edge of the parade ring before reporting back to friends their colleagues were OK. Zahra and McNeil, both Melbourne Cup-winning jockeys, were taken to hospital for observation but have escaped serious injury. The sense of shock on Caulfield’s sunbathed lawns was shared in the committee room, where gasps echoed among the establishment, according to a guest who was there. The accident, the subject of a stewards inquiry that has been adjourned to a later date, took place just metres away from where only minutes earlier the capacity 18-horse field was loaded into the gates. Not all made it home. Ohope Wins was euthanised by the on-course veterinarian, while Half Yours was to have a thorough veterinary examination on Saturday night.



Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins during trackwork in the days before the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images Worried trainer Tony McEvoy sprinted onto the track to check up on Zahra in a dramatic finish to the Cup, and then returned to the mounting yard grim-faced, but relieved to tell stressed connections horse and jockey were ok, apart from a laceration to Half Yours. Spring is when racing is supposed to shine. To mark this year’s Caulfield Cup, the Melbourne Racing Club pumped another $1 million of prizemoney for a record $6 million purse. All the money in the game, however, cannot airbrush a horse fatality during the sport’s peak period, even if racing authorities attempt to do so by editing out vision of the fall from replays on its official channels. The Victorian Racing Club will be on tenterhooks heading into the Melbourne Cup carnival after the famous race was brought to its knees by seven horse deaths in seven years from 2013 to 2020 but has remained fatality-free since 2021.



In fairness, this was a mid-race accident, unlike the Melbourne Cup in which several unsound horses had broken down. Half Yours was the first to come down, the collateral damage from a buffeting duel on the home bend between Rachel King’s Green Spaces and Kings Valley, ridden by apprentice Jabez Johnstone on his Caulfield Cup debut. Next to tumble was master trainer Chris Waller’s star staying mare Ohope Wins, who could not clear Half Yours with only a split second warning. Owned by Yulong, Ohope Wins had been destined to become a broodmare after her racing days. View post on X Waller and Yulong later released a heartfelt statement.



“A dual Oaks winner and champion in her native New Zealand, Ohope Wins was a true star of the turf, but to the people who looked after her everyday, she was so much more,” the statement read. “She was brave. She was kind. She was full of character. But more importantly, she was loved. “Our hearts go out to all involved throughout her career, especially those who cared for her on a daily basis.” Stewards will meet in the coming days to work out who or what was responsible for the devastating high-profile fall. This masthead is not suggesting that any jockey was at fault. After the race, King did not address the bumping duel but called it a “messy-run race”.



The race encapsulated the dizzying highs and lows of racing. Just minutes before Half Yours spilled, his owners conveyed their nervous excitement to this masthead of seeing their champion defend his title. It turned to disbelief. The moment the falls occurred in the Caulfield Cup. Channel Seven Some in the ownership group were in tears in the immediate aftermath, unsure of Half Yours’ welfare. “To have the excitement and the highs we had last year and [to have] this happen today, we love the horse,” managing part-owner Jason Biasin said minutes after the race.



“You just hope he’s OK. We hope Mark’s OK.” Related Article Horse racing ‘We needed to be bold … and we were’: Schofield and Tempted take down Everest champion The drama overshadowed a career-high moment for former jumps jockey Gavin Bedggood, who has long been seen as an heir apparent to dominant trainer Ciaron Maher. His unheralded stayer Kingswood, unwanted by punters at the odds of $26, overcame a bad draw to sit three wide and win the race from another grey Saint George and UK raider Enfjaar. Race favourite Cosmic Crusader finished fourth. Bedggood was unaware of the carnage behind his horse as he marvelled at the result.



“I was gutted when I saw it [the wide barrier] and thought we had to go back,” Bedggood said. “You speak to people that you need to speak to and I had a chat to Johnny [Allen] yesterday and said, ‘You’re riding it, you’ve drawn 17’. Trainer Gavin Bedggood and jockey John Allen with the Caulfield Cup trophy. Getty Images “I’ve ridden in races, and it’s easy to sit on the sidelines and say I want you to do this, I want you to do that, but it’s not an easy task from where we drew. I pretty much left it in his hands. “We were pretty much posted three-wide all the way and everyone wanted to question the horse’s credentials at a mile-and-a-half. We couldn’t condemn him on his run here, it was on a [track rating of] heavy 9 and you had to put a line through it. It’s great to be vindicated.”



He said he was grateful to former trainer Darren Weir, who told Kingswood’s owners to consider him as a training option. “He told the owners to send the horse my way, so I’m really grateful for that,” Bedggood said. “When I got it, he told me it reminded him of Puissance De Lune, not because it’s a grey, but because it’s tough, it’s got a good constitution and it’s got a good capacity. He was bang on with everything he said.” Allen said: “Gavin, he’s a trainer going places, we’ll be hearing a lot more of him after I’m retired.” John Allen (left) rides Kingswood to win the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images



Shinn makes amends Jockey Blake Shinn made up for the disappointment of being shelved for a Caulfield Cup ride on Saturday by taking out the other group 1 on the program – the $1.5 million Caulfield Guineas on Saintly Dancer. Shinn, who missed nine months of riding after breaking his leg on Melbourne Cup day last year, copped a nasty surprise during the week when told by trainer Ciaron Maher he would not be partnering Royal Supremacy in the $6 million group 1 classic. Saintly Dancer and Blake Shinn win the group 1 Thousand Guineas at Caulfield. Getty Images Maher told the star hoop that he had double-booked the ride, instead handing the reins to visiting UK jockey Jamie Spencer. It was a head-scratching decision considering the woeful record of international riders in our classic races.



But Maher threw Shinn a handy consolation prize. He also trains Saintly Dancer. Gallery Gallery icon 26 images Caulfield Cup Caulfield Cup 2026 “[It was the] first group 1 since I’ve been back, it certainly hasn’t been an easy road, but you just keep turning up and put the work in, and you get repaid with a big winner here today,” Shinn said after going back-to-back in the race. “It’s all worth it and I just want to thank everyone who’s supported me and my circle and outside too for that matter, the racing industry has been wonderful so it’s nice to come back on a big day and show what we’re made of.” Shinn was also one to look forward, overlooking Maher’s choice of Cup riders when praising the trainer.



“It takes a really tough horse and that’s what the Maher stable is all about, they turn up on these big days, they’re fit, and she’s put the writing on the wall all prep,” he said. Related Article CBD Powerbrokers, influencers, safari suits descend on Caulfield Cup The jockey’s expected $45,000 payday for the winning ride will also cover a fine from earlier in the Caulfield program. The jockey was slugged $1000 for excessive use of the whip on beaten favourite Private Eye in race 5. Maher will also have to hand over $2000 after a treatment mishap involving his imported stayer Point Of Law at the Werribee quarantine centre on Saturday morning. Maher’s right-hand man Jack Turnbull pleaded guilty to racing stewards on behalf of the trainer for using Gastropell on the galloper – a paste to prevent gastric ulcers – which is in breach of racing rules on a race day.



Point Of Law was subsequently scratched from the Caulfield Cup, which was a moot point – as the third emergency, he wasn’t getting a start. Maher’s stable hand, Samantha Waters, who usually cares for Pride Of Jenni, was also fined over the same incident after using inappropriate language towards stewards. World.title: Cummins and his men are flying. Here’s why South Africa could do the unthinkable
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Cummins and his men are flying. Here’s why South Africa could do the unthinkable Daniel Brettig October 17, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: What’s the best and most consequential batting ever seen in a Test match against Cummins, Hazlewood and Starc? Cheteshwar Pujara and Virat Kohli in Australia are contenders, as is Ben Stokes at Lord’s in 2023. But it is arguable that no team has ever combined better against Australia’s “big three” than Dean Elgar, Hashim Amla and AB de Villiers at St George’s Park in 2018. Josh Hazlewood and skipper Pat Cummins form half of the most fearsome bowling quartet in Test cricket. AP As Hazlewood alluded to this week, that game had plenty of reverse swing. But in a partnership that still sits vividly in this writer’s memory, Elgar and Amla somehow absorbed 46 overs together, during which the ball seemingly bent around corners for extended periods. Only 88 runs were scored in that time, and eventually they succumbed to Starc and Hazlewood. But by weathering the reverse movement when the ball was still relatively new, they gave de Villiers a chance to unfurl one of his most spectacular centuries, against a projectile that was somewhat less threatening, and against bowlers not quite as sharp.



“It was important for us to absorb a little bit,” Proteas skipper Faf du Plessis said at the time. “Australia are going to have times when they put you under pressure, and we absorbed brilliantly with Dean and Hashim, making sure the bowlers stay out there and bowl third and fourth spells. It set it up for an AB masterclass, which is the perfect situation for him to come in and transfer that pressure.” Editor's pick Australian cricket Reversal of fortune: Hazlewood says old-ball swing ‘crucial’ to South Africa triumph From that point, South Africa held the upper hand in the 2018 series, and it was from a place of growing desperation that Australia’s tour collapsed into infamy. It’s worth noting that the current side, much older, wiser and better adjusted, would now see that for what it was – a sublime bit of team batsmanship, rather than cause for a touring team to panic. Even so, the 2026 Proteas are casting around for similar inspiration in the city now known as Gqeberha. Amla, Elgar and de Villiers are all long-retired, and the closest thing they have to a batting star, Aiden Markram, only rejoined the team late on Friday night due to personal reasons.



David Bedingham, who fought gamely at No.3 at Kingsmead, gave an idea of the challenge the hosts feel they are facing. “I was actually speaking to my friends about it, and in first-class cricket, you face a decent bowler and then there’s maybe another decent one, and then maybe you can cash in later with the third or fourth one,” Bedingham said candidly. South African star Aiden Markram remains a force to be reckoned with. AP “But here, you get through six balls of Cummins, and then you look and it’s Starc. And then you get through their spell and it’s Hazlewood and Lyon,” Bedingham said. “It’s tough, but we’ve faced them before, so hopefully we can just do it for longer periods of time.”



Similar things used to be said about the West Indian attacks of the 1980s and 1990s, when quality and pace lurked in every bowling change. Related Article Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball Australia’s squad looks united and jovial, aided by two rounds of golf at a pair of the numerous links courses dotted around the Eastern Cape region. The major threat to what would be a 2-0 series lead lies in the return of Kagiso Rabada, who was instrumental in cleaving Australia’s batting in 2018 and is a strong-enough performer to improve the bowlers around him. Hazlewood said of Rabada, “Every time he plays against us, he seems to create a bit of havoc.” The outstanding performance by Matt Renshaw in Durban will likely need to be followed up by a more even Australian batting display here. Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith will both be eager for scores befitting the way they struck the ball last week.



The selectors may be tempted, as they often are, to call in Scott Boland as an additional seamer in the attack. There has also been plenty of time spent this week with Cooper Connolly, who has batted extensively in centre-wicket sessions and must be pushing hard for inclusion. Either move would mean pulling out another source of utility. Nathan Lyon has bowled well here in the past, while Beau Webster’s seamers and wingspan in the field are more vital as long as Cameron Green is unavailable for all-rounder duties. There is something, too, about St George’s Park, itself, that seems to bring a little extra out of South Africa. Situated up the hill from the old town, it is a beautiful cricket ground, famed for the band that plays during matches and the quaintly named Duck Pond end. In three Tests here against Australia since readmission, they have enjoyed two handsome victories, and would have had a third if not for the innings of Mark Waugh’s life, capped off by an Ian Healy six, in 1997. A forecast of heavy rain for day one may have an effect on things, but the light will also be better than at Kingsmead. As a former player quipped warily this week, “We have been one up after Durban before!” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropePope Francis Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery Nicole Winfield and Paolo Santalucia Updated October 17, 2026 — 10:24pm ,first published October 17, 2026 — 9:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Rome: Pope Leo is expected to leave hospital on Saturday afternoon (Rome local time) following surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said, after blood tests and chest imaging found him fit to return home four days after his operation. The 71-year-old pontiff, who has not been seen in public since a procedure on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will also hold his first public engagement since surgery on Sunday. He will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square at midday. This picture, released by the Vatican on Friday shows Pope Leo XIV celebrating Mass at the hospital in Rome, where he is recovering from surgery. Vatican Media via AP Pope Leo XIV gave strong indications on Friday (Rome time) that he was recovering well from lung cancer surgery and was very much in charge of running the Catholic Church, speaking on the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.



The Vatican said that during the call with Putin, “The Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.” The statement added that Leo “reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace”. The Gemelli Hospital in Rome. Getty Images Putin voiced support for “the Vatican’s intention to help create conditions for ensuring the safety of the local population and facilitating the delivery of essential supplies”, and an agreement was reached to coordinate efforts in this regard, the statement said. Also on Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his lung cancer surgery on October 13, showing him standing up at the altar in green vestments, as doctors said that tests confirmed his “continued improvement”.



Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. “His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery, Dr Stefano Margaritora. Pope Leo XIV pictured in St Peter’s Square on October 7. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and had cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Even as questions swirled about the future of Leo’s young pontificate, there were signs on Friday that it was all systems go. The Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane with him during his November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Leo’s ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change the plans at any time. But the posting of the media list signalled that at least on an organisational level, the trip was going ahead.



Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary. World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed in Bledisloe shocker
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed in Bledisloe shocker Christy Doran October 17, 2026 — 9:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The All Blacks blew the Wallabies away during a 20-minute period to run in five quick tries in the first-half. They were bigger, faster and stronger than the Wallabies and it showed. They won the collisions, generated fast ball at the ruck and Les Kiss’ men had few answers during the 43-21 defeat. So how did the men in gold rate? 1. Aidan Ross - 4.5 Was part of a tight-five that was well-beaten by the All Blacks. 2. Josh Nasser - 5.5



Made 14 tackles and didn’t miss one. Nasser fought hard and his set-piece work was acceptable. Allan Alaalatoa of the Wallabies looks on. Getty Images 3. Allan Alaalatoa - 5 Alaalatoa made 13 tackles, but missed a few as the All Blacks’ pace got the better of the Wallabies tighthead. But he wasn’t able to influence the match like he would have wanted. 4. Jeremy Williams - 5.5



Related Article Australian rugby ‘Unacceptable’: Nightmare Bledisloe as Wallabies handed reality check Scored a try in the 29th minute but was sent to the sin bin two minutes later for getting in the passing channel of Cam Roigard. It was a tough lesson to learn. Williams later made a lineout steal in the 71st minute. The second-rower also made 13 carries for 36 metres. 5. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto - 4.5 The All Blacks’ locks Scott Barrett and Fabian Holland collectively made 48 tackles. It was work-rate aplenty. Salakaia-Loto was beaten to the punch too often and outplayed by Holland, who was brilliant on his return.



Salakaia-Loto made a couple of big carries, but it wasn’t enough. The big lock dropped the ball in the 42nd minute, and the All Blacks capitalised by scoring off the back of it. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto was a part of a forward pack that was well beaten. Getty Images 6. Rob Valetini - 5 A few tough carries, but the damaging blindside flanker wasn’t able to influence the game for long enough. He also lost the ball on the deck from a kick restart after Williams’ try and the All Blacks scored soon after. 7. Fraser McReight - 5.5



Related Article Analysis

Wallabies The Bledisloe Cup used to be a great rivalry. This year proved it no longer is The Wallabies’ openside flanker might be one of the nation’s best, but for the second straight week he had little impact. The All Blacks were all over the fetcher. McReight spilled the ball at the back of the maul in the 15th minute. It proved a coach killer, with the All Blacks only leading 5-0 at the time. Dave Rennie’s side then went down the other end and scored. The tries kept coming, too. McReight was also held up over the line in the 39th minute. It was another missed chance. Rubbing salt into the wound is that Beauden Barrett intercepted Max Jorgensen a minute later to score the side’s sixth try of the first half. While McReight topped the Wallabies’ tackle count with 16, there is a school of thought that Carlo Tizzano, who is slightly bigger and more physical, could be better suited to starting against the All Blacks. His opposite Peter Lakai, meanwhile, was named player of the match.



Harry Wilson of the Wallabies is tackled. Getty Images 8. Harry Wilson - 5 Struggled to back up his brilliant Test a week earlier. Wilson tried his backside off and carried for a team-high 14 carries. He also made 11 tackles. But the impact wasn’t there. 9. Ryan Lonergan - 5 Got on the ball a couple of occasions, including a key turnover in the 14th minute. The Wallabies countered and should have made the All Blacks pay. But along with his good work over the ball, the little No.9 missed a bunch of tackles. He also couldn’t get his running game going, nor control the Test, because of the serious pace and power the All Blacks were playing with.



10. Declan Meredith - 6 Thrown in the deep end against the All Blacks, Meredith won plenty of fans for his hearty display. The Brumbies playmaker never stopped trying. He almost scored and he denied Beauden Barrett a third try too. He also set up the Wallabies’ only try of the first half by offloading to Williams to score next to the sticks. But Meredith, 27, also kicked out on the full twice from restarts in the first half and kicked dead from a penalty in the 73rd minute. Declan Meredith almost scored for the Wallabies. Getty Images 11. Harry Potter – 4 Struggled to get into the match. The Wallabies winger found the touchline from a pass in the 37th minute.



12. Isaac Henry – 4.5 A sitting duck at times in the first half as the All Blacks’ attack burned the Wallabies. Henry made a couple of strong and direct runs, but he wasn’t seen nearly enough. 13. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii – 5 The Wallabies’ most expensive player was on show early and sparked a line break with a fine offload. He also won a kick restart in the 14th minute. But Suaalii was found out a fair bit in defence, missing five tackles. The Wallabies’ midfield missed nine tackles. Getty Images



14. Max Jorgensen - 5.5 The Wallabies’ star winger experienced a real rollercoaster of a ride. Jorgensen made seven clean line breaks but his decision-making didn’t always pay off. The rising star also coughed up two tries either side of half-time, throwing an intercept for Beauden Barrett and being outfoxed by Moorby out wide. 15.Tom Wright – 5 Just like Jorgensen, Wright had a night filled with razzle dazzle but some serious lows too. He helped the Wallabies spark a couple of line breaks inside the opening 10 minutes, and he scored in the 54th minute, but he also dropped a simple pass in the second half and threw a ball into touch. The Wallabies’ back three created plenty of opportunities but couldn’t put the All Blacks away. Getty Images



Replacements 16. Billy Pollard - 5 One or two nice efforts in the second half after replacing Nasser, but didn’t look like a world beater either. 17. Angus Bell - 6 One of the Wallabies’ best. Bell replaced Ross in the second half and immediately made a difference. The loose-head prop was direct and thundering.



18. Massimo De Lutiis - 4.5 Barely sighted after replacing Alaalatoa. 19. Josh Canham - 5 Made an immediate impact when he came on and had one surging run in the 56th minute. But Canham also gave away a few penalties, including at the lineout. The Wallabies react during their loss in Sydney. Getty Images



20. Carlo Tizzano - 6 Brought onto the bench to provide some impact and energy, Tizzano got straight into the action and won a penalty in the 49th minute. 21. Kalani Thomas - 5.5 Had limited minutes, but Thomas made the most of it during his cameo. He helped deny Samisoni Taukei’aho by holding the giant hooker up along with Jorgensen. 22. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips - N/A



Wallaby 1001, McLaughlin-Phillips got seven minutes at the end and was busy. He threw one nice pass and took the ball to the line on a couple of occasions. 23. Filipo Daugunu - 5 Another who provided some energy in the second half. Daugunu scored one try but he also gave away a penalty and dropped one ball. World.title: Jayda had a light that made people stop. Hundreds just gathered to make sure it stays burning
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Jayda had a light that made people stop. Hundreds just gathered to make sure it stays burning James Costa October 17, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story contains the name and images of an Indigenous person who has died. Hundreds of people gathered for a smoking ceremony and marched to Parliament House honouring 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner, who was allegedly murdered by her partner. At least 300 people gathered on Saturday afternoon at Cardigan Street, Carlton, in front of a growing memorial with dozens of bouquets and messages of love, for an emotional smoking ceremony, where family, friends and community members remembered Bonner and called for change. Jayda’s family at the smoking ceremony in memory of Jayda Allen in Carlton. Simon Schulter The 21-year-old, who was born in Melbourne’s inner north, was found dead in an apartment complex on Cardigan Street at about 1.45am on Saturday, October 10. A 31-year-old man turned himself into police on Wednesday and was charged with murder.



The young woman with a “heart of gold” – who dreamed of moving to Queensland to help Indigenous children – had allegedly been kept isolated in the unit on Cardigan Street for months. Earlier this week, Bonner’s aunt, Kellie Carter-Bell, said the family was not allowed to see her body to say goodbye due to the nature of the injuries. But Bonner’s mother was granted one last embrace. Related Article Crime Jayda’s body was so badly injured, her mum couldn’t look as she held her hand one last time “Enough is enough,” yelled Wurundjeri woman Kathleen Terrick, a treaty assembly member for the metro region who was performing the ceremony. After a minute of silence, some in the crowd called “justice for Jayda”. As they walked through the smoke and had ash applied to their faces, family and friends sobbed, comforting each other. They invited other mourners to share in their cultural tradition



“Let’s take a stand today against domestic violence, for this young woman who deserved so much better,” Terrick said. As gatherers marched along Lygon Street, down to the State Library and then back up to parliament they chanted “not one more” and called for men to “stop killing our women”. On parliament steps, Carter-Bell said there was something about Bonner that was “difficult to explain”. “She had a special aura, a presence, a light that you felt when she was around you, and that light should not be dimming today. Jayda Allen Bonner’s aunt, Kellie Carter-Bell, at the smoking ceremony. Simon Schluter



“Our family will spend the rest of our lives carrying the pain of knowing that someone we love so dearly is never coming home.” Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisation Djirra said in a statement, endorsed by Jayda’s family and co-signed by leading Victorian Aboriginal organisations, that it was “a horrifying disgrace”. “Jayda’s death was entirely preventable, not inevitable,” the statement said. “While her death is now a criminal investigation, it is also a widespread systems failure, especially of the management of high-risk family violence offenders, the management of offenders leaving prison and how we support Aboriginal women and their families to be heard and believed.” Related Article Editorial

Domestic violence DV killings are our failure to protect the most vulnerable The Herald's View Editorial



There have been 55 women killed as a result of gendered violence in Australia in 2026, of whom Bonner was the seventh Indigenous woman allegedly murdered, according to advocacy body Australian Femicide Watch. Carter-Bell said that she thought Bonner would have been “very embarrassed but extremely proud” by the number of people who turned out to remember her. “I just wish we could have let her know how much we loved her, and [how much] he didn’t love her. “If victims just had the chance to realise how many people care, because the perpetrator’s biggest goal is to make us feel like no one cares.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, 13YARN (13 92 76), Yarning Safe’N’Strong (1800 959 563), or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: With a fall and a horse’s death, this day at Caulfield became racing’s worst nightmare
World.content:
Updated SportRacingCaulfield Cup With a fall and a horse’s death, this day at Caulfield became racing’s worst nightmare Andrew Wu and Danny Russell Updated October 17, 2026 — 8:26pm ,first published 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This was the racing industry’s worst nightmare. The death of a horse in full view of a sellout crowd cast a pall over a day that was meant to honour the history of one of the turf’s great races. As connections of the ghostly grey Kingswood celebrated an unlikely win in the 150th running of the Caulfield Cup, hundreds of metres away a green tarp was erected around one of the runners. A riderless Half Yours after the fall. Getty Images This year’s Australian Oaks winner Ohope Wins lay stricken on the track after a sickening two-horse fall involving last year’s champion Half Yours.



The mounting yard was sent into shock as medical staff raced to treat the fallen jockeys Mark Zahra (Half Yours) and Jye McNeil (Ohope Wins). Concerned hoops peered from the edge of the parade ring before reporting back to friends their colleagues were OK. Zahra and McNeil, both Melbourne Cup-winning jockeys, were taken to hospital for observation but have escaped serious injury. The sense of shock on Caulfield’s sunbathed lawns was shared in the committee room, where gasps echoed among the establishment, according to a guest who was there. The accident, the subject of a stewards inquiry that has been adjourned to a later date, took place just metres away from where only minutes earlier the capacity 18-horse field was loaded into the gates. Not all made it home. Ohope Wins was euthanised by the on-course veterinarian, while Half Yours was to have a thorough veterinary examination on Saturday night.



Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins during trackwork in the days before the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images Worried trainer Tony McEvoy sprinted onto the track to check up on Zahra in a dramatic finish to the Cup, and then returned to the mounting yard grim-faced, but relieved to tell stressed connections horse and jockey were ok, apart from a laceration to Half Yours. Spring is when racing is supposed to shine. To mark this year’s Caulfield Cup, the Melbourne Racing Club pumped another $1 million of prizemoney for a record $6 million purse. All the money in the game, however, cannot airbrush a horse fatality during the sport’s peak period, even if racing authorities attempt to do so by editing out vision of the fall from replays on its official channels. The Victorian Racing Club will be on tenterhooks heading into the Melbourne Cup carnival after the famous race was brought to its knees by seven horse deaths in seven years from 2013 to 2020 but has remained fatality-free since 2021.



In fairness, this was a mid-race accident, unlike the Melbourne Cup in which several unsound horses had broken down. Half Yours was the first to come down, the collateral damage from a buffeting duel on the home bend between Rachel King’s Green Spaces and Kings Valley, ridden by apprentice Jabez Johnstone on his Caulfield Cup debut. Next to tumble was master trainer Chris Waller’s star staying mare Ohope Wins, who could not clear Half Yours with only a split second warning. Owned by Yulong, Ohope Wins had been destined to become a broodmare after her racing days. View post on X Waller and Yulong later released a heartfelt statement.



“A dual Oaks winner and champion in her native New Zealand, Ohope Wins was a true star of the turf, but to the people who looked after her everyday, she was so much more,” the statement read. “She was brave. She was kind. She was full of character. But more importantly, she was loved. “Our hearts go out to all involved throughout her career, especially those who cared for her on a daily basis.” Stewards will meet in the coming days to work out who or what was responsible for the devastating high-profile fall. This masthead is not suggesting that any jockey was at fault. After the race, King did not address the bumping duel but called it a “messy-run race”.



The race encapsulated the dizzying highs and lows of racing. Just minutes before Half Yours spilled, his owners conveyed their nervous excitement to this masthead of seeing their champion defend his title. It turned to disbelief. The moment the falls occurred in the Caulfield Cup. Channel Seven Some in the ownership group were in tears in the immediate aftermath, unsure of Half Yours’ welfare. “To have the excitement and the highs we had last year and [to have] this happen today, we love the horse,” managing part-owner Jason Biasin said minutes after the race.



“You just hope he’s OK. We hope Mark’s OK.” Related Article Horse racing ‘We needed to be bold … and we were’: Schofield and Tempted take down Everest champion The drama overshadowed a career-high moment for former jumps jockey Gavin Bedggood, who has long been seen as an heir apparent to dominant trainer Ciaron Maher. His unheralded stayer Kingswood, unwanted by punters at the odds of $26, overcame a bad draw to sit three wide and win the race from another grey Saint George and UK raider Enfjaar. Race favourite Cosmic Crusader finished fourth. Bedggood was unaware of the carnage behind his horse as he marvelled at the result.



“I was gutted when I saw it [the wide barrier] and thought we had to go back,” Bedggood said. “You speak to people that you need to speak to and I had a chat to Johnny [Allen] yesterday and said, ‘You’re riding it, you’ve drawn 17’. Trainer Gavin Bedggood and jockey John Allen with the Caulfield Cup trophy. Getty Images “I’ve ridden in races, and it’s easy to sit on the sidelines and say I want you to do this, I want you to do that, but it’s not an easy task from where we drew. I pretty much left it in his hands. “We were pretty much posted three-wide all the way and everyone wanted to question the horse’s credentials at a mile-and-a-half. We couldn’t condemn him on his run here, it was on a [track rating of] heavy 9 and you had to put a line through it. It’s great to be vindicated.”



He said he was grateful to former trainer Darren Weir, who told Kingswood’s owners to consider him as a training option. “He told the owners to send the horse my way, so I’m really grateful for that,” Bedggood said. “When I got it, he told me it reminded him of Puissance De Lune, not because it’s a grey, but because it’s tough, it’s got a good constitution and it’s got a good capacity. He was bang on with everything he said.” Allen said: “Gavin, he’s a trainer going places, we’ll be hearing a lot more of him after I’m retired.” John Allen (left) rides Kingswood to win the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images



Shinn makes amends Jockey Blake Shinn made up for the disappointment of being shelved for a Caulfield Cup ride on Saturday by taking out the other group 1 on the program – the $1.5 million Caulfield Guineas on Saintly Dancer. Shinn, who missed nine months of riding after breaking his leg on Melbourne Cup day last year, copped a nasty surprise during the week when told by trainer Ciaron Maher he would not be partnering Royal Supremacy in the $6 million group 1 classic. Saintly Dancer and Blake Shinn win the group 1 Thousand Guineas at Caulfield. Getty Images Maher told the star hoop that he had double-booked the ride, instead handing the reins to visiting UK jockey Jamie Spencer. It was a head-scratching decision considering the woeful record of international riders in our classic races.



But Maher threw Shinn a handy consolation prize. He also trains Saintly Dancer. Gallery Gallery icon 26 images Caulfield Cup Caulfield Cup 2026 “[It was the] first group 1 since I’ve been back, it certainly hasn’t been an easy road, but you just keep turning up and put the work in, and you get repaid with a big winner here today,” Shinn said after going back-to-back in the race. “It’s all worth it and I just want to thank everyone who’s supported me and my circle and outside too for that matter, the racing industry has been wonderful so it’s nice to come back on a big day and show what we’re made of.” Shinn was also one to look forward, overlooking Maher’s choice of Cup riders when praising the trainer.



“It takes a really tough horse and that’s what the Maher stable is all about, they turn up on these big days, they’re fit, and she’s put the writing on the wall all prep,” he said. Related Article CBD Powerbrokers, influencers, safari suits descend on Caulfield Cup The jockey’s expected $45,000 payday for the winning ride will also cover a fine from earlier in the Caulfield program. The jockey was slugged $1000 for excessive use of the whip on beaten favourite Private Eye in race 5. Maher will also have to hand over $2000 after a treatment mishap involving his imported stayer Point Of Law at the Werribee quarantine centre on Saturday morning. Maher’s right-hand man Jack Turnbull pleaded guilty to racing stewards on behalf of the trainer for using Gastropell on the galloper – a paste to prevent gastric ulcers – which is in breach of racing rules on a race day.



Point Of Law was subsequently scratched from the Caulfield Cup, which was a moot point – as the third emergency, he wasn’t getting a start. Maher’s stable hand, Samantha Waters, who usually cares for Pride Of Jenni, was also fined over the same incident after using inappropriate language towards stewards. World.content:

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. LETTERS Wonder and delight

I look forward to reading Richard Glover’s book “How To Ruin A Child” (Insight, 17/10) as my experience of parenting three girls has been one of joy and delight. My guides were Jean Liedloff’s 1975 book The Continuum Concept and Rudolf Dreikurs’ idea of logical consequences in Happy

Children.

The needs of children are simple and any so-called ‘bad’ behaviour by them is generally the result of ‘bad’ behaviour by their parents, whose greatest need is to be educated on parenthood and child development.

I disagree with the idea that child-raising is difficult, as it need not be. If we could see our kids as sources of delight and wonder, and parenting them as an education, a pleasure and a privilege, I’m sure we wouldn’t see our teens desperately seeking attention and a sense of belonging by being violent and destructive.

Kids just want to belong, be approved of, and to know that warm acceptance is always there when they need it. It’s not rocket science.

Don Jordan, Mt Waverley White House hire

There is a concept and practice in the world of work called due diligence. It involves checking an applicant’s claims of qualifications and work experience, something I’ve done many times.

However, in the case of the recently hired and fired White House secretary Katie Zacharia these background checks were ignored by Donald Trump, who seems to rate blonde hair above all other considerations.

Stephen Dinham, Metung



White House fire

Zacharia Scamooched, vamoosed.

Julie Conquest, Brighton Get rid of states

Six weeks to another state election. But do Victorians benefit from having a state, let alone the political tussle of an election?

There is a strong argument that the six states and two territories cost taxpayers unnecessary expenditure. Each with its own set of rules and regulations. Each slightly different, and enough to make transferring from one to the other challenging especially for professionals such as doctors and lawyers, but also for tradies.

Each police force, fire brigade, ambulance service, schools, hospitals, clinics, universities, etc, has its own set of guidelines, uniforms, procedures that make it difficult for them to interact with one another to our frustration and expense.

There are many more examples that add cost and complexity to our lives. Surely, it’s time to scrap the states and increase the remit of councils with local knowledge and expertise.

Especially as most states are reliant on federal funding. Let the federal ministers do all the work and interact directly with much larger councils that would represent their communities.

Mike Reece, Doncaster Knowing nothing

It seems the Exclusive Brethren are actually run by Sergeant Schultz of American sitcom Hogan’s Heroes, famed for his line, “I know nothing, I see nothing, I hear nothing” abbreviated in later series to, “I know nothing, nothing”. (“Brethren leader says he knew nothing”, 17/10).

Helen Moss, Croydon Safety at stake

The Country Fire Authority launched its 2026 bushfire readiness campaign with the striking slogan “Get Fire Ready” on October 1, two weeks earlier than last year. That’s noted with concern in your masthead’s timely editorial (“State failing to protect us from fire disasters,” 17/10).

Highlighted in that column is the poor condition of the state’s ageing fire truck fleet, so dire that $1.5 billion is needed for “critical fire truck replacement and upgrade needs”. Problematically, the state’s debt “now sits at about 25 per cent of the state’s economy”.

The prospect of a change of government offers no ground for optimism, with the opposition saying “it will not find the $1 billion called for in the audit”.

If this were a federal issue, it would be easy to conjure up the money by implementing a gas export tax or by cancelling AUKUS, but there’s no such low-hanging fruit for the state to pluck.

Oh, wait on, what about the Grand Prix circus and the Big Build rorts? Labor would embellish prospects with some serious revenue recovery.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Gas cop out

Megan Herbert has picked up right where Cathy Wilcox left off. Her latest cartoon (17/10) is biting. The Albanese government is indeed pretending to sympathise with everyday Australians who are doing it tough while allowing gas giants to walk off with a wad of cash.

A 25 per cent tax on gas exports would raise about $350 million a week. That’s enough to offer real power bill relief in a cost-of-living crisis. Instead, Labor keeps letting multinational gas corporations, who are adding to our climate woes, line their shareholders’ pockets. Who is the government really working for?

Amy Hiller, Kew



Good buy

After seeing new petrol and diesel cars languishing in overgrown fields in rural Germany in 2023, I was determined to get rid of mine and replace it with an EV made in Japan.

It was second hand but in perfect condition. It’s still going strong and its battery is working at 97 per cent efficiency. Not bad after eight years. It’s proved to be a great town car, and costs virtually nothing to run.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North Into lion’s den

Anthony Albanese will face a challenge at the G20 in Florida next month, for Donald Trump, as an ally, is like sharing a cave with a lion. A lion is not a big pussy cat. Unless you continually feed it, you may be its next meal.

Even then, at a whim, it could break any unspoken truce.

Albanese has to be wary with Trump, mid-terms or not, Putin or not. The Canadian prime minister is in a position of power and can challenge Trump, as he has shown.

Albanese is not. Neither does he have the demeanour to do it. Saying no to Trump and sticking to it as Carney has done, is what we should do.

Trump is an out and out bully. His sidling up to Putin, Netanyahu and Kim Jong Un should be enough for us to say, ″⁣You are no longer an ally of ours″⁣.

Trump has few principles and we should not give ours up to appease him. He will get his comeuppance at the mid-term and next presidential elections. We have to wait it out.

Better still, we need to leave the cave as it is not a safe place to be.

Greg Tuck, Warragul Sour grapes

On Saturday, we bought some red eating grapes from our local Coles supermarket.

Imagine our surprise when we got home and were putting the grapes into a bowl when we saw that they weren’t Australian grown but were imported.

What’s happened with us when we import grapes from overseas when we grow more than enough grapes here?

The lucky country? More like the dumb country.

Stan Thomson, Sandringham Blame game

The Good Weekend story (17/10) is headlined “Don’t blame the Boomers. It’s a generation both envied and maligned but there’s another side to their story”. When I was a teenager, Sammy Davis Jr released a song called “Don’t blame it on the children” in 1967.

Is the state of the climate and property prices our fault? I think so.

David Fry, Windsor Gun violence

When will US change the gun laws? It is shocking that there are so many shootings. Its gun homicide rate is 26 times higher than other developed countries.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Cummins and his men are flying. Here’s why South Africa could do the unthinkable
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Cummins and his men are flying. Here’s why South Africa could do the unthinkable Daniel Brettig October 17, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: What’s the best and most consequential batting ever seen in a Test match against Cummins, Hazlewood and Starc? Cheteshwar Pujara and Virat Kohli in Australia are contenders, as is Ben Stokes at Lord’s in 2023. But it is arguable that no team has ever combined better against Australia’s “big three” than Dean Elgar, Hashim Amla and AB de Villiers at St George’s Park in 2018. Josh Hazlewood and skipper Pat Cummins form half of the most fearsome bowling quartet in Test cricket. AP As Hazlewood alluded to this week, that game had plenty of reverse swing. But in a partnership that still sits vividly in this writer’s memory, Elgar and Amla somehow absorbed 46 overs together, during which the ball seemingly bent around corners for extended periods. Only 88 runs were scored in that time, and eventually they succumbed to Starc and Hazlewood. But by weathering the reverse movement when the ball was still relatively new, they gave de Villiers a chance to unfurl one of his most spectacular centuries, against a projectile that was somewhat less threatening, and against bowlers not quite as sharp.



“It was important for us to absorb a little bit,” Proteas skipper Faf du Plessis said at the time. “Australia are going to have times when they put you under pressure, and we absorbed brilliantly with Dean and Hashim, making sure the bowlers stay out there and bowl third and fourth spells. It set it up for an AB masterclass, which is the perfect situation for him to come in and transfer that pressure.” Editor's pick Australian cricket Reversal of fortune: Hazlewood says old-ball swing ‘crucial’ to South Africa triumph From that point, South Africa held the upper hand in the 2018 series, and it was from a place of growing desperation that Australia’s tour collapsed into infamy. It’s worth noting that the current side, much older, wiser and better adjusted, would now see that for what it was – a sublime bit of team batsmanship, rather than cause for a touring team to panic. Even so, the 2026 Proteas are casting around for similar inspiration in the city now known as Gqeberha. Amla, Elgar and de Villiers are all long-retired, and the closest thing they have to a batting star, Aiden Markram, only rejoined the team late on Friday night due to personal reasons.



David Bedingham, who fought gamely at No.3 at Kingsmead, gave an idea of the challenge the hosts feel they are facing. “I was actually speaking to my friends about it, and in first-class cricket, you face a decent bowler and then there’s maybe another decent one, and then maybe you can cash in later with the third or fourth one,” Bedingham said candidly. South African star Aiden Markram remains a force to be reckoned with. AP “But here, you get through six balls of Cummins, and then you look and it’s Starc. And then you get through their spell and it’s Hazlewood and Lyon,” Bedingham said. “It’s tough, but we’ve faced them before, so hopefully we can just do it for longer periods of time.”



Similar things used to be said about the West Indian attacks of the 1980s and 1990s, when quality and pace lurked in every bowling change. Related Article Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball Australia’s squad looks united and jovial, aided by two rounds of golf at a pair of the numerous links courses dotted around the Eastern Cape region. The major threat to what would be a 2-0 series lead lies in the return of Kagiso Rabada, who was instrumental in cleaving Australia’s batting in 2018 and is a strong-enough performer to improve the bowlers around him. Hazlewood said of Rabada, “Every time he plays against us, he seems to create a bit of havoc.” The outstanding performance by Matt Renshaw in Durban will likely need to be followed up by a more even Australian batting display here. Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith will both be eager for scores befitting the way they struck the ball last week.



The selectors may be tempted, as they often are, to call in Scott Boland as an additional seamer in the attack. There has also been plenty of time spent this week with Cooper Connolly, who has batted extensively in centre-wicket sessions and must be pushing hard for inclusion. Either move would mean pulling out another source of utility. Nathan Lyon has bowled well here in the past, while Beau Webster’s seamers and wingspan in the field are more vital as long as Cameron Green is unavailable for all-rounder duties. There is something, too, about St George’s Park, itself, that seems to bring a little extra out of South Africa. Situated up the hill from the old town, it is a beautiful cricket ground, famed for the band that plays during matches and the quaintly named Duck Pond end. In three Tests here against Australia since readmission, they have enjoyed two handsome victories, and would have had a third if not for the innings of Mark Waugh’s life, capped off by an Ian Healy six, in 1997. A forecast of heavy rain for day one may have an effect on things, but the light will also be better than at Kingsmead. As a former player quipped warily this week, “We have been one up after Durban before!” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Olivia Dean concert stopped due to sound issues
World.content:
Olivia Dean was forced to stop her sold-out concert at Western Springs Bowl on Saturday night due to sound issues.



Dean was playing to more than 40,000 people at the revamped venue as part of her Art of Loving Live tour.



RNZ executive editor Jeremy Rees, who was at the concert, said Dean played three songs to a jubilant crowd, before leaving the stage, saying the sound needed to be "reset".



"We're looking at an empty stage at the moment and it's a real disappointment for people who had been looking forward to the Olivia Dean concert for a long, long time,” Rees said.



At 9.30pm, a stage manager announced the sound at the stadium was being reset.



Rees said the first few songs sounded very good, although Dean's voice cut out in places.



"The crowd were right into it and singing along and happy, and then just as I say, she said she had to stop. She improvised for a moment, talking about love and her latest album, while people were trying to fix the sound."



The concert restarted just after 10pm, with Dean apologising to the crowd and saying the show would not be cut short, before launching into a song.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup: Josh Moorby's try double highlights All Blacks' game of two halves
World.content:
Picking just one of the seven All Blacks tries that best summed up their 43-21 victory over Australia in a masterclass in cohesive attack and decision making in Sydney on Saturday was difficult - but Josh Moorby's second five-pointer might be it.

After a bruising run by second-five Timoci Tavatavanawai - a late replacement following the withdrawal, before kickoff, of Jordie Barrett - the ball found left wing Moorby, who showed it to Wallabies right wing Max Jorgensen and halfback Ryan Lonergan, and went over untouched.

Ultimately, that converted score was the All Blacks' final points of an extraordinary afternoon in front of 73,000 at Accor Stadium, as the Wallabies, swept again in the Bledisloe Cup for the sixth successive year, finally found something.

The home side had the better of the second half - helped by the fact the All Blacks played the final 12 minutes shorthanded - and five minutes with just 13 players - due to debutant Chay Fihaki's yellow card for a high tackle and, before that, replacement hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho's injury, which left them with no more players on the bench.

The visitors were scoring at almost a point a minute, when Damian McKenzie's conversion for Moorby's second try went over and - led by skipper Codie Taylor, loose forward Peter Lakai and a rejuvenated Beauden Barrett, who also scored a double - Dave Rennie's men looked as good as they have all year.

They committed to backing up last weekend's victory at Eden Park and, perhaps inspired by the bright afternoon sunshine, played with a continuity and skill that blew the Wallabies away in the first half.

They did it despite Jordie Barrett's calf problem, which ruled him out hours before kickoff, and fellow midfielder Quinn Tupaea's head injury within two minutes of the start.

Despite a very much reshuffled line-up, the intensity with which the All Blacks went about their work was almost as impressive as their short-passing game, which showed an incredible appreciation for time and space against a Wallabies team determined to right the wrongs of last weekend.

Beauden Barrett also had a try double against Australia. www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks had four tries in the space of 14 minutes, Moorby, Beauden Barrett, Lakai and Rieko Ioane - on for Tupaea - all finishing scores that highlighted their killer instinct.

Lock Jeremy Williams' reply for the Wallabies was only a blip, as the All Blacks made the most of Williams' yellow card for offside after the re-start for Wallace Sititi to over from a scrum and Barrett putting an exclamation on the half with an intercept try from 70m out.

"I thought we were awesome in that first 40 - just backing ourselves and playing what was in front of us - but the second 40 was a bit different," Taylor said afterwards.

Counterpart Harry Wilson said: "I'm gutted. When you give a team like the All Blacks a headstart, it's tough... we're going to have to improve a lot."

Australia fought back with two tries to one in the second half, but this was a devastating loss for them in their final home game of the year. Their next home test is in Perth on Anzac Day, 2027.

Unfortunately for them, their opponents are the All Blacks.

Wing Will Jordan's absence in the second half may spark concerns about a potential injury and Shannon Frizell's leg issue after he come into the test off the bench may also be a problem.

As Taylor hinted, the second-half performance may come under some scrutiny by Rennie and company, but maintain such intensity is difficult, when the game is all but over at halftime, and after last weekend's second-half performance at Eden Park, it was a reminder that if this team get it right, they can be devastating.

All Blacks 43 (Beauden Barrett 2, Josh Moorby 2, Peter Lakai, Rieko Ioane & Wallace Sititi tries; Damian McKenzie 4 conversions) Australia 21 (Jeremy Williams, Tom Wright & Filipo Daugunu tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 conversions, Declan Meredith conversion)

World.title: Shorthanded All Blacks too strong for Wallabies in Bledisloe Cup sweep
World.content:
The All Blacks ended the game with just 14 fit players, as they beat the Wallabies 43-21 in the second Bledisloe Cup test in Sydney.

The visitors scored seven tries to the hosts' three to claim back-to-back wins over Australia.

Midfielder Quinn Tupaea left the field for an HIA, after hitting his head on the ground early in the match and didn't return, with Rieko Ioane coming on to take his place.

Both sides started well, but the All Blacks struck first through wing Josh Moorby, who scored out wide, after a period of attack in the Wallabies 22. First-five Damian McKenzie was unsuccessful with the conversion.

The visitors were soon in again, with fullback Beauden Barrett stepping over for a try, after a nice break from flanker Peter Lakai.

McKenzie was unable to add the extras, with the All Blacks leading 10-0 nearing the 20 minute mark.

Peter Lakai of New Zealand goes over to score. www.photosport.nz

Lakai was rewarded for some good support play, taking a short ball from halfback Cam Roigard to barge over for the All Blacks' third try. McKenzie nailed the sideline conversion to make it 17-0 to New Zealand.

The All Blacks' next try was superb, with some slick handling and good running lines putting Ioane in the clear, before the replacement back beat the last defender to help the visitors extend their lead to 22-0.

Australia had barely had the ball, but they looked good when they had it, and lock Jeremy Williams scored their first try, after some nice attacking play inside the All Blacks 22. The conversion was successful to make it a 15-point game at 22-7 to the All Blacks.

Williams was then yellow-carded, after being penalised with the All Blacks hot on attack, leaving the Wallabies a man down for the last 10 minutes of the first half.

The All Blacks made the most of the numerical advantage and scored on the next play, with No.8 Wallace Sititi storming over from the back of the scrum. McKenzie added the extras to push their lead out to 29-7.

The Wallabies then went on the attack and were making inroads into the All Blacks defence, when Barrett intercepted an Australian pass and sprinted 70 metres to put a dagger in the home side's hearts just before halftime. McKenzie kicked the extras for a 36-7 lead at the break.

Beauden Barrett of New Zealand dives over to score. www.photosport.nz

A big break from midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai led to another try for Moorby, who sold a dummy to two Australian defenders, before trotting over the line. McKenzie's conversion was good to put the All Blacks ahead 43-7.

Replacement back Chay Fihaki came off the bench for his All Blacks debut and made a nice break, before not quite connecting with an attempted grubber kick.

The All Blacks had made 14 linebreaks by the 53rd minute and continued to stretch the Wallabies defence, although the hosts were also hard to handle with ball in hand and they scored next through fullback Tom Wright, who had been impressive all game.

The conversion was successful to cut the All Blacks lead to 43-14 with about 25 minutes remaining.

The Wallabies cut that lead to 43-21, with Filipo Daugunu scoring a try for the hosts, and the All Blacks then went down to 14 men for the final 11 minutes of the match, due to too many injuries.

They then had Fihaki yellow-carded for a high tackle, but managed to hold on for a 43-21 victory for 13 straight wins over Australia.

The All Blacks had already retained the Bledisloe Cup, after winning last week's first test at Eden Park 50-19.
